When I had prayed and made my vows to the great company of the dead, I took the two sheep and cut their throats over the pit, and the dark blood ran down.

"Then up out of Erebus they came swarming, the spirits of the dead and gone — brides and unmarried boys and old men worn down by their long labor; tender girls with grief still fresh in their hearts; and many men cut down in battle, run through by bronze spears, their armor still dark with blood. From every side they crowded the pit with an eerie crying, and a pale terror took hold of me. But I called to my men and told them to flay the sheep that lay there killed by the pitiless bronze, and burn them, and pray to the gods — to mighty Hades and to dread Persephone. And I myself sat with my drawn sword and would not let the powerless ghosts come near the blood until I had questioned Tiresias.

"The first to come was the spirit of my comrade Elpenor. We had not yet buried him under the wide earth; we had left his body behind us in Circe's hall, unwept and unburied, because other work pressed hard on us. I wept when I saw him, and pity took hold of me, and I spoke to him, my words flying: 'Elpenor, how did you come down here into the gloom and the dark? You came faster on foot than I did in my black ship.'

"And he answered me with a groan: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — a god's cruel doom undid me, and too much wine. I had bedded down on Circe's roof, and never thought to climb down again by the long ladder. I fell headlong; my neck snapped at the spine, and my soul went down to the house of Hades. Now I beg you, by those you left behind, by your wife, by the father who raised you when you were small, and by Telemachus, the only son you left in your halls — for I know that when you leave this place you will put in again at the island of Aeaea with your trim ship — there, my lord, remember me. Do not sail off and leave me unwept and unburied, or I may become a cause of the gods' anger against you. Burn me with all the armor that is mine, and heap me a mound on the shore of the grey sea, so men in the days to come will know my sorry story. Do this for me — and fix upon my grave the oar I pulled at while I lived, when I rowed among my friends.'

"And I answered him: 'All this, poor friend, I will do. I will not fail you.' So we two sat there trading our sad words — I on the one side, holding my sword out over the blood, and the ghost of my comrade speaking on from the other.

"Then came the spirit of my own dead mother, Anticleia, the daughter of great-hearted Autolycus. I had left her living when I sailed for sacred Troy. I wept to see her, and pity went through me — but even in all my grief, I would not let her come near the blood before I had questioned Tiresias.

"Then came the spirit of Theban Tiresias, his golden staff in his hand. He knew me and spoke: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — why have you come, you luckless man, leaving the light of the sun to look on the dead and this joyless place? Stand back from the pit and lower your sharp sword, so I may drink the blood and tell you the truth.'
"So I drew back and slid the silver-studded sword into its sheath. And when he had drunk the dark blood, the faultless prophet spoke to me at last.

"'You are searching for your sweet homecoming, glorious Odysseus,' he said, 'but a god will make it hard. For I do not think you will slip past the Earthshaker, who has set his heart in anger against you, enraged that you blinded his dear son. Even so, you and your men may still come home, for all your suffering — if you can master your own hunger and theirs when first your ship touches the island of Thrinacia, your escape from the violet sea. For there you will find grazing the cattle and the fat flocks of Helios the Sun, who sees all things and hears all things. Leave them unharmed, keep your mind fixed on your homecoming, and you may yet reach Ithaca, hard as the road will be. But if you harm them, then I foretell ruin — for your ship and for your men. And even if you save yourself, you will come home late and broken, having lost all your companions, in a stranger's ship — and you will find trouble waiting in your house: insolent men devouring your goods, courting your godlike wife, pressing their gifts on her.

"'But you will make those men pay for their outrages when you come. And after you have killed the suitors in your halls — by cunning or in the open, by the sharp bronze — then you must go out again. Take a well-cut oar and carry it on your shoulder until you come to men who know nothing of the sea, who eat their food unsalted, who have never seen ships with their painted cheeks or the oars that are the wings of a ship. And I will give you a sign so clear you cannot miss it. When another traveler, meeting you, says you have a winnowing-fan on your strong shoulder — then plant your oar in the ground and make fine offerings to lord Poseidon: a ram, a bull, and a boar that mounts the sows. Then go home and offer sacred hecatombs to the deathless gods who hold the wide heavens, to all of them, each in his turn. And death will come to you, far from the sea — a gentle death that will take you down when you are worn out in a sleek old age, your people prospering around you. All this I tell you is the truth.'

"And I answered him: 'Tiresias, surely the gods themselves have spun this out as my fate. But tell me this, and tell me true. I see the spirit of my dead mother here. She sits near the blood in silence, and cannot bring herself to look her own son in the face or say a word to him. Tell me, my lord — how can I make her know me for who I am?'

"And he answered me at once: 'That is an easy thing to tell you. Whichever of the dead you let come near the blood will speak to you, and speak the truth. But the one you refuse will turn and go back again.' And with that the spirit of lord Tiresias went back into the house of Hades, his prophecy spoken.

"But I stayed where I was until my mother came up and drank the dark blood. At once she knew me, and her grief broke into words: 'My child, how did you come down here, into all this darkness, and you still alive? It is hard for the living to look on these things. Between us and you lie great rivers and dreadful waters — Ocean first of all, which no man can cross on foot, but only in a well-built ship. Have you come here from Troy, wandering all this long while with your ship and your men? Have you not yet reached Ithaca, not yet seen your wife in your own halls?'

"And I answered her: 'Mother, I had no choice — I had to come down to the house of Hades to ask the spirit of Theban Tiresias. I have not yet come near Greece, not yet set foot on my own soil. I have been wandering in misery from the first day I followed great Agamemnon to Ilios, the land of fine horses, to fight the Trojans. But tell me this, and tell me true. What death laid you low? Was it a long sickness, or did Artemis the archer come with her gentle arrows and bring you down? And tell me of my father, and of the son I left behind. Is my honor still safe in their hands, or has some other man taken it, thinking I will never come home? And tell me what my wedded wife intends, what is in her mind. Does she still hold to me and guard all that is mine — or has one of the Greeks, the best of them, married her by now?'

"And my honored mother answered me: 'She holds out still, her heart enduring, there in your halls. Her nights and her days waste away in sorrow and weeping. No man has yet taken your fine kingship; Telemachus holds your lands in peace and sits at the feasts a man who deals out justice is asked to share, for everyone invites him. But your father stays out in the country and never comes to town. He has no bed now, no blankets, no bright coverlets. In winter he sleeps in the house where the servants sleep, in the ashes by the fire, with poor rags on his body. And when summer comes and the rich harvest-time, he lies anywhere on the ground on the slope of his vineyard, on fallen leaves, grieving, nursing the sorrow in his heart, longing for you to come — and a hard old age has come on him. That is how I too died and met my fate. It was not the keen-eyed archer Artemis who shot me down with her gentle arrows in my own halls, nor any sickness that wastes the body and drains the spirit away. It was longing for you, my glorious Odysseus — your kindness and your counsel — that took the sweet life out of me.'

"So she spoke, and I longed in my heart to hold the spirit of my dead mother. Three times I started toward her, my whole heart aching to take her in my arms; three times she slipped through my hands like a shadow, like a dream. And the grief in me grew sharper, and I spoke to her, my words flying: 'Mother, why won't you stay for me, when I long to hold you — so that even here in the house of Hades we might throw our arms around each other and take some cold comfort in our shared sorrow? Is this only some phantom that dread Persephone has sent me, to make me weep and grieve all the more?'

"And my honored mother answered: 'Oh my child, unluckiest of all men born — Persephone, the daughter of Zeus, is not deceiving you. This is the way of mortals when they die. The sinews no longer hold the flesh and the bones together; the strong fury of the burning fire destroys all that, as soon as the life leaves the white bones, and the soul flutters off like a dream and is gone. But hurry back to the light now, with all speed. And keep all this in mind, so you may tell it to your wife in the days to come.'

"So we two spoke together. And then the women came — for dread Persephone drove them up to me, all the wives and daughters of the great men of old. They crowded around the dark blood, and I wondered how I might question them each in turn. This seemed the best plan: I drew the long sword from beside my sturdy thigh and would not let them all drink the dark blood at once. So they came up one by one, and each told me her birth, and I questioned them all.

"The first I saw was high-born Tyro, who said she was the daughter of faultless Salmoneus and the wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus. She had fallen in love with a river, the god Enipeus, far the loveliest of the rivers that run on the earth, and she used to walk by his beautiful waters. There Poseidon, who holds and shakes the earth, took the river's shape and lay with her where the eddying stream runs into the sea. A dark wave reared over them, high as a mountain, curving to hide the god and the mortal woman. He loosed her maiden girdle and shed sleep over her. And when the god had finished the work of love, he took her by the hand and said: 'Be glad, woman, of this love. As the year comes round you will bear glorious children, for the bed of a god is never barren. Care for them and raise them. Now go home, and hold your tongue, and tell no one — for know that I am Poseidon, the Earthshaker.' With that he sank beneath the heaving sea. And she conceived and bore Pelias and Neleus, who both grew to be strong servants of mighty Zeus — Pelias rich in flocks, living in spacious Iolcus, and Neleus in sandy Pylos. And to Cretheus this queen of women bore others: Aeson, and Pheres, and Amythaon who fought from his chariot.

"After her I saw Antiope, the daughter of Asopus, who boasted she had slept in the very arms of Zeus, and bore him two sons, Amphion and Zethus. They were the first to found the seat of seven-gated Thebes and to wall it round, for strong as they were, they could not hold open Thebes without its walls. Next I saw Alcmene, the wife of Amphitryon, who lay in the arms of great Zeus and bore unconquerable, lion-hearted Heracles; and Megara, daughter of proud Creon, whom the tireless son of Amphitryon took as his wife.

"And I saw the mother of Oedipus, lovely Epicaste, who in the blindness of her heart did a monstrous thing — she married her own son. He had killed his own father, and married her, and the gods soon made it known to men. Yet for all his anguish he went on ruling the Thebans in their lovely land, by the cruel design of the gods; but she went down to the house of Hades, the strong gatekeeper, when she had knotted a high noose to a beam and hanged herself, mastered by her grief — and she left him agonies past counting, all that a mother's avenging Furies bring to pass.

"And I saw beautiful Chloris, whom Neleus once married for her beauty, after he had paid a fortune in bride-gifts. She was the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus, who once ruled with power in Minyan Orchomenus. She was queen in Pylos and bore him splendid children — Nestor, and Chromius, and lordly Periclymenus — and besides them she bore stately Pero, a wonder to all who saw her, whom every man around courted. But Neleus would give her only to the man who could drive off the cattle of mighty Iphicles from Phylace — a heavy task. A faultless seer alone promised to do it, but a god's harsh fate bound him fast, and the rough herdsmen and their chains. Yet when the months and the days had run their course and the seasons came round again, mighty Iphicles set him free, once he had told out all the oracles. And so the will of Zeus was done.

"And I saw Leda, the wife of Tyndareus, who bore him two strong-hearted sons — Castor, breaker of horses, and Polydeuces, mighty with his fists. The living earth holds them both, and yet they live: even under the ground Zeus gives them honor. One day they live and the next day they are dead, each in his turn, and they have won honor like the gods'.

"After her I saw Iphimedeia, the wife of Aloeus, who said she had lain with Poseidon. She bore two sons, but their lives were short — godlike Otus and far-famed Ephialtes, the tallest men the grain-giving earth ever raised, and the most beautiful by far, after famous Orion. At nine years old they were nine cubits across and nine fathoms tall, and they threatened to bring the roar of raging war up to the immortals on Olympus. They strained to pile Mount Ossa on Olympus, and leafy Pelion on Ossa, to make a stairway into heaven — and they would have done it, had they only reached the full measure of their strength. But the son of Zeus, whom fair-haired Leto bore, destroyed them both before the first down ever curled on their cheeks or covered their chins with a young beard.

"And I saw Phaedra, and Procris, and lovely Ariadne, the daughter of merciless Minos, whom Theseus once carried off from Crete toward the high ground of sacred Athens — but he had no joy of her, for first Artemis killed her on sea-girt Dia, on the word of Dionysus. And I saw Maera, and Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle, who took gold as the price of her own husband's life.

"But I could never name them all, all the wives and daughters of heroes that I saw; the immortal night would run out first. It is time now to sleep, whether I go down to the swift ship and the crew, or stay here. My setting-out will be in your hands, and the gods'."

So he spoke, and they all sat hushed and still, held in a spell through the shadowy hall. Then white-armed Arete was the first to break the silence: "Phaeacians, what do you think of this man — his looks, his stature, the steady mind within him? He is my own guest, but every one of you shares the honor of it. So do not be in a hurry to send him on, and do not stint your gifts to a man in such great need. You have many treasures in your halls, by the gods' good grace."

Then the old hero Echeneus spoke up, the eldest among the Phaeacians: "My friends, what our wise queen says is not wide of the mark or far from our own thinking — so do as she says. But the word and the work both rest with Alcinous here."

And Alcinous answered him: "Then let it stand as she has said, as surely as I am alive and rule over the Phaeacians who love the oar. Let our guest, for all his longing to be home, hold on until tomorrow, until I have made the whole gift ready. His passage will be the care of all of us, and mine most of all, for the power in this land is mine."

And Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered him: "Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all your people — if you bade me wait here even a whole year while you readied my passage and your splendid gifts, I would gladly do it. It would be far better to reach my own dear country with fuller hands; I would be more honored, more loved, by every man who saw me come home to Ithaca."

And Alcinous answered him: "Odysseus, looking at you, we do not take you for a cheat or a liar, the kind the dark earth breeds in such numbers, men who spin lies out of nothing a man could ever see. There is a grace on your words, and a sound mind within, and you have told your tale with the skill of a singer — the heavy sorrows of yourself and all the Greeks. But tell me this now, and tell me true. Did you see any of your godlike companions there, who went with you to Troy and met their fate? The night is long, beyond all measure; it is not yet time to sleep in the hall. Tell me these wonders. I could hold out until bright dawn, if only you were willing to go on telling me your sorrows here."

And Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered him: "Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all your people — there is a time for long telling, and a time for sleep. But if you still long to hear, then I will not hold back from telling you of things still more pitiful than these — the sorrows of my companions who died afterward, who came safe out of the Trojans' bitter war only to die on their return, by the will of a wicked woman.

"When holy Persephone had scattered the spirits of the women this way and that, there came the grieving spirit of Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, and around him gathered all the others who had died with him in the house of Aegisthus, meeting their fate there. He knew me at once, when he had drunk the dark blood. He wept aloud, the warm tears falling, and reached out his arms to me, longing to hold me — but the strength was gone, the firm power that had once filled his supple limbs. I wept when I saw him, and pity went through my heart, and I spoke to him, my words flying: 'Most glorious son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — what fate of pitiless death brought you down? Did Poseidon raise a dreadful blast of cruel winds and break you on the sea? Or did enemies cut you down on dry land while you were rounding up their cattle and fine flocks, or fighting for their city and their women?'

"And he answered me at once: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — no, Poseidon did not break me on the sea with a blast of cruel winds, and no enemies cut me down on dry land. It was Aegisthus who plotted my death and my doom — he and my own accursed wife. He asked me to his house, he feasted me, and he killed me as a man kills an ox at its manger. So I died, the most pitiable death, and around me my companions were slaughtered without mercy, like white-tusked pigs cut down for a wedding feast or a banquet in a rich man's house. You have seen many men killed, in single combat and in the press of battle — but your heart would have ached most of all to see how we lay among the wine-bowls and the laden tables, all through the hall, and the whole floor running with blood. The most pitiful cry I ever heard was the voice of Cassandra, Priam's daughter, whom treacherous Clytemnestra killed at my side. I lifted my hands and beat the ground as I died with the sword in me; but the brazen-faced woman turned away and would not, though I was on my way to Hades, close my eyes with her hands or shut my mouth. There is nothing more dreadful, nothing more shameless, than a woman who can set her heart on a deed like this — as she did, plotting that monstrous thing, the murder of the husband of her youth. I thought I would come home to the welcome of my children and my servants — but she, with her heart bent on utter evil, has poured shame on herself and on all the women yet to be born, even on one who does what is right.'

"And I answered him: 'It is true — far-thundering Zeus has always borne a terrible hatred against the line of Atreus, working through the schemes of women. For Helen's sake so many of us died, and Clytemnestra laid her trap for you while you were far away.'

"And he said: 'So you too — never be soft, even with your own wife. Do not tell her everything in your mind. Tell her one thing, and keep the rest hidden. And yet you, Odysseus, will not be murdered by your wife — Penelope, Icarius' daughter, is too wise, too sound of heart for that. We left her a young bride when we marched off to war, with an infant at her breast, a boy who must be sitting now among grown men. Lucky child — his father will come home and see him, and he will throw his arms around his father, as a son should. But my wife would not even let me feast my eyes on my own son; she killed me first. And here is one more thing — take it to heart. Bring your ship in to your own dear land in secret, not in the open, for there is no trusting women anymore. But tell me this now, and tell me true — have you heard anything of my son, still living? In Orchomenus, perhaps, or sandy Pylos, or with Menelaus in broad Sparta? For surely my Orestes is not yet dead and gone.'
"And I answered him: 'Son of Atreus, why ask me this? I do not know whether he is alive or dead, and it is a poor thing to speak words into the wind.'

"So we two stood trading our sad words, grieving, the warm tears falling. And then there came the spirit of Achilles, son of Peleus, and the spirits of Patroclus and faultless Antilochus and of Ajax, who in build and in beauty was the finest of all the Greeks after the matchless son of Peleus. The spirit of the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus knew me, and grieving he spoke to me, his words flying: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — reckless man, what greater thing than this could your heart still devise? How did you dare come down to Hades, where the dead live on without their wits, the worn-out husks of men who have done with their labor?'

"And I answered him: 'Achilles, son of Peleus, far the strongest of all the Greeks — I came needing Tiresias, to see if he could tell me any way to reach rocky Ithaca. For I have not yet come near Greece, nor set foot on my own land. I have nothing but trouble. But you, Achilles — no man was ever more blessed than you, nor ever will be. While you lived we Greeks honored you like a god, and now that you are here you rule with great power among the dead. So do not grieve at your dying, Achilles.'

"And he answered me at once: 'Don't gild death for me, glorious Odysseus. I would rather be a hired hand, working another man's land — a man with no portion of his own, scraping by — and be alive, than be lord over all the wasted dead. But tell me of my son, my proud boy. Did he follow the war as a leader, or not? And tell me of faultless Peleus, if you have heard — does he still keep his honor among the Myrmidons, or do they scorn him now through Hellas and Phthia, because old age has him by the hands and feet? For I am no help to him under the sun's light, the man I was on the wide plain of Troy, when I cut down the best of their army defending the Greeks. If I could come, even for a moment, to my father's house with that strength still in me, I would give any man who shames him and bars him from his honor good reason to dread these hands of mine.'

"And I answered him: 'Of faultless Peleus I have heard nothing. But of your dear son Neoptolemus I will tell you all the truth, as you ask. It was I myself who brought him over from Scyros in my trim, hollow ship, to join the well-greaved Greeks. Whenever we held council before Troy, he was always the first to speak, and he never missed the mark; only godlike Nestor and I outdid him. And when we fought on the Trojan plain, he never hung back in the crowd of men, but always charged far out in front, yielding to no one in his fury. He killed many men in the dread press of battle — I could not name them all, all the host he cut down defending the Greeks — but I will tell you how he brought down the hero Eurypylus, son of Telephus, with the bronze, and many of the Ceteians around him fell, all for a woman's bribes. He was the handsomest man I ever saw, after godlike Memnon. And when we, the best of the Greeks, were climbing into the horse that Epeus built, and the whole thing was left in my hands — to open our hiding-place or to keep it shut — then the other leaders and counselors of the Greeks were wiping the tears from their eyes, and every man's legs were shaking under him. But him I never once saw turn pale in his handsome face, or wipe a tear away. He kept begging me to let him burst out of the horse, gripping his sword-hilt and his heavy bronze spear, mad to fall on the Trojans. And when we had sacked Priam's high city, he went aboard his ship with his full share and a fine prize, not a scratch on him — never struck by a flung spear, never wounded in close fighting, the way men so often are in war, when Ares rages without rule.'
"So I spoke, and the spirit of the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus went off with long strides across the field of asphodel, glad that I had told him his son was a man of valor.

"The other spirits of the dead and gone stood grieving around me, and each one asked after those it loved. Only the spirit of Ajax, son of Telamon, held off, apart, still burning over the victory I had won against him at the ships, in the contest for the arms of Achilles. His honored mother had set them up as the prize, and the sons of the Trojans and Pallas Athena were the judges. I wish I had never won such a contest — for it laid in the earth that great head, Ajax, who in build and in deeds was the finest of all the Greeks after the matchless son of Peleus. I called out to him gently: 'Ajax, son of faultless Telamon — even in death, will you not let go your anger at me over that cursed armor? The gods set it there as a grief to the Greeks; in you we lost so great a tower of strength. We mourned you, when you died, as bitterly as we mourned Achilles himself. No one is to blame but Zeus, who hated the Greek army with a terrible hatred, and fixed your doom. Come here, my lord, and listen — master that fury, that proud spirit of yours.'

"He gave me not one word in answer, but turned and went off into Erebus, to join the other spirits of the dead. Even so, angry as he was, he might still have spoken to me, or I to him — but the heart in me longed to see the other spirits of the dead.

"And there I saw Minos, the glorious son of Zeus, his golden staff in his hand, seated and giving judgment over the dead, while around him they pressed their cases, sitting and standing through the wide-gated house of Hades. After him I saw huge Orion, herding across the field of asphodel the wild beasts he had killed himself on the lonely hills, a club of solid bronze in his hands, unbroken forever.

"And I saw Tityus, the son of Earth, stretched out on the ground, covering nine acres where he lay. Two vultures, one on either side, sat tearing at his liver, plunging their beaks into the flesh, and he could not beat them off — because he had laid hands on Leto, the honored consort of Zeus, as she went up to Pytho through the lovely fields of Panopeus.

"And I saw Tantalus too, in his cruel torment, standing in a pool that lapped at his chin. He strained with thirst, and could never reach the water to drink: every time the old man bent to it, the water would drain away and vanish, and the black earth would show at his feet, dried up by some god. And tall trees leaned their fruit down over his head — pears and pomegranates, apples gleaming bright, sweet figs and ripe olives — but whenever the old man stretched up to take them, the wind would toss the branches away to the shadowy clouds.

"And I saw Sisyphus too, in his agony, heaving a monstrous stone with both his hands. He would brace himself, hands and feet, and shove it up toward the crest of a hill — but just as he was about to push it over the top, the weight would turn it back, and down to the plain the shameless stone would come crashing again. And he would dig in once more and strain to push it up, the sweat pouring from his limbs, the dust rising from his head.

"And after him I saw mighty Heracles — his phantom, that is, for the man himself is among the immortal gods, taking his ease at their feasts, with lovely-ankled Hebe for his wife, the daughter of great Zeus and golden-sandaled Hera. Around him the dead made a din like startled birds, scattering in every direction. He came on like black night, his bow stripped bare, an arrow on the string, glaring fearsomely as if forever about to shoot. And across his chest was a terrible baldric, a strap of gold worked with marvels — bears and wild boars and lions with flashing eyes, and battles and slaughter and the killing of men. May the craftsman who put his art into that belt never make another like it. He knew me the moment he laid eyes on me, and grieving he spoke, his words flying: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — poor man, so you too drag out a hard fate, the same I bore under the light of the sun. I was a son of Zeus, son of Kronos, and yet my suffering had no end. I was bound in service to a man far worse than myself, who laid the heaviest labors on me. He even sent me down here once, to bring up the hound of Hades — for he thought he could set me no harder task than that. But I carried the hound up out of Hades, with Hermes and grey-eyed Athena to guide me.'

"With that he went back into the house of Hades, but I stayed on where I was, in case some other of the heroes of old should come — and I would have seen still more of the men of long ago whom I longed to see, Theseus and Pirithous, the glorious children of the gods. But before that, the numberless tribes of the dead came swarming around me with an eerie cry, and a pale dread seized me — that holy Persephone might send up out of Hades the head of the Gorgon, that monstrous, fearful thing. So I went straight back to my ship and told my men to climb aboard and loose the cables. They went quickly to their places at the oars, and the current carried us down the stream of Ocean — rowing at first, and then a fair wind came on."

sections.label: Book XII
sections.title: The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the Cattle of the Sun

segments.text: "Once we were clear of the river Ocean and out on the open sea again, we came back to the island of Aeaea, where the early Dawn has her dancing-grounds and the sun comes up. There we ran the ship aground on the sand, climbed out onto the shore, and lay down to sleep, waiting for the bright morning.

"And when rosy-fingered Dawn appeared at last, I sent some of the men up to Circe's house to bring back the body of Elpenor. We cut firewood and carried it to the highest point of the headland, and there, weeping, with the tears running down, we gave him his funeral rites. When the body and the armor had burned to ashes, we heaped him a mound and set a stone over it, and at the top we fixed the oar he had pulled at while he lived.

"Circe knew well enough that we had come back from the house of Hades, and she dressed herself and hurried down to us, her serving-women behind her, carrying bread and meat and gleaming red wine. She stood in the middle of us, that dread goddess, and spoke: 'You reckless men, who went down alive to the house of Hades — so you will die twice, where other men die only once. Stay here now, eat your fill, and drink the day away; you sail at first light. And I will set you your course and make everything plain, so that no trap on the land or the sea catches you off your guard and brings you grief.'

"So we agreed, and we sat and feasted all day long until the sun went down. When the sun had set and the dark came on, the men lay down to sleep by the ship's stern cables. But Circe took me by the hand and led me apart from my companions, and sat me down, and lay beside me, and asked me to tell her all that had happened. And I told her everything, in its order.

"Then the great goddess gave me my sailing directions. 'That is done, then,' she said. 'Now listen to me, and a god will keep it in your mind for you besides. First you will come to the Sirens, who bewitch every man who comes near them. Whoever draws too close, in his ignorance, and hears the voices of the Sirens — never again will his wife and little children stand around him glad that he has come home. The Sirens enchant him with their clear song, sitting in a meadow, and around them is a great heap of bones, of men rotting away, the skin shriveling on them. Row hard past them. Soften beeswax and stop the ears of your men, so that none of the rest can hear. But you yourself, if you long to listen, have them bind you hand and foot in the swift ship, standing upright against the mast-step, with the rope-ends lashed to the mast, so you may hear the two Sirens' voices and take your joy of it. And if you beg the men to set you free, if you order it — then let them tie you down all the tighter.

"'When your men have rowed you past the Sirens, I cannot tell you outright which of two roads you must take. You will have to weigh it in your own mind; I will lay both before you. On the one side there are overhanging cliffs, and against them the great waves of dark-eyed Amphitrite come thundering. The blessed gods call these the Wandering Rocks. No bird can pass them — not even the shy doves that carry ambrosia to Father Zeus; the bare rock always snatches one of them away, and the Father sends another to keep their number whole. No ship of men that ever came there got clear again; the planks of the hull and the bodies of the crew are swept off together by the sea-surge and the storms of deadly fire. One ship alone of all that sail has ever passed that way — the Argo, that all men sing of, on her voyage home from Aeetes' land; and even her the wave would have flung against the great rocks, except that Hera saw her through, for love of Jason.

"'On the other road there are two cliffs. One of them reaches the wide sky with its sharp peak, and a dark cloud caps it always and never draws off, so the top is never clear, not even in the warm days of summer and harvest. No man could climb it or get a foothold there, not if he had twenty hands and twenty feet, for the rock runs up sheer, as smooth as if it had been polished. Halfway up the cliff there is a misty cave, facing the west and the dark of Erebus, and it is past this that you must steer your ship, glorious Odysseus. Not even a strong young archer, shooting from the deck, could reach that hollow cave with his arrow. Inside it Scylla lives, and her howling is dreadful. Her voice is no louder than a new-born puppy's, but she herself is a monstrous, evil thing, and no one would be glad to look on her, not even a god who met her. She has twelve feet, all dangling, and six necks stretched out long, and on each a horrible head, and in each head three rows of teeth set thick and close, packed full of black death. Up to her middle she is sunk in the hollow cave, but she thrusts her heads out from the awful pit and fishes there, scouring the rock for dolphins and dogfish and any greater beast she can seize, of the thousands that loud-moaning Amphitrite feeds. No sailors have ever yet passed her and gone away unscathed in their ship; with each head she snatches a man and carries him off.

"'The other cliff lies lower, Odysseus — you will see it — and close to the first; a man could shoot an arrow across between them. On it grows a great fig tree thick with leaves, and beneath it monstrous Charybdis sucks the black water down. Three times a day she spews it up, and three times she swallows it again, a terror to see. Pray you are not there when she swallows: not even the Earthshaker could save you from ruin then. No — keep hard against Scylla's cliff and drive the ship past at full speed. It is far better to lose six men and keep the rest than to lose them all.'
"'But surely, goddess,' I said, 'there must be some way to escape deadly Charybdis and still beat Scylla off when she comes for my men?'

"'You hard, headstrong man,' the goddess answered, 'always reaching for the next fight, the next labor — you will not give way even to the deathless gods. Scylla is no mortal thing; she is an immortal horror, savage, monstrous, and not to be fought. There is no defense. The best thing is to flee her. If you waste time arming beside her rock, I am afraid she will dart out again and take six more of your men with her six heads. No — row past with all your strength, and call on Crataiis, Scylla's mother, who bore her to be a plague to men. She will hold her back from a second strike.

"'After that you will come to the island of Thrinacia, where the cattle of the Sun graze, and his fat flocks of sheep — seven herds of cattle, seven fine flocks of sheep, fifty in each. They never breed and they never die, and two goddesses herd them, the lovely-haired nymphs Phaethousa and Lampetie, whom shining Neaera bore to Helios who walks above us. Leave those cattle unharmed, keep your mind fixed on getting home, and you may all still reach Ithaca, hard as the way will be. But if you harm them — then I promise you the ruin of your ship and your men. And even if you yourself escape, you will come home late and broken, and every one of your companions lost.'

"By now Dawn had come up on her golden throne, and the great goddess went away inland. I went down to the ship and roused my men to climb aboard and loose the stern cables. They went quickly to their places and struck the grey sea with their oars. And behind our dark-prowed ship Circe sent us a friend, a fair wind that filled the sail and stayed steady at our back, so we had only to keep the gear in order and let the wind and the helmsman carry us on.

"Then, heavy at heart, I spoke to my men. 'Friends,' I said, 'it is not right that only one or two of us should know what Circe foretold me. I will tell you, so that whether we live or die we go in with our eyes open. First she warned us of the wonderful song of the Sirens, and their meadow full of flowers. I alone am to hear them, she said — but you must bind me with a cruel knot, standing upright against the mast-step, with the rope-ends lashed to the mast, so I cannot stir. And if I beg you to let me go, if I order it — then bind me tighter still.'

"I had hardly finished telling them everything before our trim ship came swiftly to the island of the Sirens, for a fair wind drove her on. And then, all at once, the wind dropped; a dead calm came over the water, and some god smoothed the waves to stillness. The men got up and furled the sail and stowed it in the hollow ship, then sat to the oars and whitened the sea with the polished blades. Meanwhile I took a great round of beeswax and cut it small with the sharp bronze, and worked it in my strong hands until it grew soft under the pressure and the heat of the Sun, the lord Hyperion. I stopped the ears of every man in turn; and they bound me hand and foot in the ship, upright against the mast-step, and lashed the rope-ends to the mast, and sat down again and struck the grey sea with their oars. But when we were as far off as a man's shout will carry, driving on hard, the Sirens did not fail to see our swift ship come near, and they raised their clear song:

"'Come here to us, famous Odysseus, great glory of the Greeks — bring your ship in and listen to our two voices. No man has ever yet rowed past this place in his black ship until he has heard the honey-sweet song from our lips; he goes on his way with his heart gladdened, and knowing more than he did. For we know everything the Greeks and the Trojans suffered on the wide plain of Troy, by the will of the gods; and we know all that happens anywhere on the fruitful earth.'

"So they sang, in their lovely voices, and my heart ached to listen. I signaled the men with my brows to set me free; but they only bent harder to the oars, and Perimedes and Eurylochus stood up and bound me with still more ropes, tighter than before. Only when we had rowed well past, until we could no longer hear the Sirens' voices or their song, did my faithful men take the wax from their ears and loose me from the mast.

"But the moment we left that island behind I saw smoke and a great surf ahead, and heard a roaring. The men were so afraid that the oars flew from their hands and trailed splashing in the sea, and the ship lay dead in the water, with no one rowing now. So I went up and down the ship and steadied every man with quiet words, standing over each one.

"'Friends,' I said, 'we are no strangers to danger. This is nothing worse than when the Cyclops trapped us in his cave by brute force, and even there my courage and my counsel and my cunning brought us out. We will remember this too, one day. So now — every man do as I say. Keep your oars in the surf and dig hard at the deep sea; it may be Zeus will let us slip past this ruin and live. And you, helmsman — here is your order, and take it to heart, for the ship's curved hull is in your hands. Steer her clear of that smoke and surf; hug the cliff, or before you know it she will swerve toward the other side and you will pitch us all to our deaths.'

"They did as I said, and quickly. But I never spoke of Scylla, the horror there was no fighting, for fear my men would let go their oars in terror and huddle below in the hold. And in this one thing I forgot Circe's hard command — she had told me not to arm at all, but I put on my glorious armor, took up two long spears, and went to stand on the foredeck, for it was from there I thought I would first see rock-dwelling Scylla coming with death for my men. But I could not spot her anywhere, and my eyes ached with searching every fold of the shadowy cliff.

"So we sailed up the narrow strait, groaning, for Scylla was on one side, and on the other monstrous Charybdis sucked the salt sea down in her terrible way. When she spewed it up she seethed and churned like a cauldron over a great fire, and the spray flew high over the tops of both cliffs. When she swallowed the sea down again, all of her showed, churning within, and the rock around her roared horribly, and below, the sea-bed came into sight, black with sand. Green fear took hold of my men. We were staring at Charybdis, dreading our ruin from her — and in that moment Scylla snatched six of my companions out of the ship, the strongest hands I had. I turned to look at the swift ship and at my men, and I saw their hands and feet already overhead as she swung them up, and they cried out to me, calling my name one last time, in the agony of their hearts. As a fisherman on a jutting rock lets down his long pole, his bait on the ox-horn hook to trick the little fish, and flings each one he catches gasping onto the shore — just so she swung my men up, gasping, to the rocks, and there at her cave-mouth she devoured them while they screamed and stretched out their hands to me in their last dreadful struggle. That was the most pitiful thing my eyes ever saw in all my wanderings on the paths of the sea.

"When we had escaped the rocks and dread Charybdis and Scylla, we came at last to the fair island of the Sun-god, where his fine broad-browed cattle grazed and his many flocks of sheep belonging to Helios who walks above us. While I was still out at sea in the black ship I could hear the lowing of the cattle as they were stalled, and the bleating of the sheep, and the words of the blind prophet, Theban Tiresias, came back to me, and Circe's warning too — both had told me again and again to keep away from the island of the Sun, who gives men their joy. So, heavy at heart, I spoke to my men. 'Friends,' I said, 'worn out as you are, hear me. Tiresias foretold me a thing, and Circe warned me of it too: that our worst danger lies on the island of the Sun, who gives men their light. Drive the black ship past it.'

"At that their spirit broke, and Eurylochus answered me with bitter words. 'You are a hard man, Odysseus,' he said. 'Your strength is more than ours; your limbs never tire; you must be made all of iron. Here are your men worn down with toil and want of sleep, and you will not let us set foot on dry land — on an island ringed by the sea, where we could cook ourselves a good supper — but you order us to keep wandering through the running night, driven off across the misty sea. It is at night the cruel winds rise and wreck ships. How would any of us escape sudden death if a squall came up out of the south or the west, that smashes a ship in spite of the gods? No — let us give in to the dark night now and make our supper here by the swift ship, and at dawn we will go aboard again and put out on the wide sea.'

"So Eurylochus spoke, and the rest agreed. Then I knew for certain that some god was set on our ruin, and I answered him with winged words. 'Eurylochus, I am one man, and you force my hand. But swear me a great oath, all of you: if we come on a herd of cattle or a fine flock of sheep, no man among you will be so blind, so mad, as to kill a single beast. Sit quiet, and eat the food the immortal Circe gave us.'

"So I spoke, and they swore the oath I asked. When they had sworn it through, we brought the trim ship to anchor in a curving cove beside a spring of fresh water, and the men climbed out and made their supper with care. And when they had eaten and drunk their fill, they fell to weeping, remembering their dear companions whom Scylla had snatched from the ship and devoured; and they wept until sweet sleep came over them.

"In the third watch of the night, when the stars had wheeled past their height, Zeus the cloud-gatherer raised a screaming wind, a great storm, and hid the land and the sea alike in cloud; and night came down out of the sky. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared again, we hauled the ship up into a hollow cave, where the sea-nymphs have their seats and their dancing-floors, and there I called the men together and spoke to them.

"'Friends,' I said, 'there is food and drink enough in the swift ship. Keep your hands off these cattle, or it will go badly for us. They belong to a dread god, Helios, who sees all things and hears all things.' So I spoke, and their proud hearts gave in.

"But for a whole month the south wind blew without a break, and after it no wind at all came except the south and the east. As long as the men had bread and red wine, they kept their hands off the cattle, for they wanted to live. But when all the ship's stores were gone, hunger drove them to range the island after game, fishing with bent hooks, hunting birds, taking whatever came to hand — for their bellies were eaten hollow with want. Then one day I went off alone up the island to pray to the gods, hoping one of them might show me a way home. When I had crossed the island and got clear of my men, I found a place out of the wind, and there I washed my hands and prayed to all the gods who hold Olympus. And they shed sweet sleep over my eyes.

"And while I slept, Eurylochus was laying his ruinous plan before the men. 'Hear me, friends,' he said, 'beaten down as you are. Every death is hateful to us poor mortals, but the worst of all is to die of hunger and meet your doom that way. Come — let us drive off the best of the Sun's cattle and sacrifice them to the gods who hold the wide sky. And if we ever reach Ithaca, our own land, we will build the Sun a rich temple at once and fill it with fine offerings. But if he is angry over his straight-horned cattle and means to wreck our ship, and the other gods agree — then I would rather drink down one wave and die at once than waste away by inches on a desert island.'

"So Eurylochus spoke, and the rest agreed. At once they drove off the best of the Sun's cattle from close by — for the fine broad-browed beasts were grazing not far from the dark-prowed ship — and they gathered around them and prayed to the gods, plucking the soft young leaves from a tall oak, since they had no white barley left aboard. When they had prayed, they cut the cattle's throats and flayed them; they cut out the thigh-bones, wrapped them in a double layer of fat, and laid raw flesh on top. They had no wine to pour over the burning offering, so they made their libation with water as they roasted the innards. And when the thighs were burned and they had tasted the inner parts, they carved up the rest and ran it onto the spits.

"Just then sweet sleep left my eyes, and I went down to the swift ship and the shore of the sea. And as I came near the curved ship, the warm smell of roasting fat reached me. I groaned aloud and cried out to the deathless gods: 'Father Zeus, and all you blessed gods who live forever — it was for my ruin you lulled me to sleep. See what a monstrous thing my men have dared while I was gone.'

"And Lampetie of the trailing robes ran swiftly to Helios who walks above us and told him we had killed his cattle. At once, in a fury, he spoke out among the immortals. 'Father Zeus, and all you blessed gods who live forever — make the companions of Odysseus pay for what they have done. In their insolence they have killed my cattle, the cattle I loved to look on every time I climbed the starry sky and every time I turned back from heaven toward the earth. If they do not pay me a fitting price for them, I will go down to Hades and shine among the dead.'

"And Zeus the cloud-gatherer answered him: 'Helios, keep shining on, among the immortals and over the grain-giving earth for mortal men. As for those men, soon enough I will strike their swift ship with a bright bolt and shatter it to splinters in the middle of the wine-dark sea.'
"All this I had from Calypso of the lovely hair, who said she herself had heard it from the messenger Hermes.

"When I had come down to the ship and the sea, I went up to the men and rebuked them one by one. But there was no remedy now; the cattle were dead. And straightaway the gods began to show us signs and portents. The hides crawled along the ground; the flesh on the spits, cooked and raw alike, began to bellow, and there was a sound like the lowing of cattle all around us.

"For six days my faithful companions feasted on the best of the Sun's cattle they had driven off. But when Zeus, the son of Kronos, brought on the seventh day, the wind dropped its raging at last, and we went aboard and put out on the wide sea, raising the mast and spreading the white sail. When we had left the island behind and no other land was in sight, nothing but sky and sea, the son of Kronos set a black cloud over the hollow ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it. She did not run on much longer. All at once a screaming west wind came on in a great storm, and the gale snapped both the forestays of the mast, and the mast fell backward, and all the rigging spilled into the bilge. The mast came down on the head of the helmsman in the stern and crushed every bone of his skull together, and he plunged from the deck like a diver, and his proud spirit left his bones.

"Then Zeus thundered and hurled his bolt into the ship at once. She reeled from end to end, struck by the lightning of Zeus, and filled with the reek of sulfur, and my men were flung out of her. They bobbed in the swell around the black ship like sea-crows, and the god took their homecoming from them.

"I myself kept pacing the deck until the surge tore the ship's sides from her keel, and the bare keel went drifting on the swell. The mast had snapped off close to the keel, but a backstay of stout oxhide was still fastened to it. With that I lashed the keel and the mast together, and I sat astride them and let the deadly winds carry me where they would.

"Then the west wind dropped its raging, and the south wind came up quickly, bringing fresh dread to my heart — that it would carry me back to deadly Charybdis. All that night I was swept along, and at sunrise I came again to Scylla's cliff and dread Charybdis, just as she was sucking the salt sea down. But I sprang up toward the tall fig tree and clung to it, hanging on like a bat, with nowhere to set my feet, nothing to climb on; the roots ran down far below, and the branches arched high overhead, long and great, shadowing all of Charybdis. So I held on, waiting for her to spit up the mast and the keel again — and I longed for them, and they came at last. At the hour when a judge rises from the assembly for his supper, after settling the many quarrels of young men at law, that was the hour when those timbers came up again out of Charybdis. I let go with hands and feet and dropped down with a splash, just beyond the long beams, and climbing onto them I rowed with my hands. And the father of gods and men did not let Scylla catch sight of me; otherwise I would never have escaped sheer death.

"From there I was carried for nine days, and on the tenth night the gods brought me to the island of Ogygia, where Calypso of the lovely hair lives, a dread goddess with a human voice. She took me in and was kind to me. But why tell that again? I told it all to you and your noble wife in your hall only yesterday, and it is a tiresome thing to say twice over what has already been said plainly."
So Odysseus finished, and a hush held the whole hall. They sat spellbound in the shadowy galleries, still under the charm of his story. At last Alcinous spoke.

“Odysseus,” he said, “now that you have reached my high house with its bronze floor, I am sure of one thing: you will get home this time without being driven off course again, however much you have suffered before. And to the rest of you — you who come to my halls night after night to drink the king’s wine and listen to the bard — I have something to ask. Our guest’s chest is already packed with the woven clothing and the worked gold and all the other gifts our Phaeacian counselors have brought him. Let us add to it. Let each of us give him, besides, a great tripod and a cauldron. We will make good the cost later from the people at large; no one man should have to carry a gift this generous alone.”

They all thought this well said, and went home to sleep, each to his own house. When rosy-fingered Dawn came up at last, they hurried down to the ship with their gifts of gleaming bronze. Alcinous himself went aboard and stowed everything snugly under the benches with his own hands, so nothing would shift and foul the rowers when they bent to their work. Then they came back to the palace and set about a feast. Alcinous sacrificed an ox to Zeus, the dark-clouded son of Kronos, who is lord over all. They burned the thigh-pieces and sat down to a fine meal, and Demodocus, the bard the people loved, sang to them. But Odysseus kept turning his head toward the blazing sun, willing it to set, so hungry was he to be gone. As a man who has driven a pair of oxen all day through a fallow field aches for his supper, and his knees buckle under him as the light fails and he heads home to eat — just so welcome to Odysseus was the going down of the sun. At once he spoke to the Phaeacians, and most of all to Alcinous their king.

“King Alcinous, most honored of all this people, and all of you — pour your offering and send me on my way in peace, and farewell. Everything my heart wanted, you have given: an escort home, and these gifts, which I pray the gods in heaven will let me turn to good. May I come home to find my faithful wife unharmed and my own people safe and well. And may all of you whom I leave behind here bring lasting joy to your wives and your children. May the gods grant you every blessing, and may no trouble ever come upon your people.”

They all approved his words, and agreed their guest should have his escort, for he had spoken well and fairly. Then Alcinous called to his steward: “Pontonous, mix the wine in the great bowl and carry it round to every man in the hall, so that we may pray to Father Zeus and send our guest home to his own land.”

Pontonous mixed the honeyed wine and served it to each in turn. From where they sat, every man poured out his offering to the blessed gods who hold the wide heaven; but Odysseus rose to his feet, set the two-handled cup in Queen Arete’s hands, and said to her, his words flying:

“Fare well, my queen, all your days — until old age comes upon you, and death, which waits for everyone. I am going now. Be happy here in your house, with your children and your people, and with Alcinous the king.”

With that he crossed the threshold. Alcinous sent a herald to walk with him down to the swift ship and the shore of the sea, and Arete sent serving-women after him — one carrying a fresh-washed cloak and tunic, one his strong chest of treasure, and a third bearing bread and red wine. When they came to the ship at the water’s edge, the crew took it all and stowed it aboard, every scrap of food and drink. For Odysseus himself they spread a rug and a linen sheet on the half-deck at the stern, so he might sleep soundly through the crossing. Then he too climbed aboard and lay down, without a word. They took their places at the oar-pins, in their proper order, and slipped the cable from the pierced stone where it was made fast. The moment they leaned back and the oars threw up the spray, a sleep dropped over Odysseus’s eyes — a deep, sweet, unbroken sleep, the very likeness of death.

The ship ran on. As a team of four stallions on a plain springs forward all together under the lash and devours the road, so her stern lifted and the dark wave of the loud-roaring sea boiled huge behind her. Steady and sure she held her course; not even a hawk, the swiftest thing that flies, could have kept pace beside her. So she cut through the waves at a run, carrying a man whose mind was a match for the gods — a man who had borne so much, so many wars of men and the bitter waves he had cut across, and who now slept on, still as death, forgetting all that he had suffered.

When the brightest of the stars rose, the one that comes to herald the light of early Dawn, the seafaring ship drew in to the island. There is a harbor in Ithaca that belongs to Phorcys, the old man of the sea, where two headlands run out sheer and shelving toward each other and close off the mouth; they break the great waves that the hard winds roll in from outside, so that once a ship is within, she can ride at anchor without even a line to hold her. At the head of the bay stands a long-leaved olive tree, and close by it a cave, shadowy and lovely, sacred to the nymphs men call the Naiads. Inside are great mixing-bowls and two-handled jars of stone, where the bees store their honey, and tall stone looms where the nymphs weave their sea-purple cloth, a marvel to look on, and springs that never run dry. The cave has two gates: one to the north, the way down for mortal men, and one to the south, the holier way, by which no man may enter — it is the road of the gods.

Into this harbor they rowed, for they knew it of old. The ship ran in so hard she drove half her length up onto the sand, such was the strength of the arms that had driven her. The men stepped out and first of all lifted Odysseus from the hollow ship, rug, linen sheet and all, and laid him down on the sand, still deep in sleep. Then they unloaded the treasure the Phaeacians, moved by grey-eyed Athena, had given him for the voyage home, and stacked it all together at the foot of the olive, well back from the road, in case some traveler should pass and rob him before he woke. That done, they turned for home.

But Poseidon had not forgotten the threats he had once made against Odysseus, and now he went to learn the mind of Zeus. “Father Zeus,” he said, “I shall never again be honored among the deathless gods, when even mortals show me no respect — these Phaeacians, who are my own blood. I always meant Odysseus to reach home, once he had suffered his full measure; I never robbed him of his return outright, since you had promised it with a nod of your head. But look — they have ferried him asleep across the sea in their swift ship and set him down in Ithaca, and loaded him with gifts past counting, more bronze and gold and woven goods than he could ever have carried home from Troy with his fair share of the plunder.”

Zeus, who gathers the clouds, answered him: “What are you saying, lord of the wide earth, shaker of the ground? The gods do not slight you. It would be a strange and ugly thing to deny respect to one so old and great. But if any mortal, trusting in his own strength, fails to honor you — the punishment is always yours to take, after, as you see fit. Do whatever your heart desires.”

“Then I would do it now, dark-clouded lord,” said Poseidon, the earth-shaker, “if I did not fear your anger and hold back from it. As things are, I mean to wreck that fine Phaeacian ship on her way home from the escort, out on the misty sea, so they will stop ferrying strangers ever after — and I will throw a great mountain round their city to hide it.”

“My friend,” Zeus answered, “this is how it seems best to me. When all the people are watching from the town as she runs in, turn her to stone close offshore, still in the shape of a ship, so that everyone stands amazed — and then wall their city round with the mountain.”

When Poseidon the earth-shaker heard this, he went off to Scheria, the land of the Phaeacians, and waited there. The seafaring ship came on, driving in fast and close, and the earth-shaker came up to her, struck her flat with the palm of his hand, and rooted her where she stood, turned all to stone. Then he was gone.

Up and down the shore the Phaeacians spoke to one another, the long-oared seamen famous for their ships, glancing at the man beside them: “Who in the world has rooted our swift ship in the sea, on her way home? We could see every plank of her a moment ago.” So they said, not one of them knowing what had happened. But Alcinous rose and spoke among them.

“Ah — now an old prophecy my father told me has come home at last. He used to say Poseidon would turn his anger on us for ferrying every man so safely across the sea, and that one day he would wreck a fine Phaeacian ship coming home from her escort, and throw a great mountain round our city. So the old man said, and now it is all coming true. Listen to me, and do as I say. From this day on, when strangers come to us, we give no more escorts home. And let us sacrifice twelve choice bulls to Poseidon, and pray he takes pity on us, and does not wall our city in with the mountain.” The people were afraid, and made the bulls ready. So the leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians stood about the altar and prayed to Poseidon, lord of the sea.

And just then Odysseus woke on his own native ground. He had been away so long that he did not know it again — and more than that, Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, had poured a mist all around him, so that no one would know him, and she could tell him everything herself, with neither his wife nor his townsmen nor his friends recognizing him before the suitors had paid for all their crimes. So the whole land looked strange to its own king — the long straight paths, the safe harbors, the steep cliffs, the trees in their leaf, all of it changed. He sprang up, stared at the country of his birth, and groaned. He struck both thighs with the flat of his hands and cried out in despair.

“What am I now? Whose country have I come to? Are they cruel here, savage, lawless — or are they kind to strangers, with the fear of the gods in their minds? And all this treasure — where do I carry it? Where do I even go? I wish I had stayed there among the Phaeacians. I might have gone on instead to some other great king, who would have taken me in and sent me home. As it is, I do not know where to put any of this, and I cannot leave it lying here for the first man who passes to carry off. So the Phaeacian leaders were not so wise or just after all. They have set me down in the wrong land. They swore they would bring me back to Ithaca, and they have not done it. May Zeus, who watches over those who beg for shelter, who sees all men and punishes the wrongdoer, pay them back for this. Well — let me count my goods and see whether the crew sailed off with any of it.”

He counted the lovely tripods and the cauldrons, the gold, the fine woven clothing — nothing was missing. But still he grieved for his own land, and dragged himself along the shore of the sounding sea, sick at heart. Then Athena came to him, in the form of a young man, a shepherd, but with the soft look of a prince’s son, a fine cloak doubled over his shoulders, sandals on his bright feet, and a spear in his hand. Odysseus was glad to see her, and went straight up to her, his words flying.

“Friend — you are the first soul I have met in this country, so I greet you, and I beg you, do me no harm. Save these goods of mine, and save me too; I come to you as I would come to a god, and I take you by the knees. Tell me truly, what land is this? What people? Is this an island, or the shore of some mainland that runs down to the sea?”

Grey-eyed Athena answered him: “You must be a simple man, stranger, or come from very far away, to ask what country this is. It is hardly a place without a name. Crowds of men know it — both those who face the dawn and those who live toward the dark and the setting sun. It is rough country, no good for driving horses, and not a wide island either; but it is far from poor. It grows grain beyond measure, and wine, and the rain and the dew never fail it; it is good for goats and good for cattle, there is timber of every kind, and the watering-places never run dry all year. And so, stranger, the name of Ithaca has traveled even as far as Troy — which they say lies a long way off from this land of the Greeks.”

So she spoke, and long-suffering Odysseus was glad — glad to stand again in the land of his fathers, now that Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, had named it. But even now he did not tell the truth. He held the word back on his lips and spun, out of the deep cunning that was always working in him, a false tale.

“I heard of Ithaca,” he said, “even over in Crete, far across the sea — and now here I am, with all this treasure. I left as much again behind for my children, but I am running for my life. I killed a man: Orsilochus, son of Idomeneus, the fastest runner in all of broad Crete. He tried to rob me of the spoils I had carried home from Troy, the spoils I had suffered so much for, cutting my way through the wars of men and the bitter waves — all because, he said, I would not serve his father at Troy as his man, but led a company of my own. So I lay in wait for him by the road with one comrade, and as he came in from the fields at nightfall I ran him through with my bronze spear. The night was black; no one saw it; no one ever knew I had taken his life. Once he was dead I went down to a ship and begged some Phoenicians aboard — gave them a good share of my plunder — to carry me off and set me down at Pylos, or in Elis where the Epeians rule. But the wind blew them off their course, hard, however they fought it, and brought us here in the night. We rowed in any way we could, and though we were starving not a man of us thought of supper; we just stumbled ashore and lay down where we fell. I was worn out, and a sweet sleep took me at once. They lifted my goods from the ship and set them beside me here on the sand, and then they sailed away for Sidon — and left me here, sick at heart.”

So he spoke, and grey-eyed Athena smiled. She stroked him with her hand, and changed before his eyes into a woman, tall and beautiful, skilled in the loveliest work, and her words came warm and laughing.

“He would have to be a thief and a sharp dealer indeed,” she said, “who could get past you in any kind of trickery — even a god, if a god took you on. You incorrigible man — endlessly clever, never full of your own scheming. Even here, on your own soil, you will not lay down the lies and the cunning stories you love from the bottom of your heart. Enough — let it go. We are two of a kind, you and I, both old hands at this. Of all men alive you are far the best at laying plans and spinning words, and I am famous among all the gods for my wits and my craft. And still you did not know me — Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus — I, who stand beside you and guard you through every trouble, and who made all the Phaeacians love you so. I have come now to weave a plan with you, and to help you hide the treasure they sent you home with, and to tell you all the trials you must bear inside your own house. Endure them. You have no choice. And tell no one, man or woman, that you are home from your wandering. Bear every insult in silence, and let men do their worst.”

Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered her: “It is hard, goddess, for any mortal who meets you to know you, however much he knows of the world — you take so many shapes. But this I know well: you were good to me once, in the years we Greeks fought before Troy. Yet from the day we sacked Priam’s high city and went to our ships, and a god scattered the fleet of the Greeks — from that day, Athena, I never saw you, never once felt you come aboard my ship to ward off my grief. I wandered on with a broken heart until the gods set me free at last and I reached the rich land of the Phaeacians, where you put courage in me and led me into their town. Now, by your own father’s name, I beg you, tell me the truth — for I cannot believe I am really home in Ithaca. This is some other country, and you are toying with me, telling me what you do not mean, to make a fool of me. Tell me honestly: have I truly come home to my own land?”

Grey-eyed Athena answered: “That is always the turn your mind takes — and that is exactly why I cannot abandon you in your troubles. You are quick, and shrewd, and steady-minded. Any other man, home at last from such long wandering, would have rushed straight to his house to see his wife and children. But not you — you would rather hold back and test them all first, and put your own wife to the proof, your wife who sits in your halls, wasting away, weeping out the long days and nights. As for my not coming to you — I was never in doubt; I always knew in my heart you would come home, though you would lose every one of your men along the way. But I did not want to set myself against Poseidon, my father’s brother, who nursed his anger against you for blinding his own son. Come, then — I will show you the shape of the land, and you will believe me. This is the harbor of Phorcys, the old man of the sea; here at its head is the long-leaved olive, and close by, the shadowy, lovely cave sacred to the nymphs men call the Naiads — the same vaulted cave where you burned many a fine offering to them. And there, above, is the wooded mountain of Neriton.”

As she spoke the goddess scattered the mist, and the land stood clear. Then long-suffering Odysseus rejoiced, glad of his own country, and bent and kissed the grain-giving earth. At once he lifted his hands and prayed to the nymphs: “Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus — I never thought to see you again. Now I greet you with all my love, and I will bring you gifts as I did in the old days, if Zeus’s daughter, who drives the spoils of war, will be kind and let me live, and bring my dear son up to be a man.”

“Take heart,” said grey-eyed Athena. “Do not let that trouble you now. What matters first is to stow your treasure deep in the sacred cave, where it will be safe; then we will plan how all the rest may go best.”

With that the goddess went down into the shadowy cave to find the safest hiding-places, while Odysseus carried it all in — the gold, the bronze, the well-made clothing the Phaeacians had given him. They stowed it carefully away, and Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus who carries the storm-shield, set a stone across the mouth. Then the two of them sat down at the foot of the sacred olive and laid their plans for the death of the overweening suitors.

Grey-eyed Athena spoke first: “Laertes’ son, born of Zeus, Odysseus of the many schemes — think now how you will lay hands on these shameless men who have lorded it over your house three years, courting your faithful wife, pressing their gifts on her, while she longs only for you and weeps. She gives each of them hope, and sends each man his promise, but her heart is set on other things.”

Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered her: “To think of it — I would have died in my own house the wretched death of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, if you had not told me all of this in time, goddess. Come then, weave the plan that will pay them back. Stand at my side and breathe the same fierce courage into me as on the day we tore down the bright crown of Troy’s towers. Be with me now as you were then, grey-eyed one, and I would fight three hundred men at once — with you beside me, lady, and your help.”

“I will be with you,” said grey-eyed Athena. “I will not lose sight of you once we set our hands to this work — and I think more than one of these men who are eating up your living will spatter the wide floor with his blood and brains. But first I will so disguise you that no one will know you. I will shrivel the smooth skin on your supple limbs, strip the fair hair from your head, and dress you in rags that would make any man who saw you turn away. I will dim those fine eyes of yours, until you seem a wretched thing in the sight of all the suitors, and of your wife, and of the son you left at home. Then go first to the swineherd, the man who keeps your pigs. He has always been loyal to you, and he loves your son and your steady Penelope. You will find him out by the pigs, where they feed by Raven Rock and the spring of Arethusa, fattening on acorns and dark water, the things that put good fat on a pig. Stay with him there. Sit, and ask, and learn how everything stands, while I go to Sparta, to the land of lovely women, to call your son Telemachus home — for he went off to Lacedaemon, to Menelaus, to ask after you, to learn whether you were still alive.”

Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered her: “Then why did you not tell him, when your own mind knew it all? Was it so that he too should suffer, wandering the barren sea, while strangers devour his living?”

Grey-eyed Athena answered: “Do not trouble yourself too much about him. I sent him myself, so that he would win a good name for the going. He is in no hardship; he sits at ease in the house of Menelaus, with plenty of everything around him. True, there are young men lying in wait for him in a black ship, meaning to kill him before he reaches home — but I do not think they will. The earth will close over more than one of those who are eating up your living, before that happens.”

As she finished, Athena touched him with her wand. She shriveled the smooth skin on his supple limbs and stripped the fair hair from his head; she wrapped the skin of an old man over his whole body, and dimmed his two fine eyes. She threw a poor cloak about him and a ragged tunic, filthy and grimed with smoke, and over it the great worn hide of a swift deer; and she gave him a staff, and a battered wallet full of holes, slung from a twisted cord. So the two of them laid their plans, and then they parted — and the goddess went off to bright Lacedaemon to fetch the son of Odysseus home.

From the harbor Odysseus climbed the rough track up through the woods and over the shoulder of the hill, to the place where Athena had told him he would find the swineherd — the man who, of all the servants Odysseus owned, had cared the most faithfully for what was his. He found him sitting in front of his hut, in a high yard built where the eye could see far on every side. Eumaeus had raised it himself, spacious and trim, while his master was away — built it of stones he had hauled from the ground and topped with a hedge of thorn, with no word of it to Penelope or to old Laertes; and around the outside he had driven a stockade of split oak posts, set close together. Within he had made twelve sties, side by side, for the sows to lie in, fifty breeding sows penned in each. The boars slept outside, and there were far fewer of them now, for the suitors kept eating them down, and the swineherd had to send up the best he had, day after day, until only three hundred and sixty were left. Four dogs, savage as wolves, slept always among them, for the swineherd had reared them himself. Just then he was cutting himself a pair of sandals from a good stout oxhide. Three of his men were off herding the pigs at one station or another, and he had sent the fourth into town, driving a boar the suitors had forced out of him — for them to sacrifice and gorge their fill of meat.

When the dogs caught sight of Odysseus they came at him all at once, baying furiously. Odysseus had the wit to sit straight down and let the stick drop from his hand — and even so they would have torn him there, on his own land, had not the swineherd come pounding through the gate, the oxhide flung from his fingers, shouting and pelting them with stones until he had driven them off in every direction. Then he said to his master, not knowing him: "Old man, the dogs nearly made an end of you in a heartbeat, and the shame of it would have fallen on me. The gods have given me grief enough already, without that. Here I sit, mourning a master worth all the world, and fattening his pigs for other men to eat, while he — if he is alive at all and still sees the light — goes hungry in some far-off country. But come inside. When you have had your fill of bread and wine, then tell me where you are from and what you have suffered."

So the loyal swineherd led the way into the hut and had him sit down. He spread a thick bed of brushwood and threw over it the shaggy hide of a wild goat, the great rug he slept on himself, and Odysseus, glad of such a welcome, said: "May Zeus, my friend, and all the other gods grant you your heart's desire, for the warmth with which you have taken me in."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "Stranger, it would be wrong of me to turn away a guest, even one poorer than you — for every stranger, every beggar, comes to us from Zeus. What I can give is little, but it is given gladly; that is how it is with servants, who live in fear when young lords are over them. The gods have held back the man who would have been good to me — who would have given me a holding of my own, a house, a piece of land, a wife men would court — all that a generous master grants a servant who has worked hard for him, and whose work the gods have prospered, as they have prospered mine in this place. If my master had grown old here, he would have done great things for me. But he is gone. I wish the whole breed of Helen had been wiped from the earth — she has cut the knees from under so many good men. It was that quarrel that took my master off to Ilium, the land of fine horses, to fight the Trojans for Agamemnon."

With that he hitched up his tunic and went out to the sties where the young sucking-pigs were penned. He picked two, brought them back, and killed them; he singed them, cut them up, ran the pieces onto spits, and when the meat was roasted he carried it in and set it before Odysseus, hot, still on the spit, and scattered white barley meal over it. Then he mixed wine in a bowl of ivy-wood, sat down facing him, and told him to fall to.

"Eat, stranger," he said, "such as a servant has to offer — sucking-pig. The fat hogs go to the suitors, who eat without shame and without a thought for the gods' anger.
