But the blessed gods love no such deeds; they honor fair dealing and the right. Even the cruelest raiders, who fall on another man's land and carry off plunder that Zeus lets them keep — even they, once their ships are full and they are home again, feel the cold dread of judgment settle on them. But these men here must have heard some god whisper that Odysseus is dead and will not come back; that is why they will not court his wife honestly, in their own homes, but sit on here, devouring his house at their leisure, sparing nothing. Every single day and night that Zeus sends down, they slaughter — not one beast, not two, but more — and they drain his wine like water, for he was a rich man, richer than any other, on the mainland or here in Ithaca. No twenty men together had wealth to match his. Let me tell you what he had: twelve herds of cattle on the mainland, as many flocks of sheep, as many droves of pigs, and as many sprawling herds of goats, kept by his own men and by hired hands. And here on Ithaca eleven wide-ranging herds of goats graze the far end of the island, in the charge of good herdsmen — and every one of those men drives the best goat of his flock to the suitors, day after day. And I, who watch over the pigs you see, I keep choosing out the best of them and sending it up to them too."

So he spoke, while Odysseus ate and drank, ravenous and silent, brooding all the while on the suitors and their ruin. When he had eaten his fill, the swineherd filled with wine the very cup he drank from and handed it to him, and Odysseus took it gladly and spoke to him, his words flying: "My friend, who was this master of yours, who bought you and owned you — so rich, you say, so powerful? You tell me he died for Agamemnon's sake. Tell me his name; I may have met such a man somewhere. Zeus knows, and the other gods, but I have wandered far, and I may have word of him."

The swineherd, that leader of men, answered: "Old man, no wanderer who comes here with news of him will ever make his wife or his son believe it. Tramps in need of food and lodging come full of lies, and not one of them cares for the truth. Every drifter who lands on Ithaca goes straight to my mistress with his stories, and she takes him in and makes much of him and questions him on every point, while the tears run down her cheeks, as a woman's will when her husband is lost far away. You too, old man, could soon stitch together a fine tale, if someone would give you a cloak and a shirt for it. No — by now the dogs and the swift birds have surely stripped the flesh from his bones, or the fish have eaten him in the sea, and his bones lie heaped on some beach, buried deep in the sand. He is dead and gone, and grief is all he has left his friends — me most of all. Wherever I go I will never find so kind a master again, not even if I went back to my own father and mother, in the land where I was born and raised. And I do not grieve for them as I grieve for him — though I long to lay eyes on them again in my own country. No, it is Odysseus, gone from us, that I ache for; I can hardly bring myself to say his name, stranger, he is not here, and yet he loved me and cared for me so well that I call him the master of my heart, far away as he is."

Then long-suffering Odysseus answered him: "My friend, since you are so set against it, so sure in your heart that he will never come home, I will not merely say it — I will swear it: Odysseus is coming back. And pay me for the news only when he stands here in his house; then give me a good cloak and shirt to wear. Till then I will take nothing, for all my need — for I hate, like the gates of death itself, the man who lets his poverty drive him to lies. Now I call Zeus to witness, first of the gods, and this table of guest-friendship, and the hearth of Odysseus that I have come to: everything will fall out as I tell you. Within this very year Odysseus will be here — as this moon dies and the next one rises, he will come home and take his revenge on every man who is dishonoring his wife and his son."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "Old man, I will never pay you for that news, and Odysseus will never come home. Drink your wine in peace, and let us turn to something else. Don't keep bringing this back to me; it stabs at my heart whenever anyone speaks of my honored master. We will let your oath be. But I do wish he would come — as Penelope wishes it, and old Laertes, and godlike Telemachus. It is the boy I grieve for now, Odysseus's son. The gods were raising him like a young tree, and I thought he would grow to be no worse a man than his father, in build and in face — but some god, or some man, has unsettled his wits, and he has gone off to sacred Pylos after news of his father, while the proud suitors lie in ambush for his voyage home, hoping to wipe the name of Arceisius clean off the earth, out of Ithaca forever. But let him go — let him be taken, or let him slip past them, if the hand of Zeus is held over him to keep him safe. And now, old man, tell me your own troubles. Tell me the truth, so I may know it well: who are you, and where do you come from? Where is your city, your family? What ship brought you here, and how did the crew land you on Ithaca, and who did they claim to be? For you surely did not come on foot."

Then resourceful Odysseus answered him: "I will tell you the whole of it, plainly. If only we had food and wine enough to last, and could sit here at our ease in the hut, feasting in quiet while others did the work — I could talk for a whole year and not come to the end of all the sorrows the gods have laid on me.

"I am a Cretan by birth. My father was a man of substance, with many true-born sons by his wife, but I was the son of a bought woman, a slave he kept for his bed. Still, Castor son of Hylax — that was my father, a man the Cretans honored like a god for his wealth, his good fortune, and his fighting sons — he raised me no differently from his lawful children. But when death carried him down to the house of Hades, his proud sons divided the estate and cast lots for their shares, and they handed me almost nothing, only a roof and a scrap of land. Yet by my own worth I married into a wealthy family, for I was no fool and no coward in war. All that is past me now — but look at the stubble and you can guess the standing grain; hard times enough have stripped me bare. Ares and Athena had made me brave and gave me the nerve to break a battle line. When I picked my best men for an ambush, sowing the seeds of the enemy's ruin, I never once thought of death; I would be the first to leap out and run my spear through any man who could not outrun me. That was the sort of soldier I was. But farm work was never to my taste, nor the quiet of a settled house where children are raised. What I loved were the oared ships and the wars, the polished javelins and the arrows — grim things, that make other men shudder. But one man loves one thing, another loves another; this was the life the gods turned my heart to. Before the Greeks ever sailed for Troy, I had nine times led men and ships against foreign coasts, and great wealth came to me from it — I took my pick of the plunder first, and much more fell to me by lot afterward. My house grew quickly, and I became a man feared and respected among the Cretans.

"But when far-seeing Zeus devised that terrible voyage, the one that loosened the knees of so many men, then the people called on me and on famous Idomeneus to lead the ships to Ilium, and there was no refusing — the weight of the people's blame would have crushed us. There we Greeks fought nine long years, and in the tenth we sacked the city of Priam and sailed for home, and a god scattered us over the sea. Then Zeus in his wisdom set sorrow in my path. Just one month I stayed, taking my joy in my children, my wife, and all I had. After that the longing came on me to fit out ships and make a raid on Egypt, with a good crew. I manned nine ships, and the men flocked to fill them. For six days my trusty companions feasted, and I gave them many victims, both to sacrifice to the gods and to make their own meal; on the seventh we put out from Crete and ran before a fair, fresh North Wind, as easy as a boat going downstream. Not one ship was harmed; we sat at our ease, unhurt and well, and let the wind and the steersmen hold our course. On the fifth day we reached the flowing river of Egypt, and there I anchored my curved ships. I told my faithful crews to stay by the ships and guard them, and I sent scouts ahead to high points to spy out the land.

"But my men gave way to their own reckless greed. They fell at once upon the rich Egyptian fields, carrying off the women and little children and cutting down the men. The cry of it ran swiftly to the city, and at the first light of dawn the people came pouring out, until the whole plain was full of footmen and horsemen and the glitter of bronze. Then Zeus who delights in thunder broke my men in panic; not one of them dared stand and face the enemy, for ruin had closed in on every side. There the Egyptians killed many of us with the sharp bronze, and led the rest off alive, to slave for them. But Zeus himself put a thought into my mind — and how I wish I had died there in Egypt instead, met my fate then, for worse was still waiting for me. I tore the well-made helmet from my head, slid the shield from my shoulder, dropped the spear from my hand, and ran straight out in front of the king's chariot. I caught his knees and kissed them, and he took pity, and spared me; he lifted me weeping into his own chariot and brought me home. Many of his men charged at me with their ash spears, raging to cut me down, but he held them off, in fear of the wrath of Zeus, the protector of strangers, who above all the gods is angry at cruelty.

"There I stayed seven years, and gathered a great store of wealth among the Egyptians, for every man gave me something. But when the eighth year came round, there arrived a certain Phoenician, a greedy, scheming rogue, a man who had already done the world much harm, and with his smooth tongue he talked me into sailing with him to Phoenicia, where his house and his property lay. I stayed there with him a full year. But when the months and the days had run their course and the seasons came round again to the same point, he put me aboard a ship bound for Libya — telling me a lie, that I was to help him carry a cargo there, but really meaning to sell me off and pocket a great price for me. I went with him, for all my suspicions; there was nothing else I could do.

"The ship ran before a fair, fresh North Wind, out over the open water above Crete, and Zeus plotted the death of every man aboard. For once we had left Crete behind and could see nothing but sky and sea, the son of Kronos hung a black cloud over the hollow ship, and the water went dark beneath it. Then Zeus thundered and hurled his bolt full into the ship, and she reeled and shuddered, struck by the lightning, and the air filled with the reek of sulfur. The men were flung out into the sea; black-hulled and helpless, they were swept past the ship on the swell like sea-crows on the waves, and the god took from them their day of homecoming. But Zeus himself put the ship's great mast into my hands, even in the depth of my despair, so that I might yet escape destruction. I wrapped my arms around it and drifted before the deadly winds. Nine days I drifted; on the tenth, in the black of night, a great rolling wave carried me to the land of the Thesprotians. There their king, the hero Pheidon, took me in and asked no payment, for his own son came on me, broken with cold and exhaustion, and raised me up by the hand and led me to his father's house, where they gave me a cloak and a shirt to wear.

"And there it was I first heard of Odysseus. The king told me he had given him welcome and a guest's honor, on his way home to his own land. He showed me, too, the treasure Odysseus had gathered — bronze and gold and worked iron — enough to keep a man's house for ten generations, so great was the store he had left in the halls of King Pheidon. As for the man himself, the king said he had gone to Dodona, to learn the will of Zeus from the god's great oak with its high crown of leaves — to ask whether, after so long an absence, he should come home to Ithaca openly, or in secret. And the king swore to me, pouring the wine of an oath in his own house, that the ship was launched and the crew standing ready to carry Odysseus to his own country. But he sent me off first, for it happened that a Thesprotian ship was sailing for Dulichium, that island rich in wheat, and he ordered the crew to bring me safe to King Acastus.

"But those men chose instead a wicked plan against me, to sink me into the very pit of misery. When the ship had run well out from land, they set about making a slave of me. They stripped off the cloak and shirt I wore and threw me these filthy rags you see me in now. And toward evening, when they came to the fields of sunlit Ithaca, they lashed me fast in the ship's hull with a stout twisted rope and went ashore for their supper by the water. But the gods themselves loosed my bonds with ease. I wound my rags about my head, slid down the smooth steering-oar, lowered my chest into the sea, and struck out, rowing with both hands, until I was well clear of them and came ashore where the trees stood thick. There I crouched low and hid, while they ran searching with great cries; but when it seemed no use to hunt any further, they went back to the hollow ship. So the gods themselves hid me, with no trouble at all, and led me here, to the steading of a wise man's door — for it seems my time to die has not yet come."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "Poor unlucky stranger — you have stirred my heart, telling me all this, the long tale of your sufferings and your wanderings. But there is one part of it that does not ring true, and you will never get me to believe it: what you said about Odysseus. Why should a man like you tell such an empty lie? I know the truth of my master's homecoming for myself — that the gods, every one of them, hated him; for they did not let him fall at Troy, or die in the arms of his friends once the fighting was done. The whole Greek army would have raised him a mound, and he would have won great glory for his son in days to come. Instead the storm-winds have snatched him away, and no man knows where.

"As for me, I keep clear of all that, here with my pigs. I never go down to the town unless wise Penelope sends for me, when some traveler brings word. Then they crowd around the man and question him — both those who ache for the long-lost king, and those who are glad to eat his house up for nothing. But I gave up asking such questions long ago, ever since an Aetolian fooled me with a tale. He had killed a man and wandered far over the earth, and at last he came to my hut, and I gave him a kind welcome. He swore he had seen Odysseus among the Cretans, with Idomeneus, repairing the ships a storm had wrecked, and said he would be home by summer, or by harvest-time, with all his men and a great mass of wealth. So you too, unlucky old man, since some god has brought you to my door — do not try to win me with these stories, do not soothe me with empty hopes. It is not for any such reason that I will honor you and treat you well, but out of fear of Zeus, the god of strangers, and out of pity for you yourself."

Then resourceful Odysseus answered him: "You have a heart that is hard to convince, I see. Even my oath could not win you over; you will not believe. Well then, let us strike a bargain, and let the gods on Olympus be our witnesses. If your master comes home to this house, you will give me a cloak and a shirt and send me on to Dulichium, where I want to go. But if he does not come, as I say he will, then set your men on me and fling me from the top of that great cliff — so the next beggar will think twice before going about with lies."

And the loyal swineherd answered him: "Stranger, a fine name for goodness and decency I would win for myself, now and ever after, if I first took you into my hut and gave you a welcome, and then turned and killed you and tore the dear life out of you. I would have to pray to Zeus, son of Kronos, with a clean conscience after that. But it is suppertime now, and I hope my men will be in soon, so we can cook a good supper here in the hut."

While they were talking, the swineherds came up driving the pigs, and shut them into their pens for the night, and a tremendous squealing rose as the sows were herded into their sties. Then the loyal swineherd called to his men: "Bring in the best of the boars, so I can sacrifice it for this stranger from far away — and we will get some good of it ourselves, who have toiled so long over these pigs while other men devour what our labor earns, and pay nothing."

With that he split firewood with the pitiless bronze, while the others led in a fat five-year-old boar and stood it by the hearth. The swineherd did not forget the immortals, for his heart was sound; he began by cutting bristles from the head of the white-tusked boar and throwing them into the fire, and he prayed to all the gods that Odysseus might come home again. Then he struck the boar with a billet of oak he had kept back from the splitting, and it dropped, and the others cut its throat and singed it and quickly carved it up. The swineherd laid raw strips from every limb on a coat of fat, sprinkled them with barley meal, and threw them on the fire; the rest they sliced small, spitted, roasted carefully, drew off the spits, and heaped on platters. Then the swineherd stood to share it out, for he was a fair-minded man, and divided the whole into seven portions: one he set aside, with a prayer, for the nymphs and for Hermes, son of Maia; the rest he dealt out to each man there. And he honored Odysseus with the long cuts of the chine, the back of the white-tusked boar, and gladdened his master's heart, so that resourceful Odysseus spoke up: "Eumaeus, may you be as dear to Father Zeus as you are to me, for honoring a wretch like me with the best you have."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "Eat, my strange friend, and take what pleasure you can in what is set before you. The god gives one thing and holds back another, just as he pleases in his heart — for he can do all things."

With that he made a burnt offering of the first cuts to the everlasting gods, poured a libation of gleaming wine, set the cup in the hands of Odysseus the sacker of cities, and sat down to his own share. Mesaulius set out the bread — a man the swineherd had bought for himself while his master was away, with his own goods, telling neither his mistress nor old Laertes, paying for him out of the Taphians' hands. So they reached out to the good things spread before them, and when they had put away all desire for food and drink, Mesaulius cleared away the bread, and they made for their beds, heavy and content with the feast.

Now the night came on, cruel and moonless. Zeus rained the whole night through, and a great West Wind blew, the wind that always brings wet. So Odysseus, to test the swineherd — to see whether the man who cared for him so well would strip off his own cloak and give it to him, or order one of his men to — said: "Listen to me now, Eumaeus, and all of you. I will tell you something, with a boast in it; it is the wine that draws me on, the heady wine, which sets even a steady man singing and laughing softly, and stirs him up to dance, and lets slip a word that had been better left unsaid. But I have started, so I will speak it out. I wish I were still young and my strength unbroken, as I was the day we laid an ambush below the walls of Troy. Odysseus and Menelaus led it, and I was a third in command, for they themselves chose me. When we had come up under the steep wall of the city, we crouched in the marsh among the dense reeds and brush, hunched under our shields. The night turned bitter as the North Wind came down, and snow fell on us cold as frost, and the ice crusted thick on our shields. The others all had cloaks and shirts and slept soundly enough, their shields drawn up over their shoulders; but I, like a fool, had left my cloak with my men when I set out, never thinking I would be cold, and I had come along with nothing but my shield and a bright kilt. When the night was two-thirds gone and the stars had wheeled on past their height, I nudged Odysseus, lying close beside me, with my elbow, and he came awake at once.

"'Odysseus,' I whispered, 'royal son of Laertes, man of many turns — I will not be much longer among the living. This cold is killing me. I have no cloak; some god tricked me into coming with only my shirt, and now there is no escape.'

"That was what I said, and the thought came to him at once — for he was a man who was never at a loss, in fighting or in counsel. He spoke low, with his mouth close to my ear: 'Quiet now, in case some other of the Greeks should hear you.' Then he propped his head on his elbow and called out: 'Listen, my friends. A dream from the gods came to me in my sleep. We have gone too far from the ships. I wish someone would go and tell Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, to send more men up here to us from the camp.'

"At that, Thoas, son of Andraemon, sprang up at once, flung off his purple cloak, and went running toward the ships — and I lay down in his cloak, glad of it, and slept warm until Dawn came on her golden throne. I wish I were as young now, my strength as whole, as I was then; then one of you swineherds would lend me a cloak in this steading, both for kindness and for the respect owed a good fighting man. As it is, men look down on me for the poor rags on my back."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "Old man, that was a fine story you told, and not a word of it wasted or off the mark. So you shall lack neither clothing nor anything else that a hard-pressed suppliant has a right to ask — for tonight. But in the morning you must shake your own rags about you again, for we have no spare cloaks and shirts to hand out here; each man has only the one. When Odysseus's own dear son comes home, he will give you a cloak and a shirt and send you wherever your heart is set on going."

With that he rose and made up a bed for Odysseus close to the fire, throwing down the skins of sheep and goats, and Odysseus lay down on it, and Eumaeus spread over him a great thick cloak that he kept by for a change, to put on when the weather turned truly foul. So Odysseus slept there, and the young men slept beside him. But the swineherd would not lie down to rest away from his pigs, and he made ready to go out — and Odysseus's heart warmed to see how well the man looked after his master's goods, even with his master gone. First Eumaeus slung the sharp sword over his broad shoulders, then wrapped himself in a thick cloak against the wind, took up the skin of a great well-fed goat, and caught up a sharp javelin, to keep off dogs and men. Then he went out to lie down where his white-tusked boars were sleeping, under a hollow rock that gave them shelter from the North Wind.

[Trans. note: This is the only part of the Odyssey where Homer turns from the stranger to address a character directly — "And you answered him, Eumaeus" — speaking to the swineherd by name as if he stood in the room. The Lectio Edition keeps the device rather than smoothing it to ordinary narration; it is Homer's quiet sign of tenderness toward the one humble, faithful man in the poem.]

Meanwhile Athena went to the fair city of Sparta, to tell the son of Odysseus that it was time to come home. She found Telemachus and Pisistratus bedded down in the forecourt of Menelaus's house. Pisistratus was deep in sleep, but Telemachus could find no rest the whole night through, lying awake with his thoughts running on his lost father. Athena came and stood close over him and said:

"Telemachus, you should not be wandering so far from home any longer, leaving your goods behind and such insolent men loose in your house. Be careful they do not divide everything you own among themselves and eat it up, and your whole journey come to nothing. Press Menelaus to send you off at once, while you can still find your faithful mother under your own roof. Her father and her brothers are already urging her to marry Eurymachus, who is outbidding every other suitor with his gifts, piling up the bride-price higher and higher. See that she carries nothing valuable out of the house against your will. You know how a woman's heart is: once she marries again, she sets herself to build up the house of her new husband, and forgets the children of the man she loved before, and the husband himself, now that he is dead — she no longer remembers him or cares. So go home, and put all you have in the charge of the most trustworthy of your women, until the gods show you a wife of your own. And there is one more thing you must take to heart. The chief men among the suitors are lying in wait for you in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Same, meaning to kill you before you can reach home. But I do not think they will. Sooner than that, the earth will close over some of the very men who are now eating up your house. Keep your good ship well clear of the islands, and sail on through the night; the god who watches over you will send a wind at your back. And the moment you touch Ithaca, send your ship and your crew on to the town, but go yourself, first of all, to the swineherd who keeps your pigs. He is loyal to you. Pass the night there with him, and send him into the town to tell Penelope you are home from Pylos, safe and sound."
With that she went back to Olympus. Telemachus dug his heel into Pisistratus to wake him, and said, "Up, Pisistratus, son of Nestor — yoke the horses to the chariot. We have to be on our way."

But Pisistratus answered, "Telemachus, in whatever hurry we may be, we cannot drive through the dark. It will be daybreak before long. Wait until Menelaus, that great spearman, has brought his gifts and set them in the chariot, and sent us off with a kind word. A guest remembers all his days the host who showed him friendship."

As he spoke, Dawn came up on her golden throne, and Menelaus, who had already risen and left Helen's side, came toward them. When Telemachus saw him, he pulled on his shirt in haste, threw his great cloak around his shoulders, and went out to meet him. "Menelaus," he said, "royal son of Atreus, let me go back now to my own country. My heart aches to be home."

And Menelaus answered, "Telemachus, I will not keep you against your will, since you are set on going. I have no patience with a host who fawns on his guest beyond all measure, nor with one who is cold to him — the right way lies between. It is just as wrong to push a man out the door when he wants to stay as to hold him back when he longs to go. Treat your guest well while he is under your roof, and speed him on when he wishes to leave. Only wait until I have brought you fine gifts and laid them in the chariot for you to see with your own eyes, and I will have the women set out a good meal from what we have in the house. There is honor in it, and good sense too — a man should eat before he sets out on so long a road. And if you have a mind to make a circuit through Hellas, or down through the Peloponnese, I will yoke my own horses and be your guide through every town. No one will send us away empty-handed; each will give us something to carry off — a bronze tripod, or a cauldron, a pair of mules, or a cup of gold."

"Menelaus," Telemachus replied, "I want to go straight home. When I sailed I left no one to guard what is mine, and I am afraid that while I hunt for my father I will lose my own life, or come back to find some treasure of mine gone from the house."

When Menelaus heard that, he told his wife and her women at once to set out a good meal from what was in the house. Then Eteoneus, son of Boethous, came in, just risen from his bed nearby, and Menelaus told him to light the fire and roast the meat, and he did as he was told. Menelaus himself went down to his fragrant, vaulted storeroom — not alone; Helen went with him, and Megapenthes. When they came to the place where his treasures were kept, he chose a two-handled cup for himself to give, and told his son Megapenthes to carry up a mixing-bowl of silver. Helen went to the chests where she kept the embroidered robes she had made with her own hands, and lifted out the one that was largest and richest in its needlework. It shimmered like a star, and it had lain at the very bottom of all the rest. Then they came back through the house to Telemachus, and Menelaus said: "Telemachus, may Zeus, the loud-thundering lord of Hera, bring you home to your heart's desire. Of all the treasures stored in my house, I give you the finest and the most precious. I give you this mixing-bowl, worked all of silver, its rim finished in gold — the work of Hephaestus's own hands. Phaedimus, the hero, king of the Sidonians, gave it to me when his house took me in on my way home. And now I would have it be yours."
With that he placed the two-handled cup in Telemachus's hands, while strong Megapenthes set the gleaming silver bowl before him, and fair Helen came near, the robe ready in her arms.

"I too have a gift for you, dear child," she said, "to remember the hands of Helen by — for your bride to wear on the day of your wedding. Until then let your mother keep it in her own room. And may you come with joy to your strong house and your own native land."

So she put the robe in his hands, and he took it gladly. Pisistratus laid the gifts in the basket of the chariot, gazing at each in wonder. Then Menelaus led the two of them indoors, and they took their seats on benches and chairs. A maidservant poured water for their hands from a fine golden jug into a silver basin, and drew up a polished table beside them. The grave housekeeper set out bread and many good things, giving freely of all she had, while Eteoneus carved the meat and served their portions and the son of Menelaus poured the wine. So they reached out for the good things spread before them, and when they had put away all desire for food and drink, Telemachus and the splendid son of Nestor yoked the horses, mounted the inlaid chariot, and drove out through the gateway and the echoing colonnade. Menelaus came after them, gold cup in his right hand, brimming with wine, so they might pour an offering before they went. He stood before the horses and drank their health: "Farewell to you both, young men, and give my greeting to Nestor, shepherd of the people — for he was as kind to me as a father, all the years we Greeks were fighting at Troy."

"We will be sure," said wise Telemachus, "to tell him every word of it the moment we see him, royal son of Atreus. And I wish I were as certain of finding Odysseus home again when I reach Ithaca, so I could tell him how warmly you received me, and show him all the fine gifts I carry away."

Even as he spoke, a bird flew past on the right — an eagle, with a great white goose in its talons, a tame one snatched up from the yard, and the men and women came running and shouting behind it. The eagle drew close and swept off to the right, in front of the horses, and at the sight of it their spirits lifted and the heart grew glad in every breast. Then Pisistratus, son of Nestor, spoke first: "Tell us, Menelaus, royal son of Atreus — has the god sent this sign for us, or for you?"

Menelaus, dear to Ares, turned it over in his mind, searching for the right and fitting word — but Helen, in her long robes, was too quick for him. "Hear me," she said, "and I will read it as the gods have put it in my heart, and as I believe it will come to pass. As this eagle came down from the mountain where it was bred and where its nestlings are, and seized the goose that was fattened in the house, so Odysseus, after long wandering and much suffering, will come home and take his revenge — or perhaps he is home already, and even now sowing ruin for every one of the suitors."
"May Zeus, the loud-thundering lord of Hera, grant it so," said Telemachus. "If he does, I will pray to you as I would to a god, all my days at home."

With that he laid the whip to the horses, and they sprang forward at a gallop through the town and out into open country. All day long they kept the yoke shaking on their necks, until the sun went down and the roads grew dark. Then they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles, son of Ortilochus, whose father was Alpheus, and there they slept the night, and he gave them a guest's welcome. When Dawn came with her rose-red fingers, they yoked the horses again, mounted the inlaid chariot, and drove out through the gateway and the echoing colonnade. Pisistratus touched the horses with the whip, and they flew on, glad to run, and soon came in sight of the high citadel of Pylos. Then Telemachus said:

"Pisistratus, will you do this one thing I ask of you, and promise it? We can claim a friendship that runs back to our fathers; we are of the same age; and this journey has bound us closer still. So do not carry me past my ship, son of Nestor — set me down there. If you take me to your father's house, his kindness will keep me, for he will press me to stay against my will, and I have to get home without delay."

Pisistratus thought it over in his heart, how best to do as he was asked, and in the end he judged it wisest to turn the horses toward the swift ship on the shore. There he set down the fine gifts in the stern — the gold and the woven cloth that Menelaus had given. Then he urged Telemachus on: "Go aboard now, quickly, and tell your men the same, before I can reach home and bring my father word. I know him too well in my heart: he will never let it rest. He will come down here himself to fetch you, and I tell you, he will not go back empty-handed. He will take it hard."

With that he drove his fine-maned horses back to the city of the Pylians, and soon reached home. And Telemachus called his men together and gave the order: "Set everything in order aboard the ship, men, and let us be on our way." So he spoke, and they listened and obeyed; quickly they went aboard and took their places at the oars.

But while Telemachus was busy at this, pouring an offering and praying to Athena in the stern, there came up to him a man from a far country — a seer, in flight out of Argos, for he had killed a man. He was of the line of Melampus, who had once lived in Pylos, the land of flocks; a rich man, with a great house among the Pylians, until he was driven into exile by Neleus, the proudest of living men, who seized his wealth and held it a full year by force. All that year Melampus lay a prisoner in the halls of Phylacus, suffering bitter pains, for the sake of the daughter of Neleus and the heavy madness a goddess, the dread Fury, had laid upon his heart. But he came through it with his life, drove the lowing cattle from Phylace to Pylos, paid back proud Neleus for the wrong, and won the woman as a bride for his brother. Then he left for another country, for horse-pasturing Argos — for it was fated he should live there and rule over many. There he married, built his high-roofed house, and fathered two strong sons, Antiphates and Mantius. Antiphates fathered great-hearted Oicles, and Oicles fathered Amphiaraus, rouser of armies, whom both Zeus and Apollo loved with all manner of love. Yet he never crossed the threshold of old age, but died at Thebes, betrayed for a woman's bribe. His sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus. Mantius fathered Polypheides and Cleitus. Golden-throned Dawn carried off Cleitus for his beauty, to dwell among the immortals; and Apollo made noble-hearted Polypheides the finest prophet of all mankind, now that Amphiaraus was dead. He quarreled with his father and went away to Hyperesia, and there he made his home and prophesied to all.

It was this man's son, Theoclymenus by name, who now came and stood before Telemachus as he poured his offering and prayed by the black ship. "Friend," he said, "since I find you making sacrifice in this place, I beg you, by these offerings and by the god you make them to, and by your own life and the lives of the men who follow you — tell me the truth, and hide nothing. Who are you, and where do you come from? Where is your city, and who are your people?"

And wise Telemachus answered, "Stranger, I will tell you the whole truth. I am from Ithaca, and my father is Odysseus — if ever such a man lived. But by now he has met some wretched end. That is why I have taken these men and this black ship, and gone in search of word of my father, so long away."

Then Theoclymenus, godlike man, answered him: "I too am far from my own land, an exile, for I killed a man of my own people. He has many brothers and kinsmen in Argos, the land where horses graze, and great is their power among the Greeks. To escape death at their hands, I am running for my life, doomed now to wander the earth. Take me aboard your ship, for I come to you a fugitive and a suppliant — do not let them kill me. I am sure they are on my track."
"I will not turn you away from my good ship, if you wish to come," said wise Telemachus. "Come, then, and in Ithaca you shall have such welcome as we can give."

With that he took Theoclymenus's bronze spear and laid it along the deck of the curved ship, then went aboard himself and sat down in the stern, and had Theoclymenus sit beside him. The men cast off the stern cables, and Telemachus called to them to lay hold of the rigging, and they bent to it briskly. They stepped the pine mast in its socket in the cross-beam, made it fast with the forestays, and hauled up the white sail with twisted oxhide ropes. And Athena sent them a fair wind, blowing keen and strong out of the high air, so the ship might run her swiftest course over the salt sea. So they passed Crouni and the fair streams of Chalcis.

The sun went down, and the roads of the world grew dark. The ship ran on toward Pheae, driven hard by the wind of Zeus, and on past bright Elis, where the Epeans hold sway. From there Telemachus steered for the Pointed Isles, his heart hanging between escape and capture.

Meanwhile Odysseus and the loyal swineherd were taking their supper in the hut, and the other men supped with them. When they had put away all desire for food and drink, Odysseus began to test the swineherd — to see whether he would still treat him with such warmth and press him to stay at the steading, or send him off to the town. So he said:

"Listen to me now, Eumaeus, and all of you. In the morning I mean to be gone, to go down and beg through the town, so as to be no more burden to you or your men. Give me your good advice, then, and a guide to set me on the road. Once I am there I will have to make my own way, going door to door, in hope that someone will give me a cup and a crust. I would go to the house of Odysseus too, and carry word to wise Penelope, and mingle with the overweening suitors, to see whether out of all that plenty they might give a man a meal. I would do whatever work they wanted, and do it well. For let me tell you — and mark it — by the grace of Hermes the guide, who lends beauty and a good name to the labor of every man's hands, there is no one alive who could match me as a servant: at laying fresh logs on a steady fire, at splitting dry kindling, at carving and roasting meat, at pouring the wine — all the work that lesser men do for their betters."

It troubled you to the heart to hear this, Eumaeus, swineherd, and you said: "Friend, what in the world put such a notion into your head? You are bent on getting yourself killed outright, if you mean to go in among that crowd of suitors, whose violence and arrogance reach the iron sky. They take no men like you to serve them. Their servants are young, and well turned out in fine cloaks and shirts, with their hair always sleek and their faces handsome; and the polished tables groan with bread and meat and wine. No — stay here with us. No one finds you a trouble, not I, nor any of my men. And when the dear son of Odysseus comes home, he will give you a cloak and a shirt for your back and send you wherever your heart is set on going."

Then long-suffering Odysseus answered him: "Eumaeus, may you be as dear to Father Zeus as you are to me, for sparing me the misery of the road and its hard living — there is nothing worse for a man than wandering. Still, it is the cruel belly that drives men to all their wretched troubles, the man who knows want and grief and the long road. But now, since you keep me here and bid me wait for the young master, tell me about the mother of godlike Odysseus, and his father, whom he left on the threshold of old age when he sailed for Troy. Are they still alive and looking on the light of the sun? Or are they dead now, and gone down into the house of Hades?"

And the swineherd, that leader of men, answered: "I will tell you the whole truth of it. Laertes is still living, but day after day he prays the gods to let the life slip out of his body in his own house, for he grieves without end for his son gone away, and for the wise wife he married, whose death wounded him most of all and brought old age upon him before his time. She died of sorrow for her glorious son — a cruel way to die; may no friend of mine who has dealt kindly by me come to such an end. As long as she lived, for all her grief, it was a comfort to me to go and ask after her, because she raised me herself, alongside her own daughter, long-robed Ctimene, the youngest child she bore. We grew up side by side, and she gave me almost the same honor she gave her own. But when we both came to the age that all of us long for, they married Ctimene to a man in Same and were paid a great bride-price for her; and as for me, my mistress dressed me well, in a fine cloak and shirt, with sandals for my feet, and sent me out to the farm — yet she loved me more than ever in her heart. All that is gone from me now. But the blessed gods have made my work prosper here, in the place I tend; I have enough to eat and drink, and to share with anyone worth honoring. From my mistress, though, there is no kind word to be had these days, and no kind deed, now that ruin has fallen on the house and arrogant men are in it. Servants long to speak with their mistress face to face, and learn how things stand, and eat and drink in the hall, and carry a little something back to the country with them — the kind of thing that warms a servant's heart."

Then resourceful Odysseus answered him: "Strange, then — you must have been only a small child, Eumaeus, when you were carried so far from your home and your parents. Tell me, and tell me the truth. Was it that the broad-streeted city your father and mother lived in was sacked and overthrown? Or did enemies catch you alone among the sheep or the cattle, run you down to the ships, and sell you off to the master of this house, who paid them a fair price for you?"

And the swineherd, that leader of men, answered: "Stranger, since you ask me this, then sit quiet, take your ease, and drink your wine, and listen. The nights now are endless. There is time for sleep, and time to sit up and take pleasure in talk; you have no need to go to bed before the hour — too much sleep is a weariness too. As for the rest, let any man whose heart bids him go off and sleep, and at first light eat his breakfast and follow the master's pigs out to pasture. But the two of us will sit here in the hut, eating and drinking and easing our hearts with the memory of each other's hard sorrows — for a man who has suffered much and wandered far comes in time to take a strange pleasure in his griefs once they are well behind him. Now, here is the answer to what you ask.

"There is an island called Syrie — you may have heard the name — out beyond Ortygia, there where the sun turns. It is not thickly settled, but the soil is good: rich in cattle and in sheep, full of wine, deep in wheat. Famine never comes to those people, nor any of the hateful sicknesses that fall on us poor mortals; but when the men of the city grow old, Apollo of the silver bow comes with Artemis, and brings them down with his painless arrows. There are two cities on it, and the whole land is divided between them, and over both of them my father was king — Ctesius, son of Ormenus, a man like the immortals.

"To that island there came one day some Phoenicians, famous seafarers, but greedy men, with a black ship full of trinkets and trumpery. Now there was a Phoenician woman in my father's house, tall and beautiful and skilled at fine work, and these sly Phoenicians led her astray. One of them lay with her by the hollow ship while she was washing clothes, and turned her heart with smooth words — the kind of thing that bends even an honest woman's mind. Then he asked her who she was and where she came from, and she pointed to my father's high-roofed house and said: 'I am proud to say I come from Sidon, rich in bronze, and I am the daughter of Arybas, a man rolling in wealth. But Taphian pirates snatched me up one day as I came in from the fields, and carried me here over the sea, and sold me to the master of this house, who paid them a good price for me.'

"Then the man who had lain with her said: 'Would you like to come home with us now, and see the high house of your father and mother again, and your parents themselves? For they are still alive, and they are spoken of as rich.'
"And the woman answered: 'I would, if you sailors will first swear me a solemn oath to bring me home unharmed.'

"So she spoke, and they all swore it as she asked. When they had sworn and finished the oath, the woman spoke again: 'Keep it quiet now. Let none of your men speak to me if he meets me in the street, or at the well — someone might go and tell the old man, and then in his suspicion he would clap me in cruel chains and plot the deaths of you all. So hold your peace, and get your wares bought quickly. And when your ship is loaded with cargo, send word to me at the house, and I will bring whatever gold I can lay my hands on. And there is one more fare I can pay you, gladly. There is a child of the master's in the house, in my charge — a clever little thing, who already runs out of doors at my side. I will bring him aboard for you, and he will fetch you a great price, wherever you sell him among strangers.'

"With that she went back into the great house. The Phoenicians stayed on a whole year among us, gathering a heavy cargo into the hollow ship. When at last it was loaded and ready to sail, they sent a man to carry word to the woman. A cunning fellow he was; he came to my father's house with a golden necklace strung here and there with amber beads, and while my mother and her women in the hall passed it from hand to hand, gazing at it and bidding for it, he gave the woman a quiet nod, and went off back to the hollow ship. Then she took me by the hand and led me out through the doors. In the porch she came on the cups and the tables where the men who waited on my father had been feasting — but they had just gone off to a sitting of the council and the assembly — so she snatched up three goblets and hid them in the fold of her dress and carried them off, and I went with her in my innocence. The sun went down, and all the roads grew dark, and we came quickly to the fine harbor where the Phoenician ship lay. They put us aboard and sailed out over the watery ways, and Zeus sent a wind at their backs. Six days we sailed, by day and by night alike; but when Zeus, son of Kronos, brought round the seventh day, Artemis the archer struck the woman down, and she crashed into the bilge like a sea-bird plunging, and they threw her overboard to the seals and the fishes, and I was left there grieving, all alone. The wind and the waves carried them on and brought them to Ithaca, and there Laertes bought me, paying for me out of his own goods. And that is how I first set eyes on this country with these eyes of mine."

Then royal Odysseus answered him: "Eumaeus, you have stirred my heart to the depths, telling over all the sorrows you have borne. Yet truly Zeus has set good beside your evil: for all your suffering, you came into the house of a kind master, who sees to it that you have your bread and wine, and you live a good life — while I am still wandering city to city, with no end to it."

So they talked, the two of them, and slept only a little, no more — for soon the bright Dawn was up. Meanwhile Telemachus and his men, off the coast, slackened the sails, brought down the mast, and rowed the ship in to her mooring. They threw out the anchor-stones, made fast the stern cables, then went ashore on the breaking surf, made their meal, and mixed the gleaming wine. When they had put away all desire for food and drink, wise Telemachus spoke: "Take the ship on round to the town, the rest of you. I am going up to the herdsmen and my farms. In the evening, when I have looked over my holdings, I will come down to the town, and in the morning I will set before you a good feast of meat and sweet wine to reward you for the voyage."
Then godlike Theoclymenus said: "And what of me, dear child? Whose house am I to go to, among the men of rocky Ithaca? Or shall I go straight to your house and your mother?"

"At any other time," wise Telemachus answered, "I would have sent you to our own house, where you would want for no welcome. But just now it would be the worse for you — I will be away, and my mother will not see you. She rarely shows herself to the suitors in the hall, but keeps to an upper room, weaving at her loom and away from them. Still, I can name you a man whose house you may go to — Eurymachus, the splendid son of wise Polybus, whom the people of Ithaca look upon now almost as a god. He is by far the best of them, and the most determined to wed my mother and take the place of Odysseus. But Olympian Zeus, up in his high heaven, knows whether a day of reckoning will not come down on them before any wedding."

Even as he spoke, a bird flew past on the right — a hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo. In its claws it held a dove, and tore at it, and the feathers fell to the ground between Telemachus and the ship. Then Theoclymenus drew him aside, away from the men, clasped his hand, and said: "Telemachus, that bird did not fly past on your right without a god behind it. I knew, the moment I looked at it, that it was a sign of fortune. There is no line in all Ithaca more kingly than your own. You will hold the power, you and your house, forever."

"Stranger," wise Telemachus answered, "I only wish your words may come to pass. Then you would soon know my friendship, and so many gifts from my hand that any man who met you would call you blessed."

Then he turned to Piraeus, a man he trusted: "Piraeus, son of Clytius, of all the men who came with me to Pylos you have served me the most faithfully. Take this stranger now to your own house, and treat him with all honor and kindness, until I come for him."
And Piraeus, that great spearman, answered: "Telemachus, stay away as long as you like. I will see to him, and he shall lack nothing a guest may ask for."

With that he went aboard, and ordered the men to embark and cast off the cables, and they went up and took their places at the oars. But Telemachus bound his fine sandals on his feet and took up his strong spear, tipped with sharp bronze, from the deck of the ship. They loosed the cables, thrust off from shore, and made for the town, as Telemachus had told them. And he strode on, fast and far, until he came to the steading where his great droves of swine were penned, and where the loyal swineherd slept among them — the man who, of all his master's servants, cared the most faithfully for what was his.

At first light Odysseus and the swineherd had a fire going in the hut and were getting breakfast ready, for they had already sent the herdsmen out with the pigs. When Telemachus came up the path, the dogs did not bark — they fawned around him, crowding close. Odysseus heard footsteps and saw the dogs go quiet and friendly, and he said to Eumaeus: "Eumaeus, someone is coming — a man of yours, I think, or someone the dogs know. They are not barking; they are making up to him."

The words were scarcely out of his mouth when his own son stood in the doorway. Eumaeus jumped up, startled, and the bowls he had been mixing wine in dropped from his hands as he rushed to his master. He kissed his head and both his shining eyes and wept for joy. As a father who has waited ten long years welcomes home an only son, the child of his old age, come back at last from a far country and all its hardship — so the swineherd threw his arms around Telemachus and kissed him all over, as a man kisses one back from the dead. The tears ran down, and he poured out his love: "So you are home, Telemachus, light of my eyes. When I heard you had sailed for Pylos I was sure I would never see you again. Come in, dear child, and sit, so I can have my fill of looking at you, now you are back under my roof. You don't come out to us herdsmen often — you keep close to the town. I suppose you'd rather have your eye on that crowd of suitors and what they are at."

"As you say, old friend," Telemachus answered. "But I came for your sake — to see you, and to learn whether my mother is still at home, or whether some man has finally married her, and the bed of Odysseus lies empty now, gathering cobwebs."
"She is still in the house," Eumaeus said, "breaking her heart, doing nothing but weep, day and night without end."

He took the young man's spear, and Telemachus stepped across the stone threshold and came in. Odysseus rose from his place to give it up to him, but Telemachus stopped him. "Stay where you are, stranger," he said. "I'll find another seat — there's a man here who will lay one for me." So Odysseus sat down again, and Eumaeus spread fresh green brushwood on the floor and threw a sheepskin over it for Telemachus. He set out platters of the cold meat left from the day before, heaped the baskets with bread as fast as his hands could move, mixed wine in a bowl of ivy-wood, and took his own seat facing Odysseus. They reached for the good things spread before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said to Eumaeus: "Old friend, where is this stranger from? What crew brought him to Ithaca, and who did they say they were? For he plainly did not come on foot."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "My boy, I'll tell you the whole truth. He says he is a Cretan, and that he has wandered far and wide over the earth. Just now he is on the run from a Thesprotian ship, and he has come to my hut for shelter. I put him in your hands — do with him as you like; he is your suppliant now."

"That is a hard thing you have laid on me, Eumaeus," Telemachus said. "How can I take this stranger into my house? I am young still, and have no strength of my own to fall back on if a man rises against me. My mother cannot make up her mind — whether to stay here and keep the house, out of respect for her husband's bed and the talk of the people, or to go at last with the best of the men who court her, the one whose offer is highest. But since the stranger has come to your station, I'll give him a good cloak and shirt to wear, a sword, and sandals for his feet, and send him on wherever his heart is set. Or keep him here with you, if you'd rather, and I'll send out clothes and food, so he is no drain on you and your men. Only I will not have him go near the suitors — they are too far gone in insolence, and they would abuse him in some way that would cut me to the heart. One man can do nothing against numbers, however brave he is; they will always be too many for him."

Then long-suffering Odysseus spoke up. "Friend — for I think it is right that I should say something — it tears at me to hear how these suitors carry on, riding roughshod in the house of a man like you, and you so young. Tell me: do you take it lying down, or have your own people turned against you, set on by some god? Or is it your brothers you blame — for those are the men a person leans on when a real quarrel comes? I tell you, if I were as young as you and had the heart I have now — if I were the son of long-suffering Odysseus, or were the man himself, come home from his wandering — I would let a stranger strike my head from my shoulders before I would go on bearing this. I would rather walk into that hall and be the death of every last one of them. And if their numbers beat me down, single-handed, I would still rather die fighting in my own house than stand by, day after day, and watch this — guests shoved and insulted, the serving-women hauled about for sport, wine running to waste, bread squandered, all of it for nothing, for an end that will never come."

Telemachus answered, "Then I'll tell you the truth of it, stranger. There is no quarrel between me and my people, and I have no brothers to blame — for Zeus has made ours a line of single sons. Arceisius fathered Laertes alone, and Laertes fathered only Odysseus, and Odysseus left only me behind in his house, with no good he ever had of me. That is why the place is overrun now with men who mean it harm: every lord of the islands round us — Dulichium, Same, wooded Zacynthus — and every man of weight in Ithaca itself, all of them courting my mother and eating the house bare. She neither says no outright nor brings the thing to an end, and so they devour what is mine, and before long they will devour me with it. But all that rests on the knees of the gods. Eumaeus, old friend — go quickly to the town and tell Penelope I am safe and back from Pylos. Tell her alone, and no one else, and come straight back. There are many here who would do me harm."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "I understand. You needn't say it twice. But tell me — as I'm going that way, shall I take word to poor Laertes too? He used to keep an eye on the work of his farm in spite of all his grief for Odysseus, and eat and drink with his hands when the mood was on him. But they say that from the day you sailed for Pylos he has not eaten or drunk as a man should, nor looked to his fields — he only sits and weeps, the flesh wasting off his bones."

"That grieves me," Telemachus said, "and I'm sorry for him — but we must leave him to himself for now. If men could have everything as they wished, the first thing I'd ask for is my father's return. Give your message and hurry back; don't turn aside to the farm to tell Laertes. Ask my mother to send one of her women out to him quietly, with the news."

So he sped the swineherd on his way. Eumaeus bound the sandals to his feet and set off for the town. Athena watched him well clear of the hut, and then drew near in the shape of a woman — tall, beautiful, skilled in fine work. She stood at the entrance, in plain sight of Odysseus, but Telemachus did not see her and did not know she was there, for the gods do not show themselves to everyone. Odysseus saw her, and so did the dogs; they did not bark, but slunk off whimpering to the far side of the yard. She gave him a sign with her brows, and Odysseus came out and stood before her beyond the wall. Then she said:

"Odysseus, son of Laertes, born to many turns — now is the time. Speak to your son and keep him in the dark no longer. Lay your plans for the killing of the suitors, the two of you together, and then make for the town. I will not be far behind — I am hungry for the fight myself."

With that she touched him with her golden wand. First she settled a fresh-washed cloak and a tunic about his shoulders. Then she made him taller to look on, and young again; she gave him back his dark color, filled out his cheeks, and let the beard grow black once more around his chin. Then she was gone, and Odysseus went back into the hut. His son stared, astonished, and turned his eyes away, afraid that he was looking on a god.

"Stranger," he said, "you are changed — a moment ago, and now you are not the same man. Your clothes are different, the very color of your skin is changed. Surely you are one of the gods who hold the wide sky. Be kind to me, then — I will give you sacrifices that please you, and gifts of worked gold. Only spare me."
And long-suffering Odysseus said, "I am no god. Why do you take me for one? I am your father — the man you grieve for, the man for whose sake you bear so much at the hands of lawless men."

And as he spoke he kissed his son, and the tears he had held back so long ran down at last and fell to the ground. But Telemachus could not yet believe it was his father, and he said: "You are not Odysseus, not my father — some god is mocking me with false hope, to make my grief the heavier afterward. No mortal man could do this by his own wit, make himself old and young from one breath to the next, unless a god stood at his side. A moment ago you were old and dressed in rags, and now you are like the gods who hold the sky."

Odysseus answered, "Telemachus, it is not right for you to wonder so at your own father here before you, or to stand back in such amazement. No other Odysseus will ever come; I am he. This is the man — after long wandering and much suffering, home in the twentieth year to the land of his fathers. What astonishes you is the work of Athena, who drives the spoil — she makes me what she will, for the gods can do as they please. One hour she makes me a beggar, the next a young man in fine clothes. It is an easy thing for the gods who hold the sky to lift a man up or to bring him low."

He sat down, and Telemachus threw his arms around his father and wept aloud, and Odysseus wept with him. They cried more shrilly than birds — sea-eagles, or vultures with hooked talons, whose young the country folk have stolen from the nest before they could fly — so bitterly did they let the tears fall from under their brows. And the sun would have gone down on their weeping, but Telemachus broke off and asked: "In what ship, then, dear father, did your crew bring you here to Ithaca? Who did they say they were? For you cannot have come on foot."

"I'll tell you the truth, my son," said long-suffering Odysseus. "It was the Phaeacians who brought me — great seafarers, who give safe passage to any man who reaches their shores. They carried me over the water fast asleep and set me down in Ithaca, with gifts to send me off: bronze, gold, and woven cloth. By the gods' grace those things lie hidden in a cave. And I have come here now at Athena's word, so the two of us can plan the death of our enemies. So tell me the suitors — count them, name them — that I may know who they are and how many. Then I can turn it over in my mind and judge whether the two of us can stand against them alone, or whether we must look for others to fight beside us."

Telemachus answered, "Father, I have always heard of your name — your strength in the field, your judgment in council. But this is too great a thing you speak of; the wonder of it stops me cold. Two men cannot stand against so many strong ones. The suitors are not ten, not twice ten, but many times that. Hear their count: from Dulichium, fifty-two picked young men, with six servants; from Same, twenty-four; from Zacynthus, twenty of the Greeks; from Ithaca itself, twelve, all of the best blood. With them are the herald Medon, a bard, and two men skilled at carving meat. If we go against all of these inside the hall, I am afraid your homecoming and your revenge will end in bitterness. Think hard whether there is anyone who might come and stand with us."
"Listen, then," said long-suffering Odysseus, "and think this over. Do you reckon Athena and Father Zeus enough for us, or shall I cast about for some other ally too?"
"Those two you have named are powerful helpers," Telemachus said. "They sit high among the clouds, and they hold sway over all others — gods and men alike."

"They will not hold back long from the fight," Odysseus said, "once the suitors and we two come to the test of arms in my own hall. Now, then: go home at daybreak and move among the suitors as you always do. Later the swineherd will bring me into the town, looking the part of a wretched old beggar. When you see them abusing me, harden your heart against my suffering — even if they drag me feet-first through the house or throw things at me, watch and do nothing. Speak to them gently, if you must, and tell them to stop; but they will not listen, for their day of reckoning is upon them. And mark this well, fix it in your mind: when Athena puts it in my heart, I will give you a nod. When you see it, gather up every weapon in the hall and stow it away in the inner storeroom. When the suitors miss the arms and ask, put them off with a soft answer — say you have moved them out of the smoke, that they are no longer what they were when Odysseus sailed away, but blackened and fouled with soot; and say too that you fear Zeus may set the men quarreling over their wine and turn them on each other, with arms at hand to shame the feast and the wooing — for the iron itself draws a man on. But leave a sword and a spear for each of us, and two oxhide shields we can snatch up in an instant; Zeus and Athena will quiet the rest of them soon enough. And one more thing — if you are truly my son and of my blood, let no one learn that Odysseus is in the house. Not Laertes, not the swineherd, not one of the servants, not even Penelope. Only you and I will sound out the women, and try some of the menservants too, to see who still honors us and whose hand is against us."

"Father," Telemachus said, "you will come to know my heart in time, and find no slackness in it. But I don't think this part of the plan will serve either of us — turn it over again. It would take us a long while to go round all the farms and test the men, and the whole time the suitors will be wasting your house, at their ease and without a qualm. Try the women, by all means, to learn who has been false and who is clear of it. But I would not go round trying the men just now. Leave that for later — if you really have some sign from Zeus that he is with us."

So the two of them talked on. Meanwhile the ship that had carried Telemachus and his crew from Pylos reached Ithaca. They ran her up onto the beach inside the harbor, and their attendants took the gear from them and bore the gifts to the house of Clytius. Then they sent a herald ahead to Penelope, to tell her Telemachus was in the country but had sent the ship round to the town, so that the queen would not be afraid and weep. This herald and Eumaeus met on the way, both bound on the same errand to Penelope. When they reached the house, the herald spoke out among the serving-women: "Your son, my queen, is home from Pylos." But Eumaeus went up close to Penelope and told her privately all that her son had bidden him say. Then, his message given, he left the house and its yards and went back to his pigs.

The suitors were stunned and sullen at the news. They came out past the great wall of the court and sat down in council by the gate. Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke first. "Friends, this is a serious thing Telemachus has brought off — this voyage. We were certain it would come to nothing. Quick, let us run a ship down to the water, get a crew aboard, and send word to the men out there to come home at once."

He had hardly finished when Amphinomus, turning where he sat, caught sight of the ship already inside the harbor, the crew furling her sail and laying up the oars. He laughed and said, "No need to send any message — they are here. Some god told them, or else they saw the other ship slip past and could not catch her."

At that they rose and went down to the shore. The crew hauled the ship up onto the land, and their attendants took the gear from them, and they all went together to the place of assembly — and they let no one else, young or old, sit in with them. Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke. "Curse it — see how the gods have saved this man from ruin. Day after day we kept lookouts posted along the windy headlands, and at sundown we never went ashore to sleep but lay out at sea in the ship all night, watching for dawn, hoping to catch him and make an end of him. And some god has carried him home in spite of us. Well, then — let us plan his death here. Telemachus must not slip us, for our whole business will never come off while he lives. He is sharp, and the people are by no means all on our side. We had better move before he can call the Greeks to assembly — and he will lose no time, raging as he is; he will stand up before them all and tell how we plotted his murder and missed. They will not love us for it, once they know. They may turn on us, and drive us out of our own land into exile. So let us take him first — out on his farm, away from the town, or on the road in. Then we divide his goods among us and leave the house to his mother and whatever man marries her. But if this does not sit well with you, and you would have Telemachus live and keep his father's estate, then let us stop gathering here and eating him out of house and home. Let each man court Penelope from his own hall, with his own gifts, and she can marry the one who gives the most, the man it falls to to win her."

They all sat silent until Amphinomus rose to speak. He was the son of Nisus, son of King Aretias, and he stood first among the suitors who came from the wheat-rich, grassy island of Dulichium; of all of them, his talk pleased Penelope most, for there was decency in him. He spoke plainly, with their good in mind: "Friends, I am against killing Telemachus. It is a terrible thing to spill the blood of a man of royal line. Let us first ask the will of the gods. If the oracles of Zeus approve it, I will kill him with my own hand and call on every one of you to do the same; but if the gods warn us off, then I say hold back."
His words pleased them, and they rose at once and went to the house of Odysseus, where they took their usual seats.

Now Penelope made up her mind to show herself to the suitors. She had learned of the plot against her son, for the herald Medon had overheard them at it and told her. She went down to the hall with her women, and when she came among the suitors she stood by a pillar of the roof, a fine veil before her face, and rounded on Antinous: "Antinous — you reckless schemer, you man of malice — they say you are the best speaker and the best counsel of any man your age in Ithaca, and you are nothing of the kind. Madman, why do you plot the death of Telemachus? Why do you trample on suppliants, whose witness is Zeus himself? It is a vile thing, to lay traps for one another. Have you forgotten how your own father once fled to this house, in terror of the people? They were enraged at him — he had gone off with Taphian pirates and raided the Thesprotians, who were at peace with us; the people would have torn him apart and devoured all he had. It was Odysseus who held them back and stayed their fury. And this is the house whose goods you now devour without paying, whose wife you court, whose son you would murder — breaking my heart. Stop it, I tell you, and make the others stop as well."

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered her smoothly: "Take heart, Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, and do not trouble yourself over this. The man is not born — never will be — who will lay a hand on your son Telemachus while I am alive and see the light of day. I tell you plainly, and it will come to pass: that man's dark blood will run down my spear. Many a time the city-sacker Odysseus took me on his knees and held the roast meat to my mouth and the red wine to my lips. So of all men Telemachus is the dearest to me, and he has nothing to fear from us suitors — though if death comes to him from the gods, no man can turn it aside." So he spoke, to soothe her — but in his own heart he was plotting the boy's death.

Penelope went back up to her bright room and wept for her husband, until Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyes. At evening the swineherd came back to Odysseus and his son. They had just killed a year-old pig and were busy getting supper ready; and Athena came up to Odysseus, struck him with her wand, made him an old man again, and put the rags back on him — so that Eumaeus would not know him on sight and fail to keep the secret, but run to tell Penelope.
Telemachus spoke first. "So you're back, Eumaeus. What is the word in the town? Have the suitors come in from their ambush yet, or are they still out there, waiting to take me on my way home?"

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "It never crossed my mind to ask about that, going through the town — I was set on giving my message and getting back as fast as I could. But a herald from the men who had sailed with you fell in with me; he was the first to bring the news to your mother. This much I can tell you, though, for I saw it with my own eyes: I had just climbed to the crest of Hermes' hill above the town when I saw a ship putting into the harbor, with a crowd of men aboard her, and a press of shields and spears. I took them for the suitors — but I cannot say for certain."

At that Telemachus smiled across at his father, careful that Eumaeus should not see. Then, when their work was done and the meal laid, they ate, and no man's share fell short — each had his fill. And when they had eaten and drunk all they wanted, they lay down and took the gift of sleep.

sections.label: Book XVII
sections.title: The Beggar at His Own Door

segments.text: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, Telemachus bound the sandals to his feet and took up a strong spear that sat well in his hand, for he meant to go into the city. "Old friend," he said to the swineherd, "I am off to the town now, to show myself to my mother — she will not stop grieving, I know, until she has seen me with her own eyes. As for this poor stranger, take him into the town and let him beg his bread there from anyone willing to give him a crust and a drink. I have troubles enough of my own; I cannot carry every man's. If that offends him, the worse for him — I would rather say plainly what I mean."

"I have no wish to stay either, sir," said Odysseus. "A beggar does better in the town than out here; whoever cares to can hand him something. I am too old to wait on a master's word at a country station. Let your man do as you have told him; only let me warm myself a little by the fire first, and let the day take on some heat, then take me down. My clothes are wretchedly thin, and on a frost like this morning's I would freeze on the road — and you say the city lies some way off."

At that Telemachus strode out through the yards, his mind already on the day he would pay the suitors back. When he reached the house he stood his spear against a pillar of the colonnade, crossed the stone floor, and went in.

Old Euryclea, his nurse, saw him before anyone else. She was busy spreading the fleeces over the chairs, and she burst into tears as she ran to him; the other maids crowded round too, kissing his head and shoulders in their welcome. Then Penelope came out of her room, lovely as Artemis or golden Aphrodite, and wept as she threw her arms about her son. She kissed his forehead, and both his beautiful eyes, and the words broke from her: "Light of my eyes, you are home — I had given up ever seeing you again. To think you slipped away to Pylos without a word to me, without my leave. But come, tell me everything you saw."

"Mother, do not scold me," Telemachus answered, "and do not stir up my heart when I have only just come through such danger. Wash, put on fresh clothes, go up to your room with your women, and vow whole and ample sacrifices to all the gods, if only Zeus will grant us the day of our revenge. I must go now to the place of assembly, to bring in a guest who came back with me from Pylos. I sent him on ahead with my crew, and told Piraeus to take him home and care for him until I could come for him myself."
She took her son's words to heart. She washed, put on fresh clothes, and vowed whole and ample sacrifices to all the gods, if only they would grant her the day of revenge upon the suitors.

Telemachus took up his spear and went out through the colonnade — not alone, for his two quick hounds went with him; and Athena poured such grace about him that every eye turned in wonder as he passed. The suitors gathered round him with welcome on their lips and malice in their hearts, but he gave them no opening, and went to sit instead with Mentor, Antiphus, and Halitherses, old friends of his father's house, who pressed him to tell them all that had befallen him. Then Piraeus came up, bringing Theoclymenus, whom he had escorted through the town to the assembly, and Telemachus went straight to them. Piraeus spoke first: "Telemachus, send some of your women to my house to fetch away the gifts Menelaus gave you."

"Piraeus, we cannot tell how things will fall out," Telemachus answered. "If the suitors kill me in my own house and carve up my goods among them, I would far rather you kept those gifts than that any of them got their hands on them. But if I bring those men down instead, then gladly bring the gifts to me — and I will thank you for it."

With that he led Theoclymenus home. When they came to the house they laid their cloaks over the benches and went to bathe; and when the maids had washed and oiled them and dressed them in clean tunics and cloaks, they took their places at the table. A serving-woman brought water in a fine golden jug and poured it over their hands into a silver basin, and drew up a polished table beside them; and the housekeeper set out bread and a generous share of all there was in the house. Across from them sat Penelope, leaning against a pillar of the hall and turning her spindle. They reached out to the good things spread before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Penelope said:

"Telemachus, I am going up now to lie down on that bed of mine — that grieving bed I have wet with my tears since the day Odysseus sailed for Troy with the sons of Atreus. But before the suitors come back into this house, you have still not told me plainly: did you hear anything, anywhere, of your father's coming home?"

"Then I will tell you the truth, mother," her son replied. "We went to Pylos, to Nestor, and he took me into his house and made me as welcome as a man would welcome his own son come home after long years away — he and his sons both. But he said he had not heard one word, from any living soul, of Odysseus, whether he was alive or dead. So he sent me on with a chariot and horses to Menelaus. There I saw Helen, for whose sake the Greeks and the Trojans alike, by the will of heaven, bore so much. Menelaus asked me what had brought me to Lacedaemon, and I told him the whole of it; and he said: 'So these cowards would creep into a brave man's bed? A deer might as well lay her newborn fawns to sleep in a lion's den and wander off to graze the glens and the grassy hollows — and the lion, coming home to his lair, makes a bloody end of both. Just so will Odysseus make an end of these suitors. By Father Zeus, by Athena and Apollo — if Odysseus is still the man he was that day on Lesbos, when he stood up to wrestle Philomeleides and threw him so hard the whole army roared — if he came among these suitors still that man, they would find their wedding short and their death quick.
