As for what you ask me, I will not turn it aside or soften it: what the old man of the sea told me, all of it, I will tell you. He said he had seen Odysseus on an island, in bitter grief, in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who keeps him there against his will; and he cannot win his way home, for he has no ship and no crew to carry him over the wide sea.' That was what Menelaus told me. When I had heard it I sailed for home, and the gods sent a fair wind and brought me safely back."

His words stirred Penelope to the heart. Then Theoclymenus spoke to her: "Honored wife of Odysseus, Telemachus does not see clearly into these things. Hear me, then, for I read them surely and will hide nothing. Let Zeus be my witness above all the gods, and this table of guest-friendship, and the hearth of Odysseus to which I have come — Odysseus is already here, in his own country. Whether he sits still or moves from place to place, he is learning the whole of this evil, and for every one of these suitors he is planting the seed of their ruin. Such was the omen I read aboard ship, and I told it then to Telemachus."
"May it be so," Penelope answered. "If your words come true, you will have such gifts and such goodwill from me that everyone who meets you will call you blessed."

So they talked together. Meanwhile, out in front of the house, the suitors were hurling the discus and the throwing-spear at a mark on the leveled ground, as insolent as ever. But when it came time for the meal, and the flocks were driven in from the country all around with their herdsmen as always, Medon — the one servant they liked best, who waited on them at table — called out: "Young masters, you have had your sport; come inside now and let us see to the meal. There is nothing wrong with dinner at dinnertime." They broke off their games at his word and went in, and laid their cloaks over the benches and chairs, and butchered fat sheep and goats and pigs and a full-grown heifer, and so made ready to feast.

Out at the steading, Odysseus and the loyal swineherd were setting off for the town. "Stranger," Eumaeus said, "I suppose you are still set on going down today, the way my master told you to — though for my own part I would rather have kept you here to watch the place. But I dare not cross him; he would only scold me later, and a master's tongue is a hard thing to bear. Let us be off, then. The day is at its height; before long it will be evening, and you will feel the cold worse than now."
"I know it, I take your meaning," answered Odysseus. "There is no need to say more. Let us go. But if you have a stick cut and ready, give it to me to lean on — you tell me the road is rough."

So he slung his shabby, torn old wallet over his shoulder by its cord, and Eumaeus gave him a staff that suited his hand; and the two set out, leaving the dogs and the herdsmen to mind the place. The swineherd led, and his master came behind, leaning on his staff like some broken-down old tramp, his body wrapped in rags. They worked their way down the rough, steep track, and as they neared the city they came to the fountain — the fair-flowing fountain Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor had built, where the townsfolk drew their water. A ring of water-loving poplars grew all around it, and the cold water came falling from the rock above; and over the spring stood an altar to the nymphs, where every traveler stopped to make an offering. There Melanthius, son of Dolius, overtook them, driving down the pick of his goats for the suitors' table, two herdsmen with him. The moment he saw Eumaeus and Odysseus he let fly at them with foul, abusive language that stirred Odysseus to anger.

"There they go," he sneered, "one rogue leading another — heaven matches like to like. Where do you think you are dragging this disgusting beggar, master swineherd? A thing to turn your stomach at the table. He is the sort to slouch from door to door rubbing his shoulders on the posts, whining for scraps — never for swords or cauldrons like a man, only for whatever filth will fill his belly. Hand him to me to mind my station and I will set him to mucking out the pens and bringing fodder to the kids, and he can fatten his shanks on whey to his heart's content. But no — he has learned only idleness, and would not stoop to honest work; he would rather beg his bread round the whole town to stuff that bottomless gut of his. And I tell you, and it will surely come to pass: if he sets foot in the house of Odysseus, the stools will fly at his head from every hand and break it before they throw him out."

And as he passed he kicked Odysseus on the hip, for sheer mindless spite — but Odysseus held his ground, not so much as swaying from the path. For a moment he weighed it: whether to leap on Melanthius and beat the life out of him with his staff, or seize him and dash his head against the ground. But he mastered it, and held it down in his heart. The swineherd, though, looked the man full in the face and rebuked him, and lifting up his hands he prayed aloud: "Nymphs of the fountain, daughters of Zeus — if ever Odysseus burned you the rich thigh-bones of lambs and kids, hear me now: bring him home, let some god guide him here. He would soon scatter these swaggering airs of yours, the way you strut up and down the town while your flocks go to ruin under your worthless keeping."

"Listen to the cur," Melanthius the goatherd shot back, "and the mischief he barks. One of these days I will load you onto a ship and carry you off to some far country and sell you for a tidy sum. As for that one — I only wish I were as sure that Apollo would strike Telemachus dead today, or the suitors would, as I am sure that Odysseus is never coming home."

With that he left them to follow at their own pace, and went on ahead, and was soon at his master's house. He went in and took his seat among the suitors, across from Eurymachus, who favored him above the rest; and the servers set a portion of meat before him, and the housekeeper laid out bread for him to eat. By now Odysseus and the swineherd had reached the house and halted outside it, and the sound of the lyre came drifting out, for Phemius was just lifting his voice to sing to the suitors. Then Odysseus took the swineherd by the hand and said: "Eumaeus, this is surely the house of Odysseus — a man would know it among a thousand. One building runs on into the next; the courtyard is walled and topped with a coping; the great doors are double and well made; no man would carry this by storm. And there are many feasting within, I can tell — the smell of roast meat is everywhere, and I hear the lyre, which the gods have made the companion of a feast."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "You have read it rightly, as you read most things. But let us think now what we should do. Will you go in first among the suitors and leave me here, or shall I go ahead and you wait? Only do not wait long, or someone may catch sight of you loitering and let fly something at you, or drive you off. Think it over."

"I understand and take your meaning," Odysseus replied. "Go in first; leave me here. I am no stranger to blows and to things thrown at my head. I have been knocked about too long, in war and on the sea, to be unmade by one more. Let this go with the rest. The one thing a man cannot hide is the gnawing of a hungry belly — that is the enemy that brings men endless grief; it is for the belly that ships are launched and rigged to cross the barren sea and carry war to other men."

As they were speaking, a dog that had been lying there lifted his head and pricked up his ears. This was Argos — the hound Odysseus had bred himself before he sailed for Troy, though he had never lived to get any use of him. In the old days the young men would take him out after wild goats and deer and hares; but now, with his master gone, he lay neglected, cast off on a deep heap of dung — the droppings of the mules and oxen, piled before the gates until the field hands should come to cart it off and manure the wide estate. There Argos lay, riddled with ticks. The moment he caught sight of Odysseus standing near, he dropped both ears and wagged his tail — but he no longer had the strength to drag himself any closer to his master. And Odysseus, seeing him across the yard, turned his face aside and brushed away a tear, easily hiding it from Eumaeus, and said: "Eumaeus, it is a strange thing — a dog as fine as that lying on a dung-heap. He is well built; but I cannot tell whether he had the speed to match his looks, or whether he was only one of those table-dogs that men keep about them for show."

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "That hound belonged to a man who died far from home. If he were now what he was in body and in work the day Odysseus left for Troy, you would soon marvel at his speed and his strength. No creature he started in the deep woods ever got away from him; he ran a scent like nothing else. But now he has fallen on hard days. His master is dead in some distant land, and the women give him no care. Servants lose half their worth the moment there is no master's hand over them; Zeus takes the better half of a man away the day the yoke of slavery comes down on him."
With that he went on into the house, into the hall where the suitors were, and Argos, in the very moment he had seen his master again in the twentieth year, was taken by the darkness of death.

Telemachus was the first by far to see Eumaeus come in, and he gave him a quick nod to come and sit by him. The swineherd looked about, found the stool the carver used when he was serving out the suitors' portions, carried it over to Telemachus's table, and sat down across from him; and a server set a portion of meat before him and gave him bread from the basket.

Right behind him came Odysseus, in the look of a wretched old beggar, leaning on his staff with the rags hanging off him. He sat down on the ash-wood threshold just inside the doorway, with his back against a post of cypress that the carpenter had once planed smooth and set true to the line. Telemachus took a whole loaf from the basket, and as much meat as his two hands would hold, and said to Eumaeus: "Carry this to the stranger, and tell him to make his round of the suitors and beg from each — a beggar cannot afford to be ashamed." So Eumaeus went and stood by him: "Stranger, Telemachus sends you this, and says you are to go round the suitors and beg, for a beggar cannot afford to be ashamed."

"King Zeus grant Telemachus every happiness," Odysseus answered, "and give him all his heart desires." Then he took what was sent him in both hands and set it down on the filthy old wallet at his feet, and ate while the bard was singing; and as the song ended, so did his meal. The suitors broke into noise, and Athena came to Odysseus and stirred him to go begging crusts from each of them in turn, to learn which were decent men and which were not — though not one of them would she spare for it in the end. So he went round from left to right, holding out his hand to each as if he had begged all his life. Some pitied him and wondered who he might be and where he came from; and the goatherd Melanthius spoke up: "Suitors of my noble queen, I can tell you this much of the stranger — I have laid eyes on him before. The swineherd brought him here. But of the man himself, of where he is from, I know nothing."

At that Antinous turned on the swineherd. "You prize fool," he cried, "what did you mean, hauling this fellow into town? Have we not tramps and beggars enough plaguing us as we eat? Is it a small thing to you that they swarm here eating up your master's living — and you must drag in one more?"

And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd: "Antinous, your blood is good, but your words are not. Who goes out to fetch a stranger from abroad, unless it be one who serves the people — a seer, a healer of hurts, a worker in wood, or a singer who can charm us with his voice? Those men are welcome the world over; but no one calls in a beggar to eat him out of house. You are always the hardest of all the suitors on the servants of Odysseus, and on me above the rest — but I do not care, so long as Telemachus and wise Penelope still live in this house."

"Hush," said Telemachus, "do not answer him. Antinous has the cruelest tongue of all of them, and he eggs the others on." Then he turned to Antinous: "How fatherly of you, Antinous, to look after my interests so — telling me to drive this stranger from my house with harsh words. God forbid. Take something and give it to him yourself; I do not begrudge it — I am telling you to do it. Never mind my mother, nor any servant in the house of Odysseus. But you have no such thing in mind: you would far rather eat it yourself than hand it to another."

"What a high-handed speech, Telemachus," Antinous answered. "If every suitor gave him as much as I will, this house would not see his face again for three whole months." And as he spoke he dragged out from under the table the footstool his sleek feet had been resting on, and brandished it. But the others all gave the beggar something and filled his wallet with bread and meat; and he was about to go back to the threshold and eat what the suitors had given, when first he stopped before Antinous and said:

"Give me something too, friend. You do not look the poorest man here — you look a prince, the first among them; so you should give the most freely, and I will carry the fame of your bounty far and wide. I too was a rich man once, with a fine house of my own, and many a wanderer like this I gave to in those days, whoever he was and whatever he needed. I had servants without number and all the things that make a man's life full and call him wealthy. But Zeus took it all from me — it was his will. He sent me off with a band of roving raiders to Egypt, a long voyage, and it was my undoing. I drew up my ships in the river of Egypt and bade my men stay close and stand guard while I sent scouts to look out from the high ground. But they would not hold to my orders; they followed their own greed and fell to plundering the Egyptian fields, killing the men and carrying off the women and children. The cry reached the city, and at first light the people poured out until the whole plain was thick with men on foot and in chariots, ablaze with bronze. Then Zeus broke my men's nerve, and not one of them would stand and face the enemy, for ruin closed on us from every side. They cut down many of us with the bronze, and the rest they took alive to work as slaves. I was given to a stranger who happened by, to carry off to Cyprus — Dmetor, son of Iasus, a great lord there. And from there I have come here, by way of misery upon misery."

Then Antinous said: "What spirit has sent us this plague to spoil our dinner? Stand off, out in the open of the court, or you will have your Egypt and your Cyprus over again, for the bold and shameless beggar you are. You have made your round of all of them, and they have given you freely — there is no holding back where there is plenty, and free with other men's goods is an easy thing."

Odysseus drew back, and said: "For shame — your looks are better than your heart. In your own house you would not spare a beggar so much as a grain of salt, you who sit here at another man's table with plenty all around you, and cannot bring yourself to break off one piece of bread."

That stung Antinous, and he glared at him: "Then I think you will not get out of this hall in one piece, after talking like that." And he caught up the footstool and hurled it, and struck Odysseus on the right shoulder, high on the back. But Odysseus stood firm as a rock; the blow from Antinous did not so much as rock him on his feet. He only shook his head in silence, brooding on his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down, and laid his full wallet at his feet, and said:

"Hear me, you suitors of the great queen, while I say what my heart bids me. There is no grief, no smart, in being struck while a man fights for his own — for his cattle or his white-fleeced sheep. But Antinous has struck me on account of my belly, that cursed, ruinous thing that brings men so much trouble. Yet if there are gods anywhere for the poor, and powers that avenge them, then I pray the end of Antinous comes before his wedding day."

"Sit and eat in silence, stranger, or take yourself elsewhere," Antinous shouted. "One more word and the young men will drag you out by the hand and foot through the whole house and strip the skin from your bones."

But this was too much even for the others, and one of the high-born young men spoke up: "Antinous, it was an ugly thing to strike that luckless wanderer. You will pay for it, if he should turn out to be some god from heaven. For the gods take the likeness of strangers from far countries, and in every kind of shape they walk the cities of men, watching who does violence and who keeps the right." So the suitors said, but Antinous paid them no mind. And Telemachus, though no tear fell from him, raged in his heart at the blow struck against his father, and only shook his head in silence, brooding on his revenge.

Now when Penelope, in her room, heard that the stranger had been struck in the hall, she said before her maids: "May Apollo strike you, Antinous, the same way." And her housekeeper Eurynome answered, "If our prayers were granted, not one of them would live to see the sun rise." "Nurse," Penelope said, "I hate every one of them, for there is nothing in them but mischief — but Antinous I hate like black death itself. A poor luckless wanderer comes begging through the house for sheer need, and everyone gives him something to put in his wallet; but Antinous lets fly a footstool and strikes him on the right shoulder."

So she talked with her women, sitting in her own room, while down in the hall Odysseus was finishing his meal. Then she called the swineherd to her and said: "Eumaeus, go and tell the stranger to come to me. I want to welcome him and ask him whether he has heard or seen anything of my unhappy husband, for he has the look of a man who has wandered far."

And you answered her, Eumaeus, swineherd: "If only these Greeks would hold their peace, my queen, you would be spellbound by the tale he tells. I had him three days and three nights in my hut — for that was the first place he came to, fresh from his ship — and even so he has not reached the end of his sorrows. The way a man hangs on the words of a bard taught by the gods, with the song spilling sweet from his lips, that is how I sat in my hut and hung on his words. He says there is an old guest-friendship between his house and the house of Odysseus; that he comes from Crete, where the line of Minos still lives; and that, driven from land to land by every kind of misfortune, he has heard word of Odysseus alive and near at hand, among the Thesprotians, and bringing home great wealth besides."

"Call him here, then," said Penelope, "that I may hear it from his own mouth. As for those men — let them take their pleasure indoors or out, it is all the same to them. They have nothing to grieve over: their own corn and wine lie untouched in their houses, with only the servants to use them, while they haunt our house day after day, slaughtering our oxen and sheep and fat goats for their feasts and swilling our wine without a care. No house could bear such waste; there is no Odysseus here now to fight off the ruin. But if he came home, he and his son would soon take their revenge."

As she spoke Telemachus gave a sneeze so loud the whole house rang with it, and Penelope laughed and said to Eumaeus: "Go now and call the stranger in. Did you not hear how my son sneezed on my very words? It can only mean that death is coming to all the suitors, and not one of them will escape it. And mark this, lay it to your heart: if I am satisfied the stranger speaks the truth, I will dress him in a good cloak and tunic."

When he heard this, Eumaeus went straight to Odysseus: "Stranger, my queen, the mother of Telemachus, has sent for you. Heavy as her grief is, she longs to hear whatever you can tell her of her husband; and if she is satisfied you speak the truth, she will give you a cloak and a tunic — the very things you most need. As for bread, you can fill your belly with that, begging round the town from any who will give."

"I will tell Penelope nothing but the strict truth," answered long-suffering Odysseus. "I know all about her husband; we have borne hard fortune together. But I am afraid of this savage pack of suitors, whose insolence reaches to the sky. Just now, as I went about the hall doing no harm to anyone, a man struck me a cruel blow, and neither Telemachus nor anyone else lifted a hand for me. So tell Penelope to be patient and wait in her room until the sun goes down. Then let her ask me about her husband's return — but let her seat me close to the fire, for my clothes are wretched, as you know yourself, since it was you I first begged for help."

The swineherd heard him and went back, and as he stepped over the threshold Penelope said: "Why do you not bring him, Eumaeus? Is he afraid of being ill-used, or only too shy to come into the house? A beggar cannot afford to be ashamed."

And you answered her, Eumaeus, swineherd: "He speaks good sense, my queen — only what any man would think. He is keeping clear of those overbearing men. He asks you to wait until sundown; and it will be far better so, for then you can have him to yourself, to hear him and question him as you please."

"He is no fool, whoever he is," Penelope answered. "It may well be as he says, for there are no men in all the world so set on evil as these." When she had spoken Eumaeus went back into the crowd of suitors, his errand done, and bent close to Telemachus so no one else could hear: "My dear lad, I will go back now to the pigs, to look after the property — yours and what is mine. You see to things here, but above all keep yourself safe; there are many in this house who wish you harm. May Zeus bring them to ruin before they bring it down on us."

"So be it," said Telemachus. "Have your meal first, then go. And in the morning come back, and bring the beasts for the day's sacrifice. The rest I will leave to me and to heaven." At that Eumaeus sat down again, and when he had eaten and drunk his fill he left the courts and the hall behind, with the men still at their meat, and went back to his pigs. As for the suitors, they gave themselves over to dancing and song, for the day was wearing on toward evening.

Now there came a public beggar who used to go cadging all over the town of Ithaca, a man with a name for bottomless eating and drinking. There was no strength in him and no staying power, but he was a great hulk to look at. His real name, the one his mother gave him, was Arnaeus; but the young men all called him Irus, because he would run and carry a message for anyone who sent him — a man's twist on Iris, the runner of the gods. The moment he arrived he set about insulting Odysseus, trying to drive him from his own door.

"Off with you, old man," he cried, "away from the doorway, before you are dragged out by the foot. Can you not see them all winking at me, wanting me to throw you out? I am ashamed to do it, that is all. Get up and go on your own, or it will come to blows between us."

Odysseus frowned at him and said, "My friend, I am doing you no harm. People give you plenty; I do not grudge it. There is room in this doorway for the two of us, and you have no cause to begrudge me what is not yours to give. You look to be a tramp like myself — and perhaps the gods will grant us both better luck one day. But do not talk so freely of fighting, or you will rouse me; and old as I am, I will paint your chest and your mouth with blood. I would have more peace tomorrow if I did, for you would never come back to the house of Odysseus again."

Irus was furious. "Listen to the glutton run on," he said, "chattering away like an old kitchen-hag. I have a mind to set both fists on you and knock the teeth out of your head like a boar's tusks. Gird yourself, then, and let all these men stand by and watch. How will you fight a man so much younger than you?"

So the two of them traded insults on the smooth pavement before the great door. And when Antinous saw what was brewing, he gave a great laugh and said to the others, "Friends, here is the finest sport heaven ever sent into this house. The stranger and Irus have fallen out, and they mean to fight. Let us match them now, this minute."

Up they all sprang, laughing, and crowded round the two ragged beggars. "Hear me," said Antinous. "There are goat stomachs down at the fire, stuffed with fat and blood, that we set by for our supper. Whichever of these two wins and proves the better man, let him come and take his pick — and from now on he eats at our table, and we will let no other beggar near the house."

They all liked the sound of it. But Odysseus, throwing them off the scent, said, "Sirs, an old man worn down with hardship is no match for a young one; yet my wretched belly drives me to it, though I know it will earn me a beating. Only swear me this first: that not one of you will strike me a foul blow to favor Irus and hand him the win."

They swore it as he asked. And when the oath was done, Telemachus put in a word. "Stranger," he said, "if your heart bids you take this man on, do not fear any of the rest. Whoever strikes you will have more than one man to answer to. I am your host, and Antinous and Eurymachus, both men of sense, are of the same mind as I am."

Every man there agreed. Then Odysseus girded his old rags tight about his loins, and out came his great thighs, broad and bare, and his wide chest and shoulders and the mighty arms; and grey-eyed Athena came close and made his limbs stronger still. The suitors were struck with wonder, and a man would lean to his neighbor and say, "Irus will soon be un-Irused, and asking for it too. Look at the thigh the old fellow has hauled out of his rags."

Irus felt his courage drain away as he heard them, but the servants girded him up and hauled him out, his flesh quaking on his bones with fear. And Antinous rounded on him: "You swaggering bully — better you had never been born than to stand there trembling at this broken old tramp. But I tell you, and it shall surely come to pass: if he beats you and proves the better man, I will pack you onto a black ship and send you to the mainland, to King Echetus, who maims every man who comes near him. He will cut off your nose and your ears with the pitiless bronze, and tear out your privates to throw raw to the dogs."

That made Irus shake the harder. But they led him into the open of the court, and the two men put up their hands. Then Odysseus weighed it in his mind: whether to lay him out with one blow and finish him on the spot, or to strike lighter and only drop him in the dust. In the end he judged the lighter blow the wiser, for fear the Greeks should begin to wonder who he was. So they squared off, and Irus struck Odysseus on the right shoulder; but Odysseus caught him on the neck, below the ear, and crushed the bone within, and the red blood came welling up through his mouth. Down he went groaning into the dust, grinding his teeth and drumming his heels on the ground — and the suitors threw up their hands and nearly died of laughter. Then Odysseus took him by the foot and dragged him out through the doorway and across the yard to the gate of the court, and propped him against the wall, and put his staff in his hand. "Sit there now," he said, "and keep off the dogs and the pigs. Wretch that you are, do not set up as king of the beggars again, or you will fare even worse."

Then he slung his shabby, torn old wallet over his shoulder by its cord, and went back to sit on the threshold. And the suitors filed in laughing and saluting him: "May Zeus and all the other gods, stranger, give you whatever you most desire, for stopping the mouth of that bottomless tramp. We will soon ship him off to the mainland, to King Echetus, who maims every man alive."

Odysseus took their words for a good omen. Antinous set before him a great goat's stomach, stuffed with fat and blood; and Amphinomus took two loaves from the basket and brought them to him, and lifted a golden cup and drank his health. "Good luck to you, father stranger," he said. "You are hard pressed enough now; I hope better days are coming."

And Odysseus answered, "Amphinomus, you strike me as a man of good sense, as well you might, being the son you are — for I have heard your father, Nisus of Dulichium, well spoken of, a man both brave and rich. They tell me you are his son, and you have the look of one who knows how to listen. So listen now, and take to heart what I say. Of all things that breathe and crawl across the earth, the earth breeds nothing feebler than a man. While the gods grant him strength and spring in his knees, he never thinks any evil will reach him later; and when the blessed gods send him sorrow instead, he bears that too, and against his will, with an enduring heart. For the mind of a man down here is only what the father of gods and men makes it, day after day. I too looked to be a fortunate man once, and did much wrong out of my own headstrong pride, trusting in my father and my brothers to back me. So let no man ever be lawless; let him take whatever the gods give him and hold his peace. Look at the suitors here, and the harm they do — wasting the goods and dishonoring the wife of a man who, I tell you, will not long be gone from his own people. He is close. May some god lead you home and away before then, so you are not in this hall the day he comes back to his own country. For once he is under this roof, I do not think the suitors and he will part without blood."

With that he poured a libation and drank, and put the cup back in Amphinomus's hands; and Amphinomus walked off through the hall with his head bowed and his heart heavy, for some shadow of evil had fallen on him. Yet for all that, he did not escape his doom; even then Athena had bound him to go down under the spear of Telemachus. So he went and sat down again in the place he had risen from.

Now grey-eyed Athena put it into the mind of Penelope, daughter of Icarius, to show herself to the suitors — to set their hearts beating all the harder for her, and to stand higher than before in the eyes of her husband and her son. So she gave a hollow laugh and said, "Eurynome, my heart has turned, for all that I loathe them: I have a mind to show myself to the suitors. And I would say a word to my son, too — that he do better than keep such company. They have fair words on their lips and nothing but mischief behind them."

"All you say is true, my child," Eurynome answered. "Go, then, and speak plainly to your son. But first wash, and put oil on your face. Do not go down with your cheeks all furrowed with crying. Endless grieving does no good; and your son is grown — a bearded man now, the very thing you always prayed to the gods you might live to see."

"I know you mean well, Eurynome," Penelope said, "but do not press me to wash and anoint myself. Whatever beauty I had, the gods took from me the day my husband sailed away in the hollow ships. No — only send Autonoe and Hippodamia to me, that they may stand beside me in the hall. I will not go down among the men alone; that would not be seemly."

So the old woman went off through the house to call the maids and hurry them to their mistress. And meanwhile grey-eyed Athena had another thought, and poured a sweet sleep over the daughter of Icarius, so that she sank back on her couch and her limbs went slack, while the goddess gave her gifts that would leave the Greeks marveling. First she washed her lovely face with the divine balm that fair-crowned Aphrodite wears when she goes to the lovely dancing of the Graces; she made her taller to the eye, and fuller, and her skin whiter than fresh-sawn ivory. When this was done the goddess departed, and the white-armed maids came in from their room and woke her with their chatter, and sleep let her go.

She passed her hands across her cheeks. "What a soft sleep," she said, "folded itself around me in all my misery. I wish pure Artemis would grant me so soft a death this very moment, that I might stop wearing my life away in grief and longing for my husband — a man who was best in every way among the Greeks."

Then she came down from her bright upper room — not alone, but with two of her women attending her — and when she reached the suitors she stood by the pillar that bore the roof of the hall, holding a shining veil before her face, and a faithful maid on either side. And the knees of the suitors went weak; love so bewitched them, every one, that each man prayed to lie beside her in her bed. But she turned to her son.

"Telemachus," she said, "your mind and your judgment are not what they were. When you were a child you had a better sense of what was fitting. But now you are grown — and any stranger who looked at your height and your good looks would call you the son of a fortunate house — your judgment and your sense of what is right are no longer what they should be. How could you let such a thing happen here in our hall, this stranger so shamefully abused? What if a guest, sitting under our roof, had come to real harm in a brawl like that? It would have been your disgrace before the world."

"Mother," Telemachus answered, "I am not surprised you are angry. But I do take in everything now, and I know in my own heart when things go right and when they go wrong; when I was younger I could not. Even so, I cannot keep everything in good order. These men hem me in on every side with their malice, and I have no one at my back. Still, the fight between the stranger and Irus did not go the way the suitors wanted, for the stranger had the better of it. By Father Zeus, by Athena and Apollo — I wish the suitors in this house lay beaten the same way, some out in the court and some inside, every one of them slack-limbed as Irus over there by the courtyard gate, nodding his head like a drunk man, unable to stand on his feet or find his way home, with all the strength knocked out of him."

So mother and son spoke together. Then Eurymachus turned to Penelope. "Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope," he said, "if every Greek in Iasian Argos could see you now, you would have still more suitors feasting in your halls by tomorrow's dawn, for there is no woman in the world to match you — in beauty, in stature, and in the good sense within."

"Eurymachus," Penelope answered, "whatever excellence I had, of face or form, the gods destroyed the day the Greeks took ship for Troy and my husband Odysseus went with them. If he came home and took up the care of my life again, then my name might stand higher and fairer than it does. As it is, I am eaten up with grief, so many sorrows has heaven let fall on me. And he foresaw it all. When he was leaving, he took me by the right wrist and said, 'Wife, I do not think all of us well-greaved Greeks will come home safe from Troy. The Trojans are fighters, with spear and bow, and quick in the chariot — and that, more than anything, decides the day in a hard, even battle. So I do not know whether the gods will bring me back, or whether I will fall there at Troy. Look after everything here. Care for my father and mother, as now, and even more while I am gone. But when you see our son with a beard on his cheek, then marry whom you will, and leave this house behind.' That is what he said, and now it is all coming true. The night is near when this hateful marriage will fall to a miserable woman whose happiness Zeus has stripped away. And here is what cuts deepest of all: your way of courting is not the custom. When men woo a woman of good family, a worthy bride, and rival one another for her, they bring oxen and fat sheep of their own to feast her friends, and lay rich gifts before her — they do not eat up another man's living and pay nothing for it."
And Odysseus, hearing her, was glad — glad that she was charming gifts out of them with honeyed words, while her real heart was set elsewhere.

Then Antinous spoke. "Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope," he said, "take whatever gifts any of us cares to bring you, for it is not well to refuse a gift. But we will not go back to our own lands, or stir from here at all, until you have married the best man among us."

The others all said yes to that, and every man sent a herald off to fetch his gift. For Antinous the man brought a wide, lovely robe, beautifully worked, with twelve clasps of pure gold, fitted with curving sheaths. For Eurymachus, a chain of cunning craft, of gold strung with amber beads, glowing like the sun. Two servants of Eurydamas brought earrings, each a triple cluster of mulberry drops, and the grace of them shone out. From the house of Lord Pisander, son of Polyctor, came a servant with a neckband, a thing of rare beauty. And so each of the Greeks brought his own fine gift.

Then the queen went back up to her room, and her women carried the lovely gifts after her. And the suitors gave themselves over to dancing and to the sweetness of song, and so passed the time until evening came down on them. The dark of evening overtook them still at their pleasure, and they set up three braziers about the hall to give light, and heaped them with firewood long dry and well seasoned, splitting fresh kindling among it; and they kept torches burning, the maids of long-suffering Odysseus holding them up by turns. Then Odysseus himself said to the women,

"You maids of Odysseus, your master so long gone — go inside to the queen's chamber. Sit with her and lighten her heart; turn the spindle, or card the wool in your hands. I will keep the light burning for all these men. Let them stay till the bright Dawn herself; they will not wear me down, for I can bear a great deal."

At that the maids glanced at one another and laughed; and one of them, the pretty Melantho, began to taunt him to his face. She was a daughter of Dolius, but Penelope had raised her like her own child and given her playthings to her heart's content; yet for all that she felt nothing for her mistress's grief, but had taken up with Eurymachus and shared his bed.

"You poor fool of a stranger," she said, "have you gone clean out of your mind? Why not go and sleep in some smithy, or a tramps' shelter, instead of running your mouth here, bold as you please, in front of all these men? The wine has gone to your head — or perhaps your wits are always this loose, and that is why you babble so. Or has beating the tramp Irus turned your head? Take care a better man than Irus does not stand up against you and pound your skull with his fists and send you out of the house dripping blood."
Odysseus scowled at her. "You bitch," he said, "I will go straight to Telemachus and tell him what you said, and he will have you cut to pieces on the spot."

His words scattered the women in fear, and they fled away into the body of the house, the knees shaking under them, for they believed he meant it. But Odysseus took his stand by the burning braziers, holding up the light and watching them all — and his mind ran far off, on things that would surely come to pass.

And Athena would not let the proud suitors hold off their cruelty for a moment, so that the bitterness might sink the deeper into the heart of Odysseus. She set Eurymachus, son of Polybus, to mock him, and raise a laugh among the rest. "Hear me, you suitors of the great queen," he said, "while I say what is on my mind. This man has not come into the house of Odysseus for nothing — the gods themselves have led him. Look, I do believe the gleam of the torches is coming off the man himself — off the top of his head, for there is not a hair left on it, not so much as a wisp."

Then he turned to Odysseus. "Stranger," he said, "would you go to work for me, if I took you on out at the far end of the country — building up dry-stone walls, planting tall trees? I would keep you in bread the year round, and find you clothes and sandals for your feet. But no — you have learned only bad habits, and you will not put your hand to honest work; you would rather go cringing round the town to feed that belly of yours."

"Eurymachus," Odysseus answered, "I only wish there could be a contest of work between us, you and I, in the long days of spring, when the days run on and on. Give me a good curved scythe, and take one yourself, and let us go fasting into the deep meadow grass from first light till dark, and see who mows the cleaner and the longer. Or give us a yoke of oxen each, big tawny beasts, well matched and full of strength and never tiring, in a four-acre field with the sod ready to turn, and you would see whether I could not cut a straight furrow before me from end to end. Or let Zeus stir up war this very day, somewhere — give me a shield and two spears and a helmet of bronze set close on my temples, and you would find me up among the foremost in the fighting, and you would not be jeering at this belly of mine. But you are insolent, and your heart is hard; and you think yourself some great man because you keep company with a few small men, and poor ones. If Odysseus came home to his own country — those wide doors would seem narrow enough to you, for all their width, as you scrambled to get out through the porch and away."

Eurymachus burned with rage at that. He glared at him and let fly: "You wretch — I will make you pay, mouthing off like that in front of everyone, and not a shred of fear in you. The wine has gone to your head, surely, or your wits are always loose, that you babble so. Or has beating the tramp Irus turned your head?" And as he spoke he snatched up a footstool. But Odysseus dropped down at the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium in fear of Eurymachus; and the stool caught the wine-steward on the right hand, so that the jug rang as it hit the floor, and the man fell back in the dust with a cry. The suitors broke into an uproar in the shadowy hall, and a man would lean to his neighbor and say, "I wish this stranger had died somewhere else in his wanderings before he came to us — then he would not have brought all this turmoil among us. Here we are, brawling over a beggar, and there will be no joy left in the feast at all, now that worse has the upper hand."

Then Telemachus stood up among them. "Sirs," he said, "you are out of your minds. You can no longer hide that you have eaten and drunk too much; some god is goading you. You have feasted well — go home now and lie down, whenever your hearts move you. I drive no man out."

They bit their lips and marveled that Telemachus dared speak so boldly. But Amphinomus rose — Amphinomus, son of Nisus, who was son of King Aretias — and said, "Friends, no one should take offense at a fair word, or strike back at it in anger. Lay no hand on the stranger, nor on any servant in the house of Odysseus. Come — let the steward pour for our cups, that we may make our libations and go home to our rest. As for the stranger, let us leave him to Telemachus to deal with, for it is to his house that the man has come."

His words pleased them all. So the lord Mulius, a herald of Dulichium and servant to Amphinomus, mixed the bowl and carried it round and served every man in turn; and they poured out to the blessed gods and drank the honey-sweet wine. And when they had made their offerings and drunk their fill, they went off, each man to his own house, to lie down for the night.

sections.label: Book XIX
sections.title: By the Fire, and the Scar

segments.text: Odysseus stayed behind in the hall, turning over in his mind how, with Athena's help, he might bring the suitors down. At last he said to Telemachus: "We must carry the weapons out of here and stow them away inside. When the suitors miss them and ask, put them off with some excuse. Tell them you have moved the arms out of reach of the smoke, that they are not what they were when your father sailed but have grown dull and grimed with soot. And add something heavier than that: say you are afraid Zeus may set them quarreling over their wine and they will turn the iron on each other, fouling both the feast and the courtship — for steel within a man's reach has a way of drawing his hand to it."

Telemachus thought his father spoke well, so he called the nurse Eurycleia and said: "Nurse, keep the women shut in their quarters while I carry my father's arms down into the storeroom. No one tends them now that he is gone; they have gathered soot all through my boyhood. I mean to put them where the smoke cannot reach them."

"I only wish, child," Eurycleia answered, "that you would take the whole house into your own hands at last and look after everything yourself. But who is to go with you and light your way? You will not let the maids carry a torch for you."
"The stranger," said Telemachus. "A man who eats my bread can earn it, wherever he comes from."

Eurycleia did as she was told and bolted the women inside. Then Odysseus and his son fell to it, carrying the helmets and the bossed shields and the long spears within; and Athena went before them holding a golden lamp that filled the room with a soft, marvelous light. Telemachus stopped and stared. "Father," he whispered, "my eyes are seeing a great wonder. The walls, the rafters and crossbeams, the pillars that bear them — everything glows as if a fire were running over it. There is surely a god here, one of those who hold the wide heaven."

"Hush," said Odysseus. "Hold your tongue and ask nothing. This is the way of the gods who live forever. Go now and lie down. Leave me here to talk with your mother and the maids. She will be heavy with grief, and there is much she will want to ask me."

So Telemachus went by torchlight across the court to the room where he always slept, and there he lay until morning. And Odysseus was left alone in the hall, still turning over in his mind how, with Athena's help, he might bring the suitors down.

Then Penelope came down from her room, lovely as Artemis or golden Aphrodite. They drew up for her, near the fire in her usual place, a chair inlaid with whorls of silver and ivory — the work of the craftsman Icmalius, who had built a footstool into it, all of a piece, and spread it thick with a fleece. There she sat, and the maids came out of the women's quarters to join her. They began clearing away the tables where the shameless suitors had dined, carrying off the leavings of bread and the cups they had drunk from, and they raked the dead coals out of the braziers and piled them high with fresh wood for light and warmth. And Melantho started in on Odysseus a second time. "Still here, stranger?" she said. "Do you mean to slink about the house all night and spy on the women? Get out, you wretch, and be glad of the supper you've had — or you'll have a firebrand at your back to drive you through the door."

Odysseus gave her a dark look. "My good woman," he said, "why come at me so hard? Because I am filthy, and dressed in rags, and have to beg my way through the world like other tramps? Need does that to a man. I too was rich once, with a fine house of my own, and in those days I gave to many a wanderer like the one I am now, whoever he was and whatever he needed. I had servants past counting and all the comforts of a man called wealthy. Then Zeus took it from me — such was his will. So take care, woman, that you do not someday lose the high place you flaunt now over the other maids; take care your mistress does not turn against you in her anger, or that Odysseus does not come home — for there is still a hope of it. And even if he is dead, as you suppose, there is his son Telemachus, whom Apollo keeps, and nothing the women do amiss in this house escapes him now. He is no longer a boy."

Penelope heard him, and turned on the maid. "You brazen creature," she said, "do not think your insolence is hidden from me — you will pay for it with your own head. You knew well, for I told you so myself, that I meant to see the stranger and ask him about my husband, who is the reason I live in such endless grief."
Then she said to her head housekeeper Eurynome: "Bring a chair, and a fleece to lay on it, so the stranger can sit while he tells his story and listens to what I have to say. I want to question him."

Eurynome brought the chair at once and spread a fleece on it, and when Odysseus had sat down Penelope began: "Stranger, the first thing I will ask is this — who are you, and where do you come from? Where is your city, and who are your people?"

"Lady," Odysseus answered, "who on the whole wide earth could find a word of blame for you? Your fame goes up to the very floor of heaven. You are like some blameless king who fears the gods and holds the right, ruling a great and warlike people: under him the dark earth bears its wheat and barley, the trees hang heavy with fruit, the flocks bring forth without fail, the sea gives up its fish — all because he governs well, and his people prosper under him. So ask me anything else here in your house, but do not press me about my birth and my country, or you will fill me with fresh grief over the memories. I am a man weighed down with sorrow, and it is not fitting to sit weeping and wailing in another's house — there is no good in grieving on and on without end. One of your women might take it ill, or you yourself, and say my eyes swim because I am heavy with wine."

"Stranger," Penelope answered, "whatever grace I had of face or form, the gods stripped from me the day the Greeks set sail for Troy and my husband went with them. If he were to come home and take up my life again, I would be better thought of, and show a fairer face to the world. As it is, I am bowed down with sorrow; some god has heaped grief on grief upon me. All the chiefs who hold power in the islands — Dulichium, Same, wooded Zacynthus — and the lords of rocky Ithaca too, are courting me against my will and bleeding my house white. So I can pay no heed to strangers, or to suppliants, or to heralds who serve the people; I do nothing but ache for Odysseus. They press me to marry, and I have had to spin out my tricks. First some god put it in my heart to set up a great loom in my hall and begin weaving a wide web of fine thread. And I said to them: 'Young men, my suitors — since noble Odysseus is dead, hold back from this marriage, eager as you are, until I have finished this cloth, so the threads will not be wasted. It is a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day death takes him down in its long sleep — for I would not have the women of this land reproach me, if a man who won so much should lie without a shroud.' So I spoke, and their pride gave way. Then by day I would weave at the great web, and by night, with torches set beside me, I would unravel it again. Three years I fooled them and kept them believing it. But when the fourth year came round with the turning seasons, and the months waned and the long days were done, those worthless girls, my own maids, gave me away, and the suitors broke in and caught me at it, and raged at me — so I was forced to finish it, willing or not. And now I can find no way out of this marriage, no further dodge. My parents are pressing me hard to take a husband, and my son chafes at the way these men devour his living, for he sees it all clearly now; he is a grown man, well able to keep his own house, and the gods have given him a good heart. But for all that — tell me who you are, and where you come from. You were not born of the oak of old stories, or sprung from a rock."

Then Odysseus answered: "Honored wife of Odysseus, since you will not let it go, I will tell you — though it costs me something, as it must cost any man who has been an exile as long as I have, and suffered among as many peoples. Still, I will answer what you ask. There is a land called Crete, in the middle of the wine-dark sea, fair and fertile, ringed with water — a crowded land, with ninety cities, and many tongues mingled in it: there are Achaeans, and the true-born Cretans, and Dorians in their three tribes, and the noble Pelasgians. The great city among them is Cnossus, where Minos was king, who every ninth year took counsel with mighty Zeus himself. Minos was the father of Deucalion, and Deucalion was my father, for he had two sons — Idomeneus and myself. Idomeneus sailed for Troy in the curved ships, and I, the younger, am called Aethon; my brother was the elder and the better man. It was in Crete that I saw Odysseus and gave him welcome, for a storm had driven him off his course on his way to Troy, carrying him past Cape Malea and into Amnisus, by the cave of Eileithyia, where the harbors are hard to enter and he barely rode out the gale. The first thing he did was come up into the town and ask for Idomeneus, calling himself his sworn and honored friend — but Idomeneus had already sailed for Troy, ten or twelve days before. So I took him into my own house and gave him a guest's full welcome, for I had plenty of everything. I fed his crew from the town's stores, and gathered up wine and oxen for their sacrifices, until they had eaten and drunk their fill. The Greeks stayed with me twelve days, for a great north wind was blowing, so fierce a man could hardly keep his feet on land — some unfriendly god had raised it. On the thirteenth the wind dropped, and they put out to sea."

Many another likely tale he told her, and Penelope wept to hear it, for her heart was melting. As the snow melts on the high mountains when the West Wind has heaped it up and the East and South winds breathe upon it, until the rivers run full and overflow their banks — so her fair cheeks ran with weeping for the husband who sat there beside her all the while. Odysseus pitied his wife as she wept, but he held his eyes steady as horn or iron in their lids; he did not let so much as a flicker show, so cunningly did he master his own tears. And when she had eased her heart with weeping, she turned to him again: "Now, stranger, I think I will test you, and see whether it is true that you took my husband and his men into your house, as you say. Tell me, then — what kind of clothes did he wear, and what sort of man was he to look at, and the companions with him?"

"Lady," Odysseus answered, "it is hard to say after so long. It is twenty years now since he left my country and went his way. But I will tell you the picture my mind still holds. Odysseus wore a thick wool cloak, dyed sea-purple and lined double, and it was fastened with a brooch of gold, with two sheaths for the pin. On the face of it was worked a marvel: a hound holding a dappled fawn pinned beneath its forepaws, gripping it as it struggled — and everyone wondered at the workmanship, the way the hound, all of gold, throttled the fawn while the fawn writhed with its hooves to be free. I noticed the tunic against his skin too, smooth as the skin off a dried onion, soft as that, and shining like the sun; the women could not take their eyes from it. But I tell you, and mark it well — I cannot say whether Odysseus wore these things from home, or whether one of his comrades gave them to him aboard ship, or some host on his travels made him the gift; for he had friends everywhere, and few among the Greeks were his equal. I myself gave him a bronze sword, and a fine double cloak of sea-purple, and a tunic that fell to his feet, and I saw him off to his ship with every honor. He had a herald with him, a little older than himself, and I can tell you his look as well: round-shouldered, dark-skinned, with thick curling hair. His name was Eurybates, and Odysseus held him closer than any of the others, because the man's mind ran with his own."

At this Penelope was moved more deeply still, for she knew the signs Odysseus laid before her were true beyond doubt. And when she had wept her fill she said to him: "Stranger, I pitied you before, but now you will be honored and made welcome in my house. It was I who gave him those clothes. I took them from the storeroom and folded them myself, and I pinned on the bright brooch to set them off. But I shall never welcome him home again. It was a cruel fate that sent him sailing off to that city I will not even name — the name of ruin."

Then Odysseus answered: "Honored wife of Odysseus, do not waste your fair face and wear out your heart any longer weeping for your husband — though I will not blame you for it. Any woman grieves for the man she married and loved and bore children to, even were he a lesser man than Odysseus, who they say was like the gods. But dry your tears now and hear me, for I will tell you the truth and hide nothing: I have heard, lately and close at hand, that Odysseus is alive and on his way home. He is among the Thesprotians, in their rich country, and bringing back great treasure that he has gathered up and down the land. He lost his ship and all his men on the wine-dark sea, leaving the island of Thrinacia, for Zeus and the Sun were angry that his crew had slaughtered the cattle of the Sun, and every man of them went down. But Odysseus clung to the keel and the waves carried him to the shore of the Phaeacians, who are close kin to the gods. They honored him as though he were a god himself, gave him many gifts, and would have brought him home safe of their own accord. Odysseus would have been here long ago, except that he judged it wiser to go on from land to land, gathering wealth — for no man alive is as cunning as he is; there is no one to match him. Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, told me all this, and swore to me, pouring the wine of his oath, that the ship was hauled down to the water and the crew was ready to bring Odysseus home to his own country. But me he sent off first, for a Thesprotian ship happened to be sailing for Dulichium, where the wheat grows. He showed me the treasure Odysseus had heaped up — enough lying in King Pheidon's house to keep a man's family ten generations. As for Odysseus, the king said, he had gone to Dodona to learn the will of Zeus from the great oak, whether after so long away he should come back to Ithaca openly or in secret. So you may be sure he is safe and near, and will be here soon — he cannot stay away from his own much longer. And I will give you my oath on it: let Zeus be my witness, first and highest of the gods, and this hearth of Odysseus to which I have come — everything I have told you will come to pass. This very year Odysseus will be here, between the waning of this moon and the rising of the next."

"May it be so," Penelope answered. "If your words come true, you will have such gifts and such goodwill from me that everyone who meets you will call you blessed. But my own heart tells me how it will go. Odysseus will not come home, and you will not get your escort either, for there are no longer any masters in this house such as Odysseus was — if ever there truly was such a man — to welcome an honored stranger and speed him on his way. Even so — wash his feet, you maids, and make him a bed: a couch with rugs and bright blankets, so he can lie warm until the golden Dawn. And early in the morning bathe him and rub him with oil, so he can sit at meat in the hall beside Telemachus. It will be the worse for any of those hateful men who vexes him — say what they like, they will get nothing more done in this house. For how, stranger, are you to know whether I am better than other women in heart and in good sense, if I let you sit at my table unwashed and dressed in rags? Our lives are short. A hard man, who deals hardly, is cursed by all while he lives and mocked when he is dead; but a man who is just, and acts justly — strangers carry his name far over the earth, and many call him good."

Odysseus answered: "Honored wife of Odysseus, I have had no use for rugs and bright blankets since the day I first lost sight of the snowy mountains of Crete and went down to my ship. I will lie as I have lain through many a sleepless night before. Night after night I have passed in some rough bed, waiting for the holy Dawn. And as for washing my feet — I want none of it. No young girl of those who serve your house is going to lay a hand on my feet. But if there is some old woman here, faithful, who has borne as much trouble in her life as I have in mine, I will let her wash them."

"Dear guest," Penelope said, "of all the strangers who have ever come to my house from far away, not one has spoken so wisely and so well as you. There is an old woman here, faithful and full of good sense — the same who took my poor husband into her arms the night he was born, and nursed him at her breast. She is feeble now, but she shall wash your feet." Then she called out: "Come, Eurycleia, and wash this man — he is your master's age. Odysseus must by now have hands and feet much like his, for hard trouble ages a man fast."

At those words the old woman hid her face in her hands and broke into tears, and her grief poured out of her: "Oh, my child, what can I do for you! Surely Zeus has hated you above all men, god-fearing as your heart was. No mortal ever burned the Thunderer so many rich thigh-bones, or gave him such fine offerings, praying to reach a green old age and see your own son grow into a man — and yet he, of all men, you he has shut out from the day of his homecoming. I dare say the women in some far palace where Odysseus has come are jeering at him now, the way these shameless sluts here have jeered at you, and no wonder you would not let them touch you and add their insults to it. But I will wash your feet gladly — for Penelope's sake, and for your own, for you have stirred my heart to its depths. And hear this, for there is something in it: many a worn stranger has come to this house in his trouble, but never yet, I swear, have I seen one so like Odysseus — your build, your voice, the very set of your feet."
"Old woman," Odysseus answered, "that is what everyone says who has seen us both — that we are wonderfully alike. You have an eye, to have marked it."

Then the old woman took the gleaming basin she used for washing feet and poured in cold water, a good deal of it, and added hot to warm it. Odysseus sat by the hearth, but he turned himself quickly toward the dark, for it had come to him all at once that when she took his leg in her hands she might know the old scar, and the whole truth would come spilling out. And so it was: the moment she came near and laid hold of her master, she knew the scar — the wound a boar had given him, years before, with its white tusk, the day he hunted on Mount Parnassus with the sons of his grandfather Autolycus. Autolycus was the finest thief and the best swearer of oaths in all the world; the god Hermes himself had given him that gift, for Autolycus burned for him the pleasing thigh-bones of lambs and kids, and the god went gladly at his side. Once, when Autolycus had come to the rich land of Ithaca, he found his daughter's child newly born; and when supper was done Eurycleia set the baby on his knees and said: "Autolycus, find a name yourself now for your daughter's son. He is a child long prayed for."

And Autolycus answered: "My daughter, and my son by marriage, give him the name I tell you. I have come here a man who has been angered at many in my time — men and women both, the whole world over. So let the boy's name be Odysseus: the child of anger. And when he is grown and comes to his mother's great house on Parnassus, where my wealth lies, I will give him a share of it and send him home rejoicing."

So when Odysseus was grown he went to Parnassus to claim the gifts. Autolycus and his sons took his hand and welcomed him warmly, and his grandmother Amphithea threw her arms around him and kissed his head and his two bright eyes. Autolycus called on his sons to make the meal ready, and they did as he asked, and led in a five-year-old bull, flayed it and dressed it, and cut it into joints, and carved the joints small and ran them on the spits and roasted them through, and shared out the portions. So all day long until the sun went down they feasted, and no man wanted for his fair share. And when the sun had set and darkness came on, they lay down and took the gift of sleep.

When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, the sons of Autolycus went out to hunt with their hounds, and noble Odysseus went with them. They climbed the steep, wooded flank of Parnassus and soon came up into its windy folds; and just as the sun, fresh-risen from the deep, smooth flood of Ocean, began to strike the fields, the beaters came down into a glen. The hounds ran ahead, casting for the scent, and behind them came the sons of Autolycus, and among them Odysseus, close on the dogs, swinging a long spear. There, in a thicket so dense the wet winds could not pierce it nor the bright sun get through, with the fallen leaves lying deep on the ground, a great boar lay in his lair. He heard the tramp of the men's feet and the baying of the hounds closing in, and he charged out to meet them, his bristles standing up along his spine, fire flashing from his eyes, and stood at bay. Odysseus was the first to drive in, lunging with the long spear to kill — but the boar got there first and gored him above the knee, ripping a long furrow of flesh as he came in sideways, though the tusk did not reach the bone. Odysseus caught him through the right shoulder, and the bright point drove clean out the other side, and the boar dropped in the dust with a scream and his life went out of him. The sons of Autolycus saw to the carcass, and bound up the wound of faultless, godlike Odysseus with care, and stanched the dark blood with a charm, and got him home to their father's house. And when Autolycus and his sons had healed him well, they sent him back to his own land of Ithaca with splendid gifts, glad of him and he of them. His father and mother were overjoyed to see him, and asked him about everything — how he had come by the scar — and he told them the whole of it: how the boar had ripped him with its white tusk when he was up on Parnassus hunting with the sons of Autolycus.

This was the scar the old woman now ran her flat hands over, and knew, and let go his foot. The leg dropped into the basin; the bronze rang, and it tipped, and the water went pouring out across the floor. Joy and grief seized her at once, and her eyes filled with tears, and her voice caught in her throat. She reached up and took Odysseus by the chin and said: "You are Odysseus, my own dear child — you are, and I never knew you, not until I had my hands on the body of my master."

And she looked toward Penelope, to tell her that her own husband was here in the house. But Penelope could not meet her eyes or take in what was passing, for Athena had turned her mind away. Then Odysseus, with his right hand, caught the old woman by the throat, and with his left he pulled her close, and said: "Nurse — do you want to destroy me, you who nursed me at your own breast, now that after twenty years of pain I have come home at last to my own country? You have found me out; a god has put it in your heart. Then be silent. Let no one else in the house hear a word of it. For I tell you this, and it will be done: if the god gives these proud suitors into my hands, I will not spare you, my nurse though you are, when I come to kill the other women in this house."

"My child," Eurycleia answered, "what a thing to say! You know how firm I am — nothing can bend me or break me. I will hold as hard as stone, as iron. And hear me on this, and keep it close: when the god has put the proud suitors under your hand, I will tell you which of the women in the house have shamed themselves, and which are blameless."
"Nurse," Odysseus answered, "why should you name them? There is no need. I will mark them well enough myself, every one. Keep silent, and leave the rest to the gods."

At that the old woman went off through the hall to fetch fresh water, for the first had all been spilled. And when she had washed him and rubbed him with oil, Odysseus drew his chair nearer the fire again to warm himself, and hid the scar under his rags. Then Penelope began to speak to him once more.

"Stranger," she said, "there is one small thing more I would ask you. It is near the hour of rest — at least for anyone whom sweet sleep can take in spite of grief. But to me the gods have given a sorrow past all measure. By day, even at my work, looking after the house and the women, I find no comfort but in mourning and tears; and when night comes, and the others go to their beds, I lie awake, and my heart is torn by trouble that will not let go. As the daughter of Pandareus, the pale-brown nightingale, sings out her sweet song in the new spring, perched in the thick leaves of the trees, and pours it out in run after trembling run, mourning her own child Itylus, the son of King Zethus, whom she killed by mischance with the bronze — so my own heart goes this way and that, torn whether I should stay here with my son and keep all safe: my house, my servants, my high roof, out of respect for my marriage bed and the word of the people; or whether I should go now with the best of these Greeks who court me in the hall and bring the richest gifts. While my son was still a child and had no understanding, he would not hear of my leaving his father's house; but now that he is grown a man, he begs me to go, fretting at the way the suitors eat up his inheritance. But listen now to a dream of mine, and read it for me if you can. I keep twenty geese about the house, that come up out of the water to eat the soaked grain, and I love to watch them. I dreamed a great eagle with a hooked beak swooped down off the mountain and broke all their necks and killed them, and they lay scattered dead about the hall, and the eagle soared back up into the bright sky. And I wept and wailed there in my dream, and the fair-haired women of the town gathered round me, while I cried my heart out because the eagle had killed my geese. Then he came back and settled on a jutting beam of the roof, and checked my grief, and spoke to me in a human voice: 'Take heart, daughter of far-famed Icarius. This is no dream but a waking truth, and it will come to pass. The geese are the suitors; and I, who was the eagle, am your own husband, home again at last, and I will bring a foul death down on every one of them.' At that I woke, and looked, and there were my geese in the yard at their grain, just as before."

"Lady," Odysseus answered, "there is no twisting this dream to mean anything else, since Odysseus himself has told you how he will make it good. The suitors' death is clear, every one of them; not one will get away from his fate."

"Stranger," Penelope answered, "dreams are slippery things, hard to read, and not all of them come true for the people who see them. There are two gates through which our fleeting dreams pass: one is made of horn, the other of ivory. The dreams that come through the carved ivory are deceivers, carrying words that come to nothing; but those that come through the polished horn bring true things to pass, for the one who sees them. I do not think my own strange dream came through there — much as my son and I would welcome it if it did. And one thing more I will tell you, and hold it in your heart: the dawn is coming now whose evil light will cut me off from the house of Odysseus. For I am going to set the suitors a contest, the axes. Odysseus used to stand twelve axe-heads in a row down the hall, like the ribs set up to build a ship, and then stand well back and send an arrow clean through the whole twelve. Now I will set the suitors to do the same; and whichever of them strings the bow most easily in his hands and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes, with him I will go, leaving behind this house of my marriage, so fine a house, so full of good things — the house I think I shall remember even in my dreams."

Then Odysseus answered: "Honored wife of Odysseus, do not put off this contest in your house. Odysseus will be here, the man of many turns, before these men can take that polished bow and string it and shoot the iron through."

"Stranger," Penelope answered, "if you would only sit here in my hall and go on talking to me, sleep would never fall on my eyes. But no one can do without rest forever; the gods have set every mortal his measure of all things, even of sleep, here on the grain-giving earth. So I will go up now to my own room and lie down on that bed of mourning, the bed I have soaked with my tears since the day Odysseus sailed away to that city of ruin I will not name."
So she went up to her bright upper room, not alone, for her women went with her; and there she wept for Odysseus, her dear husband, until Athena cast sweet sleep over her eyelids.

sections.label: Book XX
sections.title: The Last Night Before the Reckoning

segments.text: Odysseus lay down to sleep in the forecourt. He spread an undressed ox-hide on the floor, heaped over it a pile of fleeces from the sheep the suitors were forever slaughtering, and Eurynome threw a cloak across him once he had settled. There he lay, wide awake, turning over in his mind how he would bring death to the suitors. And as he lay there the women of the house who had been sleeping with those men came slipping out, laughing and joking with one another as they went. The sight set his heart boiling. He weighed it hard — whether to rush in and kill every one of them on the spot, or to let them go to the suitors this one last time. His heart growled inside him. As a bitch standing over her pups will growl and bare her teeth at a stranger, ready to fight, so his heart growled within him at the wickedness he was watching. But he struck his chest and rebuked his own heart: "Endure, my heart. You have borne worse than this. You bore it the day the Cyclops, that savage with no restraint in him, devoured your brave companions one by one — and you held on, in silence, until your cunning brought you out of that cave where you were sure you would die."

So he spoke, calming the heart in his breast, and it obeyed him and held steady. But his body would not be still. As a man turns a sausage thick with blood and fat over a blazing fire, this way and that, hungry to have it roasted through, so Odysseus tossed from side to side, racking his mind to see how he, one man alone, could ever lay hands on so great a crowd of them. Then Athena came down from heaven to him, in the likeness of a woman, and stood over his head and spoke: "Why are you still awake, you most unlucky of men? This is your own house. Your wife is safe inside it, and your son too — a young man any father would be proud of."

"All of that is true, goddess," Odysseus answered. "But here is what gnaws at me. How am I, one man, to lay hands on these shameless suitors, who are never here in less than a crowd? And beyond that — a harder thing still — even if I do kill them, with Zeus's help and yours, where am I to escape to afterward, with all their kinsmen out for my blood? I ask you to think on that."

"You have no faith," said Athena. "A man will lean on a weaker friend than I am — a mortal, with none of my wisdom. And I am a goddess, who has watched over you through every trouble you have had. Hear me plainly: if fifty companies of fighting men stood around the two of us, hot to kill, you would still drive off their cattle and their fat sheep and walk away. Now sleep. To lie awake the whole night through, on guard, is a wearing thing. You are nearly clear of your troubles."
As she spoke she poured sleep over his eyes, and went back to Olympus.

While sleep was loosening the cares from Odysseus's limbs, his faithful wife woke. She sat up in her soft bed and wept; and when she had wept until the grief eased, she prayed to Artemis: "Artemis, great goddess, daughter of Zeus — drive an arrow into my breast and take my life now, this moment. Or let a storm-wind catch me up and carry me down the paths of darkness and drop me where the streams of Ocean pour back into themselves — as the winds once carried off the daughters of Pandareus. The gods killed their father and mother and left them orphans in their house; but Aphrodite fed them on cheese and honey and sweet wine, and Hera made them lovelier and wiser than other women, and holy Artemis gave them height and bearing, and Athena taught them every fine handiwork. Then, while Aphrodite had gone up to high Olympus to ask Zeus — who knows all things, what is fated and what is not — to grant the girls a happy marriage, the storm-winds snatched them away and handed them over to be servants to the hateful Furies. Let the gods on Olympus blot me out the same way. Or let fair Artemis strike me, so that I might pass under the dreadful earth still looking on Odysseus, and never gladden the heart of a lesser man. A grief is bearable, however a person weeps by day, so long as sleep comes at night — for sleep closes the eyes and wipes out everything, the good and the bad alike. But some god sends me even evil dreams. This very night one lay beside me who was the image of Odysseus as he looked the day he sailed; and my heart leapt, for I thought it no dream but the waking truth at last."

So she spoke, and at once golden Dawn came on. Odysseus caught the sound of her weeping, and it troubled him; half-dreaming, it seemed to him that she already knew him and was standing at his side. He gathered up the cloak and the fleeces he had slept on and laid them on a chair in the hall, and carried the ox-hide outside. Then he lifted his hands to heaven and prayed: "Father Zeus — if it was truly your will to bring me home over land and sea, after all the suffering you laid on me, then let one of those now waking in the house speak a word of good omen for me, and send me some other sign as well, from outside."

So he prayed, and Zeus the counselor heard him. At once he thundered out of shining Olympus, high above the clouds, and Odysseus's heart lifted. And inside the house a woman grinding grain spoke the word of omen, close by, from the room where the mills of the master stood. Twelve women in all worked there, grinding barley and wheat, the marrow of men's strength. The others had finished their measure and lain down to rest, but this one had not yet stopped, for she was the frailest of them. Now she let her millstone rest and spoke the words that were a sign for her master: "Father Zeus, lord of gods and men — how loud you have thundered out of a clear sky, with not one cloud in it. That is a sign for someone. Then grant this too, to me, poor wretch that I am: let this be the last day, the very last, that the suitors take their pleasant feast in the house of Odysseus. They have broken my knees with the bitter grinding of their meal. Let this be the last supper they ever eat."
So she spoke, and Odysseus rejoiced at the word of omen and at the thunder of Zeus; for he knew now that he would have his revenge on the guilty.

The other women of the house were rising now and kindling the fire on the hearth, the flame that would not die. And Telemachus got up from his bed and dressed, a godlike man. He slung his sharp sword over his shoulder, bound the fine sandals on his feet, and took up his strong bronze-tipped spear; then he came and stood in the doorway and said to Euryclea: "Nurse, did you see the stranger looked after in the house — a bed, a meal — or has he been left to fend for himself?
