That would be like my mother: shrewd as she is, she will fuss over some second-rate man and turn a far better one out the door."

"Do not blame her, child, when there is no blame to give," the wise Euryclea answered. "The stranger sat and drank his wine as long as he wished. He had no more appetite for bread — your mother asked him. And when he thought of sleep, she told the maids to make up a bed; but he is so battered and luckless a man that he would not lie on a bed under blankets. He slept in the forecourt, on an undressed ox-hide with some fleeces over it, and I laid a cloak across him myself."

So Telemachus went out through the hall, his spear in his hand and his two quick hounds trotting beside him, on his way to the place of assembly where the Greeks were gathering. And Euryclea, that good woman, daughter of Ops son of Peisenor, called out to the maids: "Up with you, and to work. Sweep the hall and sprinkle it down to lay the dust; throw the purple covers over the chairs; sponge the tables clean; rinse out the mixing-bowls and the fine cups. Some of you, off to the spring for water, and be quick. The suitors will not stay away long this morning — they will come early, for today is a feast for all the people."

So she spoke, and they jumped to it. Twenty of them went off to the deep-running spring, and the rest got busy through the house. The serving-men of the suitors came in and set to splitting firewood, deft hands at it. The women came back from the spring; and after them came the swineherd, driving in three fat hogs, the best of his herd. He left them to root about the good courtyard, and said to Odysseus, kindly enough: "Stranger, are the suitors treating you any better now, or are they riding you as hard as ever?"
"May the gods pay them back, Eumaeus," Odysseus answered, "for the outrages they pile up so insolently, in another man's house, with no shame in them at all."

So the two of them talked. And now Melanthius the goatherd came up, driving in the best of his goats for the suitors' dinner, with two herdsmen at his side. He tied the goats under the echoing gateway, and then he turned on Odysseus with his sneering tongue: "Still here, are you, stranger — still pestering the house with your begging? Still in the way? I can see the two of us are not going to part before we have given each other a taste of the fist. There is no decency in the way you beg. Are there no other feasts among the Greeks, that you have to glue yourself to ours?"

Odysseus said nothing in answer. He only bent his head and brooded, turning his dark thoughts over inside him. Then a third man came up — Philoetius, the chief of the herdsmen — leading in a barren heifer and some fat goats. The ferrymen had brought him across, the men who carry over anyone who comes to them. He tied his beasts carefully under the echoing gateway, and went to the swineherd and asked: "Swineherd, who is this newcomer, this stranger in our house? Where does he claim his people are, where is he from? Poor fellow — and yet for all his rags he carries himself like a king. But the gods send hard days even to wandering men, and spin out trouble even for kings, when it is their will."

And as he spoke he stepped over to Odysseus and took his right hand in greeting, and said: "Good day to you, father stranger. Things go badly for you now, but may better days come. Father Zeus — there is no god crueler than you. You feel no pity for the men you fathered yourself; you let them fall into hard living and into bitter pain. The sweat broke out on me and my eyes filled the moment I saw this man, for he put me in mind of Odysseus. I cannot help thinking my master too is dressed in rags like these, knocking about the world somewhere — if he is even still in the light of the sun. But if he is dead already and gone down to the house of Hades — then bitter grief for the good Odysseus, who set me over his cattle while I was still a boy, among the Cephallenians. The herds have grown past counting; no man could have bred them better; broad-browed cattle thick as standing grain. And now strangers order me to drive them in for their own eating. They take no thought for the son of the house, though he is right here; they have no fear of the gods' anger; they are itching already to share out the goods of a master gone so long away. I have turned it over and over in my mind — only it would be a wrong thing while his son lives — to load the cattle and go off to some other country, to strangers. But that is a hard road too. So I stay here and put up with it, minding cattle for other men's pleasure, and it has become more than I can bear. I would have run off long ago and put myself under some other great lord, for life here is past enduring — but I keep thinking of my unlucky master, that he might yet come home and scatter these suitors through the house."

"Herdsman," said Odysseus, "you strike me as no fool and no bad man, and I can see for myself you have sense in you. So I will tell you something, and swear a great oath on it. Witness it, Zeus before all the gods, and this table of guest-friendship, and the hearth of noble Odysseus that I have come to: while you are still here, in this very place, Odysseus will come home. And if you have a mind to it, you will see with your own eyes the killing of the suitors who lord it here."

"Stranger, if only Zeus would bring that to pass," the herdsman answered, "you would see what strength is in these hands, and how I would use it." And Eumaeus prayed in the same way, to all the gods, that wise Odysseus might come home again.

So the three of them talked. Meanwhile the suitors were busy hatching death and doom for Telemachus. But a bird came to them on the left — a high-flying eagle with a trembling dove in its talons. And Amphinomus rose and spoke: "My friends, this plan of ours, this killing of Telemachus, will never come off cleanly. Let us turn our minds to the feast instead." So said Amphinomus, and his words pleased them. They went into the house of noble Odysseus, laid their cloaks over the chairs and benches, and set to slaughtering the great sheep and the fat goats, the well-fed hogs and the heifer of the herd. They roasted the inner meats and shared them round, mixed the wine in the bowls, and the swineherd handed out the cups. Philoetius, chief of the herdsmen, passed the bread in fine baskets, and Melanthius poured the wine. And they all reached out to the good things laid ready before them.

Telemachus, working a plan of his own, seated Odysseus inside the strong-built hall, by the threshold of stone, with a mean little table and a poor chair. He set a portion of the inner meats before him and poured his wine into a gold cup, and said: "Sit there now, and drink your wine among your betters. I will keep the gibes and the fists of every suitor off you myself. This is no public house. It is the house of Odysseus, and he won it for me. So you suitors — hold your tempers, keep your hands and your tongues to yourselves, or there will be a quarrel and a fight."

So he spoke, and they all bit their lips and marveled that Telemachus had the nerve to speak so. Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said: "Hard as it is, Greeks, let us swallow what Telemachus says, threats and all. Zeus would not let us, or we would have shut his ringing mouth long ago, here in this hall." So Antinous spoke, but Telemachus paid him no mind.

Now the heralds were leading the sacred offering, the hundred beasts, up through the city, and the long-haired Greeks were gathering under the shady grove of Apollo the archer. When the suitors had roasted the outer meat and drawn it off the spits, they shared it out and feasted in splendor; and those who served set a portion before Odysseus equal to their own, for so Telemachus, the dear son of godlike Odysseus, had commanded.

But Athena would not let the proud suitors hold back from their galling insolence — she wanted the pain to bite still deeper into the heart of Odysseus. There was among them a man of lawless mind named Ctesippus, whose home was in Same. Trusting in his great wealth, he had come courting the wife of the long-absent Odysseus; and now he spoke up to the arrogant suitors: "Hear me, you proud suitors, while I say a word. The stranger has had his fair share all along, as he should — there is no decency in slighting a guest of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house. But come, let me give him a guest-gift of my own — something he can pass on to the bath-girl, or to any other servant in the house of godlike Odysseus."

And with that he snatched up a cow's hoof from the basket where it lay and flung it with a strong hand. But Odysseus tipped his head just aside and dodged it, and inside himself he smiled — a grim, bitter smile — while the hoof struck the solid wall. Then Telemachus rounded on Ctesippus: "It is well for your own skin, Ctesippus, that you missed the stranger — that he dodged your throw. Had you hit him, I would have run you through the middle with my spear, and your father would be busying himself with your funeral here, not your wedding. So let me see no more loutishness from any of you in this house. I see now, and understand, both the good and the bad of things; I am no longer the child I was. I have borne the sight of all this long enough — my sheep slaughtered, my wine drunk, my bread eaten — for one man cannot hold off many. But let there be no more violence done to me out of spite. And if it is your pleasure to cut me down with the bronze, then I would rather die — far rather — than go on watching these foul deeds day after day: guests knocked about, and the serving-women dragged through this fine house in shame."

So he spoke, and they all fell dead silent. At last Agelaus, son of Damastor, said: "Friends, when a thing is fairly said, no one should round on it in anger or answer it with hard words. Leave off mishandling the stranger, and any other servant in the house of godlike Odysseus. But to Telemachus and his mother I would speak a gentle word, if it might find a welcome in both their hearts. As long as you could still hope in your hearts that wise Odysseus would come home, there was no fault in waiting and holding the suitors off in your halls. That would have been the better way, had he come back. But by now it is plain enough he never will. So sit down beside your mother and tell her this: let her marry the best man, the one who offers the most, so that you may keep all your father's goods to yourself, to eat and drink in peace, while she keeps another man's house."

"No, Agelaus," Telemachus answered. "I swear it by Zeus, and by the sufferings of my father, who is dead or wandering far from Ithaca — I put no obstacle in the way of my mother's marriage. I urge her, in fact, to wed whom she will, and I will give her gifts beyond counting. But to drive her from this house against her will, with a hard word — that I cannot bring myself to do. God forbid I should."

So spoke Telemachus. But Pallas Athena set the suitors laughing — laughing until they could not stop, until their wits went wandering. They were laughing now with jaws that were not their own. The meat they ate ran with blood; their eyes brimmed over with tears; and their hearts foreboded grief. Then Theoclymenus, the godlike seer, spoke out among them: "You poor doomed men — what is this horror coming over you? Night has wound itself around your heads, your faces, your knees. The hall is loud with the sound of wailing; your cheeks are wet with tears. The walls are spattered with blood, and the fair crossbeams above. The porch is crowded with ghosts, and the courtyard too — ghosts hurrying down into the dark of Hades. The sun has perished out of the sky, and an evil fog has rolled over everything."

So he spoke, and they all laughed at him, easy and loud. Eurymachus, son of Polybus, took the lead: "This stranger who has just blown in from somewhere has lost his mind. Quick, you servants — show him out the doors, out into the marketplace, since the hall seems as dark as night to him."

But the godlike Theoclymenus answered: "Eurymachus, I have no need of anyone to guide me out. I have eyes, and ears, and two good feet of my own, and a sound mind in my breast besides — nothing wrong with any of them. By these I will take myself outside. For I see the evil coming on you, and not one of you suitors will dodge it or escape it — not one of you who, in the house of godlike Odysseus, do violence to men and plot your wicked deeds."

So he spoke, and walked out of the well-built hall, and came to Piraeus, who took him in gladly. But the suitors only looked at one another, and went on baiting Telemachus by jeering at his guests. One of the high-handed young men would say: "Telemachus, no man is worse served in his guests than you. First there is this filthy tramp, good for nothing but begging his bread and his wine, with no strength in his hands and no stomach for a fight — a dead weight on the ground. And now up gets this other one, to play the prophet. Take my advice, for it is the better course: let us throw the pair of them aboard a ship of many oars and sell them off to the Sicels. That would fetch a decent price." So the suitors talked. But Telemachus paid them no mind. He sat in silence, watching his father, waiting always for the moment he would lay his hands on the shameless crowd.

And the daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope, had set her lovely chair facing them, just across the way, so that she heard every word each man spoke in the hall. For all the laughter, they had made a fine, rich dinner of it, with all those beasts slaughtered. But never was there a supper less to be envied than the one a goddess and a strong man were about to set before them — for it was they themselves who had begun the foul work first.

Now Athena put it into the mind of wise Penelope to set the suitors a contest with the bow and the gray iron axes, there in the halls of Odysseus — the beginning of their slaughter. She climbed the high stair of the house and took in her strong hand the storeroom key, a fine thing of bronze with an ivory handle. Then she went, with her maids behind her, to the inmost storeroom at the back of the house, where her husband's treasures lay: gold, and bronze, and wrought iron. And there too lay the springing bow, and the quiver full of arrows, every one of them heavy with grief to come.

He had been given that bow long ago, in Lacedaemon, by Iphitus son of Eurytus, a man like the gods. The two of them had fallen in together at Messene, in the house of Ortilochus. Odysseus had come there to collect a debt owed him by the whole people, for the Messenians had carried off three hundred sheep from Ithaca in their ships, shepherds and all. He was still a young man then; his father and the other elders had sent him on the long journey to get them back. Iphitus had come for his own loss — twelve brood mares, and the sturdy mule-foals running with them. Those mares would be the death of him in the end. For when he went to the house of Heracles, that stubborn-hearted son of Zeus who did such mighty deeds, Heracles killed him under his own roof — killed a guest, with no fear of the gods' eyes upon him and no shame for the table he had set before the man — and kept the mares for himself. It was while Iphitus was hunting for those mares that he met Odysseus, and gave him the great bow that mighty Eurytus had carried in his day and left to his son when he died. Odysseus gave him in return a sharp sword and a strong spear, the first tokens of a friendship between guest and host — though they never came to sit at each other's tables, for Heracles killed Iphitus first. That bow Odysseus never took to Troy. He had kept it at home, a keepsake of a friend he honored, and there it stayed while he sailed to war.

Penelope came to the storeroom and stepped up onto the oak threshold, which a carpenter had once planed smooth and true to the line, and fitted with doorposts and hung with shining doors. Quickly she slipped the strap from the door-handle, drove the key home, and shot back the bolts. The doors flew open with a groan like a bull bellowing in a meadow — so the great bolts gave way under the key. She climbed onto the high platform where the chests stood, holding sweet-smelling clothes, and reached up and lifted the bow down from its peg, still in the bright case that sheathed it. Then she sat with it across her knees and wept aloud, and drew her husband's bow out of the case. And when she had had her fill of tears and grieving, she went back to the hall, to the proud suitors, carrying the springing bow and the quiver with its many arrows of grief. Her maids came after her, bearing a chest packed with the iron and bronze her husband had won as prizes. When she reached the suitors, that lady among women drew her bright veil before her face and took her stand by a pillar that held up the roof, a faithful maid on either side of her. And she spoke out to the suitors:

"Hear me, you proud suitors. You have fallen on this house and eaten and drunk in it without end, all the long while its master has been gone, and the only excuse you can put forward is that you want to marry me. Well — here is the prize, and here it is set before you. I bring out the great bow of godlike Odysseus. Whoever among you strings it most easily, in his bare hands, and shoots an arrow clean through all twelve axes — him I will follow. I will leave this house that took me as a bride, this fine house, so full of the goods of living, that I think I will remember even in my dreams."

So she spoke, and told Eumaeus, the loyal swineherd, to set the bow and the gray iron before the suitors. And Eumaeus wept as he took them and laid them down. Close by, the herdsman wept too at the sight of his master's bow. But Antinous turned on them both and snapped: "You fool farmhands — no thought in your heads beyond the day in front of you. Why are you blubbering, you two, working up grief in your mistress, when her heart is heavy enough already with a husband lost? Sit and eat in silence, or take your crying outside and leave the bow here for us — the suitors — to settle. No light test, this, the stringing of such a bow. There is not a man in this whole company the equal of Odysseus. I saw him myself, I remember him, though I was only a child."

So he said. But all the while his own heart was sure he would string the bow and send the arrow through the iron — he, who was to be the first to taste an arrow from the hands of Odysseus, the man he was dishonoring in his own hall, and stirring up the rest to dishonor too.

Then Telemachus spoke out, in his clear young voice. "Well now — Zeus himself must have stripped me of my wits. Here is my own dear mother, sensible as she is, saying she will go off after another man and leave this house, and I stand here laughing, light-hearted, like a fool. Come then, suitors. The prize is set before you, a woman with no equal anywhere — not in all Achaean land, not in sacred Pylos, not in Argos, nor Mycenae, nor here in Ithaca, nor on the dark mainland. You know it as well as I do; what need is there for me to praise my own mother? Come, no more excuses, no more putting it off. String the bow, and let us see. I will try the bow myself, for that matter. If I can string it and shoot through the iron, then it will not break my heart to watch my mother leave this house with a stranger — not when I am left behind, man enough to take up the contests my father won."

With that he sprang up, threw off his crimson cloak, and lifted the sword from his shoulders. First he set the axes up, all twelve, digging one long trench for them and lining them straight to a measured cord, then stamping the earth firm around them. Everyone watching was amazed to see how neatly he set them in their row, though he had never once seen it done. Then he went and stood on the threshold and put the bow to the test. Three times he strained at it, hauling with all his strength, hungry to bend it; and three times he had to let it go, though in his heart he had not given up hope of stringing it and shooting through the iron. And the fourth time, pulling hard, he would have strung it — but Odysseus caught his eye and stopped him, for all his eagerness. So the boy spoke out among them again:

"It seems I am to be a weakling all my days, and good for nothing. Or else I am still too young, with no strength yet in my arms to fend off a man who picks a fight with me. Come then, you others, stronger than I am — try the bow, and let us see this contest through." And he set the bow down on the floor, leaning it against the smooth, close-fitted doors, propped the swift arrow against the bow's fine tip, and sat back down in the seat he had risen from.

Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said to them: "Stand up and come forward, all of you, one after another, from left to right — starting from the place where the wine is poured." So said Antinous, and his words pleased them. The first to rise was Leiodes, son of Oenops. He was their priest at the sacrifices, and always sat in the inmost corner, by the fine mixing-bowl; and he was the only one of them who hated their reckless ways, and was sickened by the rest. Now he was the first to take up the bow and the swift arrow. He went and stood on the threshold and tried the bow — and could not bend it. Before he could, his soft, unworked hands grew tired on the string. And he said to the suitors: "My friends, I cannot string it. Let another man take it. This bow is going to take the life and the spirit out of many a great man here — and better to die than to go on living and miss the very thing we have all gathered and waited so long for. There is a man among us even now, hoping in his heart, longing to marry Penelope. But once he has handled this bow and seen what it is, let him go court some other fine Achaean woman with his gifts, and let Penelope marry the man who brings the most, the one it is fated she will wed."

So he spoke, and set the bow down, leaning it against the smooth doors, the swift arrow propped against its fine tip, and sat back in his seat. But Antinous rounded on him: "Leiodes — what is this that has slipped past the wall of your teeth? Hard words, ugly words; it makes me angry to hear them. This bow is going to take the spirit out of great men, is it — just because you cannot string it? No, your mother never bore you to be a bowman. But there are others here who will string it soon enough."

Then he called out to Melanthius the goatherd: "Quick now, Melanthius — light a fire in the hall, set a big bench beside it and a fleece over the bench, and bring out a great cake of fat from the stores inside. We young men will warm the bow and grease it well, and then try it again, and bring the contest to its end." So Melanthius lit the tireless fire, drew up a bench and threw a fleece across it, and brought out a great cake of fat from within. The young men warmed the bow and tried it — and not one of them was strong enough; they fell far short of stringing it. But Antinous still held back, and so did Eurymachus, godlike Eurymachus, the two ringleaders, far the best of them all.

Now the swineherd and the cowherd went out of the house together, and behind them went godlike Odysseus himself. When they were past the gates and out in the courtyard, he spoke to them gently, drawing them close: "Cowherd — and you, swineherd — there is something I could say to you. Or should I keep it to myself? No, my heart tells me to speak. What sort of men would you be, if it came to standing by Odysseus — if some god brought him home, suddenly, out of nowhere? Would you fight for the suitors, or for Odysseus? Tell me, just as your heart and spirit move you."

And Philoetius, the loyal cowherd, answered: "Father Zeus — if only you would grant it, that the man come home, and some god guide him here. Then you would see what these hands of mine can do." And Eumaeus prayed the same to all the gods, that wise Odysseus might come home to his own. So when Odysseus knew their minds for certain, he said to them: "It is here. The man himself. It is I. After twenty years of suffering I have come home to the land of my fathers. And I see that of all my servants, you two alone have longed for my return — for I have heard no other praying that I might come back. So I will tell you the truth, the way it will be. If a god strikes down these proud suitors under my hand, I will find wives for you both, and give you each goods of your own and a house built close to mine, and from that day you will be to me brothers and companions of Telemachus. And here — let me show you a clear sign, a thing you cannot doubt, so you will know me in your hearts. This scar — the wound a boar gave me with its white tusk, the day I hunted on Mount Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus."

And with that he drew his rags aside from the great scar. The two of them looked, and knew it, and broke into weeping, and threw their arms around wise Odysseus, and kissed his head and his shoulders in welcome; and Odysseus kissed their heads and their hands. The sun would have gone down on their weeping, had he not checked them and said: "Enough crying now, or someone may come out from the hall and see us and carry word inside. Go back in, but one at a time, not together — I first, you after. And here is the sign between us. The suitors, every one of them, will refuse to let the bow and quiver be put into my hands. But you, good Eumaeus, carry the bow through the hall all the same and place it in my hands; and tell the women to bolt the close-fitting doors of their quarters. If any of them hears groaning, or the crash of men fighting through the house, she is not to come out — she is to stay where she is, in silence, at her work. And you, Philoetius — your task is the gate of the courtyard. Lock it, bar it fast, and tie it shut on the instant."
So speaking he went back into the well-built house and sat down again in the seat he had left. And his two servants came in behind him, one after the other.

By now the bow was in the hands of Eurymachus, who was turning it this way and that in the heat of the fire to warm it. Even so he could not string it, and his proud heart groaned within him. He heaved a deep sigh and said: "This is bitter — bitter for me, and for us all. I do not grieve so much for the marriage, hard as that is — there are other Achaean women enough, here in sea-girt Ithaca and in the other towns. What cuts me is this: that we should fall so far short of godlike Odysseus in strength that we cannot even string his bow. The shame of it will follow us, for men not yet born to hear of."

But Antinous answered him: "Not so, Eurymachus — and you know it yourself. Today is a feast day of Apollo, holy across the land. Who would be bending a bow today? Set it down quietly. The axes can stand where they are; no one is going to walk into the house of Odysseus and carry them off. Let the wine-steward come round and pour for the offerings, and we will let the bow rest. In the morning we will have Melanthius bring in goats, the best of all the herds, and burn the thigh-pieces to Apollo the great archer — and then we will try the bow again, and bring the contest to its end."

So said Antinous, and his words pleased them. The stewards poured water over their hands, and boys filled the bowls to the brim with wine and served it round to every man, the first drops poured out for the gods. And when they had made their offerings and drunk their fill, then crafty Odysseus, with a plan turning in him, spoke up: "Hear me, you suitors of the famous queen. I will say what the heart in me moves me to say — and most of all to Eurymachus and to Antinous, who spoke just now, and rightly. Lay the bow down for tonight; leave the matter to the gods, and in the morning the god will give the victory to whomever he chooses. But for now, hand me the polished bow, so that I may test my hands and my strength among you — to see whether the old power is still in these bent limbs, or whether the road and the rough years have worn it clean away."

At that they were all furious, afraid he might actually string the polished bow. And Antinous turned on him and said: "You miserable stranger — there is not a wit left in you. Be content that you are allowed to eat in peace among your betters, with a fair share like the rest of us and nothing held back, and to sit and hear us talk — when no other beggar or stranger is let near our conversation. It is the wine that has run away with you, the honeyed wine that ruins any man who gulps it down past measure. Wine was the ruin of the centaur Eurytion, in the house of great-hearted Peirithous, the day he came among the Lapiths. When the wine had blinded his mind, he ran wild and did foul things under Peirithous's roof. The heroes there sprang on him in their fury, dragged him to the porch, and sheared off his ears and his nose with the pitiless bronze; and off he went, raving, carrying his ruin in a darkened mind — and from that came the long war between men and centaurs. But he brought it down on himself, first of all, by drowning his wits in drink. So I tell you plainly: it will go hard with you if you string that bow. You will get no mercy from anyone in this hall. We will ship you straight off, in a black hull, to King Echetus, the mangler of all mankind, and there will be no saving you. Drink, then, and hold your peace, and pick no quarrels with men younger than yourself."

Then wise Penelope said to him: "Antinous, it is neither right nor decent to abuse a guest of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house. Do you really suppose that, if this stranger trusts his hands and his strength and manages to string the great bow of Odysseus, he will take me home and make me his wife? Not even the man himself nurses such a hope in his heart. So let none of you eat his dinner here with that weighing on him. It does not bear thinking of."

And Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered her: "Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope — none of us thinks this man will carry you off. That would be unthinkable. What we shrink from is the talk of men and women, the chance that some lesser Achaean will go about saying: 'See — far weaker men than the hero are courting his wife, and not one of them could string his polished bow. Yet some drifting beggar came to the house and strung it easily, and shot clean through the iron.' That is what they will say, and it will be our disgrace."

But wise Penelope answered: "Eurymachus, there can be no good name among men for those who devour and dishonor the house of a great man. Why should you turn this into a disgrace? The stranger here is a big, well-made man, and he says his father was a man of standing. So give him the polished bow, and let us see. I tell you this, and it will be done: if he strings it, and Apollo grants him the glory, I will clothe him in a fine cloak and tunic, and give him a sharp javelin to keep off dogs and rough men, and a two-edged sword, and sandals for his feet, and send him on wherever his heart desires to go."

Then Telemachus, with his good sense, said to her: "Mother, when it comes to the bow, no Achaean has more right than I to give it or refuse it to whom I please — not one of all who rule in rocky Ithaca, or in the islands toward horse-grazing Elis. None of them will force my hand against my will, not even if I choose to give this stranger the bow outright, to carry away with him. So go to your room and see to your own work, the loom and the distaff, and keep the maids at their tasks. The bow is the men's concern — and mine above all, for the rule of this house is mine." And she went back in, astonished, taking her son's strong words to heart. She climbed to her upper room with her women, and there she wept for Odysseus, her dear husband, until Athena cast sweet sleep over her eyelids.

Now the loyal swineherd had taken up the bow and was carrying it across, when the suitors all raised an uproar at him through the hall, and one of those arrogant young men cried out: "Where are you taking that bow, you wretched swineherd — out of your mind, are you? Soon the swift dogs you raised yourself will eat you out among your pigs, alone, with no man near, if Apollo and the other gods are kind to us." At that Eumaeus took fright at the shouting that broke out all around him, and set the bow down then and there. But Telemachus shouted across at him, hard, from the other side: "Bring the bow on, old friend — you will be sorry soon if you listen to all of them. Young as I am, I will chase you back to the fields with a hail of stones, for I am the stronger. If only I were as far above all these suitors here in the house, in strength of hand, I would soon send a few of them packing, sick and sorry, out of our home — for the mischief they mean."

So he spoke, and all the suitors laughed merrily at him, and let go of their hard temper toward Telemachus. The swineherd carried the bow on through the hall and put it in the hands of wise Odysseus. Then he called the nurse Eurycleia aside and said: "Eurycleia, Telemachus orders you to bolt the close-fitting doors of the women's quarters. If any of them hears groaning, or the crash of men fighting inside, she is not to come out — she is to stay where she is, in silence, at her work." So he spoke, and his words stayed unwinged on her lips: she went and bolted the doors of the fair women's hall.

And Philoetius slipped out without a word and locked the gates of the walled courtyard. There was a ship's cable of papyrus fiber lying under the colonnade; with it he lashed the gates fast, then came back in and sat down again in the seat he had left, his eyes on Odysseus. And Odysseus by now had the bow in his hands and was turning it every way, testing it up and down, to see whether the worms had eaten into the horn while its master was far away. And one suitor would glance at the man beside him and say: "This one is a real connoisseur of bows — a cunning hand. No doubt he has one like it stored at home, or means to make one — the way the rascally old beggar turns it over in his hands." And another of the arrogant young men would say: "May he have just as much luck in everything else as he is ever going to have in stringing that bow."

So the suitors talked. But Odysseus, the man of many turns, once he had lifted the great bow and looked it over end to end — easily, as a man skilled in the lyre and in song slips a new string onto its peg, looping the twisted sheep-gut fast at either end, so without effort Odysseus strung the great bow. Then he took it in his right hand and tried the string; and it sang sweetly under his touch, with a voice like a swallow's. A sharp grief ran through the suitors, and the color drained from every face. And Zeus thundered loud, sending forth his sign. Long-suffering, godlike Odysseus rejoiced that the son of crooked-counseling Kronos had sent him an omen.

He took up one swift arrow that lay bare on the table beside him — the rest were still inside the hollow quiver, though the Greeks would taste those soon enough. He laid it against the bridge of the bow, drew back the string and the arrow's notch, all the while sitting just as he was in his seat, and let fly, aiming true. He did not miss a single axe of all of them: through the first ring, and on through every one, the heavy bronze-tipped arrow drove its way clean out the other side. Then he turned to Telemachus and said: "Telemachus, the stranger sitting in your hall has not shamed you. I did not miss the mark, and I did not labor long to string the bow. My strength is still whole in me, whatever the suitors say to mock me. But now it is time to make the Greeks their supper, while the daylight lasts — and then the rest, the song and the lyre, that are the crown of any feast." And as he spoke he gave the sign with his brows. Telemachus, the dear son of godlike Odysseus, girt his sharp sword about him, closed his hand on his spear, and took his stand beside his father's seat, armed in the gleaming bronze.

Then Odysseus tore the rags from his body and leapt to the great stone threshold, the bow in his hand and the quiver full of arrows at his side. He poured the arrows out at his feet and said, "That contest is finished. Now I will see whether I can hit a mark no man here has hit before — and whether Apollo will grant it to me."

And with that he leveled a bitter arrow at Antinous. The man was just then reaching for a fine two-handled gold cup, lifting it to drink, with no thought of death in his head. Who, at a feast among so many, would imagine that one man, however hard, would stand alone against the whole crowd and bring him down? The arrow caught Antinous square in the throat, and the point drove clean through the soft of his neck. He pitched sideways. The cup dropped from his hand, and a thick jet of blood came spurting from his nostrils. His foot kicked out and overturned the table, and the bread and the roasted meat slid off and were fouled on the floor.

The suitors broke into an uproar when they saw the man go down. They sprang up from their seats in a panic, every one of them, and their eyes went searching along the walls — but there was no shield anywhere, no spear to lay a hand on. And they turned on Odysseus in their fury: "Stranger, you will pay for shooting men. You have killed the finest young man in Ithaca, and it is the last shot you will ever take. The vultures will have you."

So they raged, for they still believed he had hit Antinous by accident. The fools did not understand that the noose had already drawn tight around every neck in the room. Odysseus looked at them with a black stare and said: "Dogs. You told yourselves I would never come home from Troy. So you ate my house bare, you forced my serving-women to your beds, and you courted my wife while I was still alive — with no fear of the gods who hold the wide sky, and no fear of the anger of men to come. Now the day of reckoning has caught up with the whole pack of you."

The blood drained out of their faces as he spoke, and every man looked about him for a way to run. Only Eurymachus found his voice. "If you are truly Odysseus, then every word of it is just. The Greeks have done you great wrong, here in your halls and out on your lands. But the man who was the head and front of it all lies dead already — Antinous. He drove the whole thing. It was never the marriage he cared for, not really; he had another aim, one that Zeus has now denied him. He meant to kill your son and make himself the king of Ithaca. He has met the death he had coming. So spare the rest of us, your own people. We will make it all good. Every one of us will pay you back for what we ate and drank in your house — a fine worth twenty oxen apiece, in bronze and in gold, and we will keep on paying until your heart is satisfied. No one could blame you for your anger before that."

Odysseus answered with the same black stare. "Eurymachus, not if you handed me every last thing you own — all you have now and all you could ever scrape together — would I hold back my hands from killing until the suitors have paid in full for everything they did. Now you have a choice in front of you. Stand and fight, or run for your lives. But I do not think a single one of you will get away."

Their knees went weak where they stood. But Eurymachus spoke up again: "Friends, this man will not stop. He has the bow and the arrows, and he will plant himself on that threshold and shoot us down to the last man unless we stop him. So set your minds on fighting. Draw your swords. Hold the tables up against his arrows. Then rush him all together — drive him off the threshold and out the doorway, and break into the town and raise the alarm. He will not loose many more shots after that."

And as he spoke he drew his sharp bronze sword, two edges to it, and threw himself at Odysseus with a terrible cry. In the same instant Odysseus let fly. The arrow took Eurymachus in the chest beside the nipple and buried itself in his liver. The sword fell from his hand. He doubled over the table and crashed down across it, spilling the food and the two-handled cup onto the floor, and he beat his forehead against the ground in his agony and thrashed the chair with his heels — until the dark closed over his eyes.

Then Amphinomus drew and charged straight at Odysseus, to try and force him from the door. But Telemachus was the quicker. He drove his spear into the man's back from behind, between the shoulders, and the point came out through his chest. He went down hard and struck the floor full with his face. Telemachus sprang back at once, leaving the spear standing in the body — he was afraid that if he stooped to wrench it free, one of the Greeks might run in and cut him down or stab him while he was bent over. So he ran to his father's side and said quickly: "Father, let me bring you a shield and a pair of spears and a bronze helmet for your head. I will arm myself as well, and carry armor out to the swineherd and the herdsman. We are better off in armor."
"Run and fetch it," Odysseus said, "while I still have arrows to hold them off. Once they are gone they will rush me and force me from the door, and I will be one man alone."

Telemachus did as his father told him and went to the storeroom where the war-gear was kept. He took out four shields, eight spears, and four bronze helmets with horsehair crests, and carried them back at a run. He armed himself first, and then the herdsman and the swineherd put on the bronze and took their stand beside Odysseus. And Odysseus, as long as the arrows lasted, kept shooting the suitors down one after another, and they fell in heaps. When the last arrow was spent he stood the bow against the doorpost by the wall, slung a four-layered shield across his shoulders, set a strong helmet on his head — the horsehair crest nodding down over it — and took up two heavy bronze-tipped spears.

Now in the wall of the hall there was a small raised door, a vent, and at the end of the threshold a way out into a narrow passage, shut by a close-fitting door. Odysseus posted Philoetius to guard it, since only one man could come at it at a time. But Agelaus called out to the others: "Can no one get up to that vent and shout to the town what is happening here? One alarm and help would come, and we would soon finish this man and his shooting."

"That cannot be done, Agelaus," said Melanthius the goatherd. "The mouth of the narrow passage is too close to the courtyard gate — one good man there could hold off an army. But I know what I can do. I will bring you arms from the storeroom. That is surely where Odysseus and his son have hidden them."

And with that the goatherd Melanthius slipped up through the back passages of the house to the storeroom. There he chose twelve shields, twelve helmets, and twelve spears, and carried them back as fast as he could and handed them around to the suitors. The heart in Odysseus sank when he saw the men buckling on the armor and shaking their long spears. He understood at once how much the danger had grown, and he said to Telemachus, "One of the women in the house is helping them against us — or else it is Melanthius."

"The fault is mine, father, mine alone," Telemachus answered. "I left the storeroom door standing open, and they kept a sharper watch than I did. Go, Eumaeus, shut it fast — and find out whether it is one of the women doing this, or Melanthius son of Dolius, which is what I think."

While they were speaking, Melanthius went up to the storeroom a second time, to fetch more armor. But the swineherd saw him and said to Odysseus at his side: "Odysseus, son of Laertes, there he goes — that scoundrel Melanthius, the one we suspected, off to the storeroom again. Tell me plainly: if I get the better of him, shall I kill him, or shall I bring him here to you, to pay for all the wrongs he has done in your house?"

"Telemachus and I will hold the suitors here, however hard they press," Odysseus said. "You two go and bind his hands and his feet behind his back, throw him into the storeroom, and make the door fast. Then run a rope around his body and haul him up a tall pillar to the rafters, and leave him there alive — to suffer a long time before he dies."

They went and did exactly as he said. They reached the storeroom unheard, for Melanthius was deep inside it rummaging for arms, and they took their stand on either side of the door and waited. Out he came at last, a helmet in one hand and in the other an old shield, dry-rotted and gone soft, that Laertes had carried in his young days and laid aside long ago, the straps perished. The two of them seized him, dragged him back inside by the hair, and threw him down on the floor. They wrenched his hands and feet up behind his back and lashed them there, hard and cruel, as Odysseus had ordered, and they ran a rope about him and hauled him up the high pillar to the rafters. And the swineherd Eumaeus stood over him and jeered: "Now you can keep watch through the whole night, Melanthius, stretched on the soft bed you have earned. You will not miss the dawn coming up from the streams of Ocean — your hour for driving in the goats to feast the suitors."

So they left him there, racked in his bonds. They put their own armor back on, shut the storeroom door, and went back to take their stand beside Odysseus — the four of them now in the hall, full of fight and fury. And the suitors against them were still many, and still dangerous. Then Athena came, in the shape and voice of Mentor. Odysseus was glad to see her and called out, "Mentor, stand by me. Remember your old companion, and all the good I did you. We are the same age, you and I." But all the while he knew well enough it was Athena, marshaler of armies.

From across the hall the suitors raised an outcry when they saw her, and Agelaus shouted his threats: "Mentor, do not let Odysseus talk you into siding with him against us. This is how it will go. When we have killed those two, father and son, we will kill you with them. You will pay for what you mean to do with your own head. And once you are dead we will take everything you have, indoors and out, and throw it in with the goods of Odysseus. We will not let your sons live on in your house, nor your daughters, nor will your wife walk the streets of Ithaca again."

That only made Athena angrier, and she rounded on Odysseus with hard words — to test him: "Odysseus, where is the strength and the daring that was in you for nine long years at Troy, fighting over white-armed Helen? You killed your men by the score in those days, and it was your scheme that brought down the wide streets of Priam's city. How is it that here, on your own ground, with your own house and your own goods to fight for, you flinch at standing up to these suitors? Come here beside me, friend, and watch. You will see how Mentor son of Alcimus repays a kindness in the thick of his enemies."

But she would not yet hand him the victory outright. She wanted to go on proving the courage and the strength of Odysseus and his brave son. So she flew up to a crossbeam in the smoke-blackened roof and perched there, looking down — in the likeness of a swallow.

Now the suitors were led by Agelaus son of Damastor, and by Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander son of Polyctor, and Polybus. These were the best of the men still on their feet and fighting for their lives; the rest had already gone down under the arrows. Agelaus called to them: "Friends, the man will have to give over soon. Mentor has flown off after all his big talk and left them standing there alone at the door. So do not throw all at once. Let six of you cast first, and pray that Zeus lets you bring Odysseus down. Once he falls, the others are nothing to fear."

So they threw, the six of them, hard and eager. But Athena turned every spear aside. One struck the doorpost of the strong-built hall, one the close-fitting door, and another's heavy bronze head buried itself in the wall. When the four had let the volley go by, Odysseus said to his men: "Friends — now it is our turn. Throw into the middle of them, before they add our deaths to all the rest of the harm they have done."

They took aim straight ahead and threw. Odysseus killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus killed Euryades, the swineherd killed Elatus, and the herdsman Philoetius killed Pisander. The four of them bit the floor together, and as the rest fell back into a corner of the hall the four attackers rushed in and pulled their spears free from the bodies of the dead.

Then the suitors threw again, hard and eager — and again Athena turned most of it aside. One spear struck a pillar of the hall, one the close door, another's bronze point lodged in the wall. Still, Amphimedon grazed Telemachus across the wrist, just skimming the skin, and Ctesippus reached over the swineherd's shield to nick his shoulder, though the spear flew on and dropped to the floor. And the four threw back into the press of suitors. Odysseus struck Eurydamas, Telemachus struck Amphimedon, the swineherd struck Polybus. Then the herdsman Philoetius caught Ctesippus full in the chest, and called out over him: "Foul-mouthed son of Polytherses — no more of your big crude talk now. Leave the last word to the gods. They are far stronger than men. Take that as my gift in return for the ox-hoof you threw at Odysseus when he was begging through his own house."

So spoke the herdsman of the cattle. And Odysseus closed in and ran the son of Damastor through with his spear, and Telemachus drove his spear into the belly of Leocritus son of Evenor, so that it came out the other side and the man dropped face-down on the floor. Then Athena, from her place on the rafter, lifted high the aegis that destroys men — and the hearts of the suitors broke. They scattered down the hall like a herd of cattle that the darting gadfly has maddened in the long warm days of spring. And as hawks with hooked beaks and crooked talons come stooping down out of the hills on the smaller birds, who flee low across the plain with no cover above them and no fight in them, and the hawks fall on them and kill, and there is no help and no escape — so the four fell on the suitors and cut them down through the hall, this way and that. A hideous groaning rose as the skulls were struck in, and the whole floor ran with blood.

Then Leiodes ran and caught Odysseus by the knees, pleading: "Odysseus, I beg you, take pity on me. I never did wrong to any of the women in your house, in word or in deed, and I tried to hold the others back from it. They would not listen. So they have come to this end for their own wickedness. But I was only their priest at the offerings, and I did nothing — and now I am to lie among them and die, with no thanks for any good I did."

Odysseus looked down at him grimly. "If you were truly their priest at the offerings, then many a time you must have prayed in this house that my homecoming would never come, and that my wife would be yours and bear your children. For that you will not escape death." And with that he caught up a sword from the floor where Agelaus had let it fall in his dying, and struck Leiodes across the back of the neck. The head was still speaking when it rolled in the dust.

But Phemius the bard, son of Terpes, who had been made to sing to the suitors against his will, was still trying to save his life. He stood near the vent with his clear-toned lyre in his hands, torn between two thoughts — whether to slip out of the hall and crouch at the great altar of Zeus in the courtyard, where Laertes and Odysseus had burned the thighs of many oxen, or to go straight to Odysseus and clasp his knees. In the end he judged it better to clasp the knees of Odysseus. So he laid the lyre down on the floor between the mixing-bowl and the silver-studded chair, and he ran to Odysseus, took hold of his knees, and begged: "Odysseus, I beg you, have pity on me, spare me. You will grieve for it afterward if you kill a singer — one who sings for gods and men alike. I am self-taught; a god has planted every kind of song in me, and I could sing for you as for a god. Do not be in such a hurry to take off my head. Your own son Telemachus will tell you the truth of it — that I never came to your house willingly, never wanted to sing to the suitors after their feasts. They were too many and too strong. They forced me."

Telemachus heard him, and stepped quickly to his father's side. "Hold — this man is innocent. Do him no harm. And let us spare Medon the herald too, who looked after me all through my boyhood — unless Philoetius or Eumaeus has already killed him, or he has crossed your path while you were storming through the hall."

Medon caught the words. He was crouched under a chair where he had hidden, wrapped in a fresh-flayed ox-hide, and now he threw off the hide, sprang out, and clasped Telemachus by the knees. "Here I am, my dear lord — hold your hand, and tell your father, before he kills me in his rage at the suitors for eating his house bare and slighting you the way they did."

Odysseus smiled at him and said, "Take heart. My son has saved you, and brought you out alive — so that you may know in your own bones, and tell other men, how much better a good deed fares in the end than an evil one. Now go out of the hall and sit in the courtyard, clear of the killing, the two of you, the bard and the herald, while I finish my work here inside."

The pair went out into the courtyard as fast as they could and sat down by the great altar of Zeus, glancing about them, still half-expecting death. And Odysseus searched the whole hall, looking to see whether any man was left alive and hiding. But he found them all fallen in the blood and the dust, the whole crowd of them — like fish that the fishermen have dragged up out of the gray sea in the meshes of their net and poured out on the curve of the shore, where they lie heaped on the sand, gasping for the saltwater, while the burning sun takes the life out of them. So the suitors lay heaped, one against another.

Then Odysseus said to Telemachus, "Go and call the nurse Eurycleia. There is something I must tell her." Telemachus went and knocked at the door of the women's quarters and called, "Up, old mother, come out. You who keep watch over all the serving-women of the house — my father wants you. He has something to say."

Eurycleia did not stop to answer. She opened the doors of the hall and came, with Telemachus leading the way. And she found Odysseus among the bodies of the slain, spattered with blood and gore — like a lion that has just fed on an ox of the field, his chest and his jaws on both sides smeared red, a thing terrible to look on. So was Odysseus fouled, from his feet to his head and his hands. When she saw the dead, and all that blood, she opened her mouth to cry aloud in triumph, for she saw the greatness of what had been done. But Odysseus stopped her, held her back from it, and said: "Keep your joy in your heart, old woman. Do not cry out. It is no holy thing to gloat over slain men. The doom of the gods and their own foul deeds brought these men down. They honored no one who came among them, low or high. So they have come to a hard end for their own wickedness. Now tell me which of the women in the house have shamed themselves, and which are guiltless."

"I will tell you the truth, my child," the nurse answered. "There are fifty serving-women in the house, women we trained in their work — to card the wool and carry the load of the household. Of those, twelve in all have gone the way of shamelessness, with no respect for me, or even for Penelope. Telemachus they obeyed, for he is only lately grown and his mother never let him give orders to the women. But let me go up now and tell your wife everything. Some god has laid sleep on her."
"Do not wake her yet," said Odysseus. "First send me the women who have disgraced themselves."

So Eurycleia went off through the hall to call the women and bring them to him. And Odysseus called Telemachus and the herdsman and the swineherd to him and said: "Begin carrying out the dead, and make the women help you. Then sponge down the fine chairs and the tables with water. And when you have set the whole hall in order, take the women out, between the round storehouse and the wall of the courtyard, and put them to the sword — every one — until you have driven the life out of them, and the memory of the love they made in secret with the suitors."

The women came down together, in a huddle, weeping bitterly. First they carried the dead out and set them down under the gateway, propped against one another, while Odysseus stood over them and drove them at the work, and they bore the bodies out under his eye. Then they scoured the tables and the chairs with water and sponges, while Telemachus and the two herdsmen scraped the floor clean of the caked blood and the filth, and the women carried it all out of doors. When the whole hall was clean and in order, they led the women out and hemmed them into the narrow ground between the round storehouse and the courtyard wall, with no way through. And Telemachus said, "I will not give these women a clean death — not after the shame they heaped on my head and my mother's, lying with the suitors."

And with that he made a ship's cable fast to a great pillar and looped it high around the round storehouse, drawn taut, so that none of them could reach the ground with her feet. As thrushes with their long wings, or doves, come flying into a snare set across a thicket, and find a cruel bed where they had thought to roost — so the women hung in a row, the nooses about their necks, to die the most pitiful death. Their feet kicked out a little while. It did not last long.

Then they brought Melanthius out through the hall into the courtyard. There they cut off his nose and his ears with the pitiless bronze, and tore out his manhood to throw raw to the dogs, and in their fury hacked off his hands and his feet.

When that was done they washed their own hands and feet and went back into the house to Odysseus, for the work was finished. And Odysseus said to the dear nurse Eurycleia, "Bring sulfur, old woman — it cleanses every pollution — and bring me fire, so that I may purify the hall. And go tell Penelope to come down, with her women, and have all the serving-women of the house come too."
"All that you say is true, my child," Eurycleia answered. "But let me first bring you a shirt and a cloak to put on. It is not right that you should stand in your own hall in these rags any longer."

"Light me the fire first," said Odysseus. So she brought the fire and the sulfur, and Odysseus purified the whole hall, and the house, and the courtyard. Then the old woman went through the house to call the loyal women and tell them all that had happened, and they came out of their quarters with torches in their hands and crowded around Odysseus, welcoming him home — taking his hands, kissing his head and his shoulders. And a sweet longing to weep came over him, for in his heart he knew every one of them.

Eurycleia went up the stairs laughing, to tell her mistress that her dear husband was home at last. Her old knees turned young again, and her feet were light with joy. She bent over Penelope's head and spoke: "Wake up, dear child. Wake and see with your own eyes the thing you have longed for all these years. Odysseus is home. He has come at last, and he has killed the suitors who ate up the house and tormented your son."

"Dear nurse," Penelope answered, "the gods have driven you out of your mind. They can make a wise woman foolish and lift a foolish one into sense, and they have unsettled you, who were always so steady. Why do you mock me, with grief enough on me already, waking me out of the sweetest sleep I have known since the day my husband sailed for that city I cannot bring myself to name? Go back down to the women's room. If any other woman had roused me with such nonsense, I would have sent her off with a scolding she would remember. Your age alone protects you."

"I am not mocking you, dear child," said Eurycleia. "It is the truth. Odysseus is home. He was the stranger they all abused in the hall. Telemachus knew it all along, but he kept his father's secret, so that the two of them could take their revenge on those proud men."

At that Penelope sprang up from the bed and threw her arms around the old woman, weeping for joy. "Then tell me, dear nurse," she said, "if he has truly come, how did one man bring down the whole shameless crowd of them? There were always so many."

"I did not see it," Eurycleia answered. "I do not know. I only heard the groaning of men being killed. We sat huddled in a corner of the women's room with the doors shut fast, until your son came to fetch me, sent by his father. And there I found Odysseus standing among the dead, and they lay all around him on the hard ground, one upon another. It would have warmed your heart to see him, splashed with blood and filth, like a lion over its kill. Now the bodies are heaped together by the courtyard gate, and he has lit a great fire to purify the house with sulphur. He sent me to bring you. Come, so that the two of you may be glad together at last. Your heart's long wish has come true: your husband is home, and he has found you and your son alive, and has paid the suitors back in his own halls for all the wrong they did."

"Dear nurse, do not be so sure of your joy yet," said Penelope. "You know how everyone in this house would welcome Odysseus home — I most of all, and the son the two of us share. But what you tell me cannot be true. It is some god who has killed the suitors, angry at their pride and their cruelty; for they respected no one in the world, high or low, who came near them, and their wickedness has brought them down at last. As for Odysseus, he is dead, far from the land of the Greeks. He will never come home again."

"My child, what a thing to say," the nurse answered. "Your husband is here, at his own hearth this very moment, and still you swear he will never come. But here is one more proof. When I washed him, I felt the scar the wild boar gave him long ago. I wanted to tell you, but he clapped his hand over my mouth — that was his cunning — and would not let me. Come down with me. And I will stake my own life on it: if I have deceived you, kill me by the cruelest death you can think of."
"Dear nurse, however wise you are, you cannot hope to read the purposes of the gods," Penelope said. "Still, let us go down to my son, so that I may see the suitors dead and the man who killed them."

So she came down from her room, and all the way her heart was divided — whether to keep her distance and question her husband, or go straight to him, take his hands, and kiss him. But when she had crossed the stone floor of the hall, she sat down across from Odysseus, in the firelight, against the far wall. He sat by one of the great pillars, his eyes on the ground, waiting to see what his wife would say to him now that she saw him with her own eyes. For a long while she sat in silence, lost in wonder. One moment she looked him full in the face and seemed to know him; the next, the filthy rags threw her off, and she could not. At last Telemachus could bear it no longer, and turned on her.

"Mother — though you are too hard for me to call you that — why do you keep away from my father like this? Why not sit beside him and speak to him, ask him your questions? No other woman alive would hold off from her husband, come home at last after twenty years and everything he has suffered. But your heart was always colder than stone."

"My son," Penelope answered, "I am so stunned that I have no words — I cannot ask him anything, I cannot even meet his eyes. But if this truly is Odysseus, home again, the two of us will know each other well enough soon. There are signs between us that no one else knows, signs hidden from everyone in the world."

Odysseus smiled at that, and said to his son: "Telemachus, let your mother test me however she likes. She will be sure of me soon enough. For now she turns away, because I am caked in dirt and dressed in rags, and she cannot believe it is me. But let us think what to do next. When a man has killed even one other man — one who leaves few friends behind to avenge him — he still has to flee his country and abandon his own people. And we have struck down the flower of Ithaca, the props of the whole town. Think on that."

"Look to it yourself, father," said Telemachus. "They say there is no mind in the world like yours, that no other man can match you. We will follow you with all our hearts, and we will not fail you, as long as the strength is in us."

"Then here is what seems best to me," Odysseus said. "Wash now, and put on clean shirts, and have the women dress as well. Let Phemius take up his lyre and lead off a dance, so that anyone passing in the street, or any neighbor who hears, will think there is a wedding in the house. Word of the suitors' deaths must not run through the town before we have slipped away to my own land out in the country. There we will see what plan the gods give us."

They did just as he said. The men washed and put on their shirts; the women made ready; Phemius took up his lyre and woke in them all a hunger for song and stately dancing. The great house rang with the beat of dancing feet, and out in the street people said to one another, "So the queen has married at last. The faithless woman — she had not the heart to keep her husband's house safe until he came home." That was their talk; they had no idea what had truly happened inside.

Meanwhile the housekeeper Eurynome bathed Odysseus and rubbed him with oil and dressed him in a fine cloak and shirt. And Athena poured grace and beauty over him: she made him taller to look on, and stronger, and set the hair thick and curling on his head, like blossoms of hyacinth. As a craftsman skilled by Hephaestus and Athena in every art lays gold over silver and makes a thing of beauty, so the goddess gilded his head and shoulders with grace. He came from the bath looking like one of the deathless gods, and went and sat down again across from his wife, in the seat he had left. "You strange woman," he said. "The gods have given you a harder heart than they gave any other woman alive. No other wife could keep herself away from her husband, come home at last after twenty years and everything he has suffered. Nurse — make up a bed for me. I will sleep alone. Her heart is iron."

"You strange man," Penelope answered. "I am not too proud, and I do not think too little of you. But I know very well what you were like the day you sailed from Ithaca. — Eurycleia, make up the strong bed for him, outside the bedchamber my husband built with his own hands. Carry the bed out here, and pile it with fleeces and good blankets and warm coverlets."

She said it to test him, and Odysseus flared up at his faithful wife. "Woman," he said, "that word cuts me. Who has moved my bed? It would be hard for the best craftsman alive — unless a god came down and shifted it with his own hand. No living man, however young and strong, could pry that bed from its place. There is a secret built into it, a marvel I made myself, and no one else. A long-leaved olive tree was growing inside the courtyard, in full life, thick as a pillar. I built my bedchamber around that tree, and walled it in with close-set stone, and roofed it over, and hung strong doors that shut tight. Then I cut away the leafy crown of the olive, and squared the trunk up from the root, and smoothed it true with the adze, and drew the line down it, and made of it the standing bedpost. Around that post I built the rest of the bed, and inlaid it with gold and silver and ivory, and stretched across it oxhide thongs dyed glowing red. That is my secret. And what I do not know, woman, is whether my bed still stands where it stood — or whether some man has cut through the olive's root and carried it off."

At that — the sure sign she alone could know — Penelope's knees went loose, and her heart with them. She knew him now, past all doubt. She burst into tears and ran straight to him, threw her arms around his neck, and kissed his head. "Do not be angry with me, Odysseus," she wept. "In all things you were the wisest of men. The gods gave us sorrow; they grudged us the years of growing old side by side. Do not hold it against me now, that I did not run to you the moment I saw you. My heart was cold with dread — that some man might come and trick me with a smooth story. There are so many cruel and scheming men in the world. But now you have spoken the secret of our bed, the sign no living soul has seen but you and I, and the one maid my father gave me when I came here, who keeps the door of our room — now, hard as I was to win over, I doubt you no longer."

Her words broke something open in him, and he wept, holding his dear and faithful wife. As welcome as land is to swimmers, when Poseidon has smashed their ship far out in the heaving sea, and only a few struggle in out of the grey water to the shore, their bodies crusted with salt, and they climb out glad to be alive and free of death — so welcome to her was the sight of her husband, and she would not loosen her white arms from his neck. And rosy-fingered Dawn would have risen on their weeping, had Athena not thought of one more thing. She held the long night back at the edge of the world, and kept golden Dawn waiting beside the streams of Ocean, and would not let her yoke the swift horses, Lampus and Phaethon, that carry the morning to mankind.

At last Odysseus said, "My wife, we have not yet come to the end of all our trials. There is still a long, hard labor left for me, and I must see it through. So the ghost of Tiresias told me, the day I went down into the house of Hades to ask the way home for myself and my men. But come now, let us go to bed, and take the sweet gift of sleep together."

"Your bed is ready whenever you wish it," Penelope said, "now that the gods have brought you home to your own house and your own land. But since some god has put this in your mind, tell me about the labor still to come. I will have to learn of it sooner or later — better to hear it now."

"You strange woman, why press me to tell you?" Odysseus answered. "Still, I will not hide it. Though it will give you no joy — it gives me none. Tiresias told me to take a well-cut oar and carry it on my shoulder, on and on, until I come to men who know nothing of the sea, who eat their food unsalted, who have never seen ships with their painted cheeks, or the oars that are the wings of a ship. And he gave me a sign I could not miss: when another traveler, meeting me on the road, says I have a winnowing-fan on my shoulder, then I am to plant my oar in the ground and make fine offerings to lord Poseidon — a ram, a bull, and a boar that mounts the sows — and then go home and offer sacred hecatombs to all the deathless gods who hold the wide heaven, each in his turn. And death, he said, will come to me far from the sea — a gentle death that will take me when I am worn out in a sleek old age, with my people prospering around me. All this, he said, would surely come to pass."
"If the gods mean to grant you a kinder old age," said Penelope, "then there is hope you will find some rest from your troubles at the last."

So the two of them talked. Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse made up the bed with soft coverlets by torchlight. When it was ready, the old nurse went off to her rest, and Eurynome lit them to their room and left them. And gladly they came together again to the rites of the bed they had known of old. As for Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd, they ended the dancing, and the women left off too, and they lay down to sleep through the shadowed halls.

When Odysseus and Penelope had taken their fill of love, they turned to the joy of talking, each telling the other everything. She told all she had borne in the house, watching that crowd of ruinous men slaughter her cattle and her sheep and drain cask after cask of wine, all on her account. And Odysseus told her all the grief he had dealt others and all he had suffered himself, every hardship of it, and she listened with delight and would not let sleep touch her eyes until he had told it to the end.

He began with the Cicones, and how from there he came to the land of the Lotus-eaters; all that he did to the Cyclops, and how he made him pay for the brave companions he had eaten without mercy; how he came to Aeolus, who took him in kindly and sped him on, though it was not yet his fate to reach home, for a storm caught him up and carried him back out over the fish-filled sea, groaning; how he came to Telepylus of the Laestrygonians, who destroyed his ships and his men, every one but himself; the cunning of Circe and all her arts; how he sailed down to the dank house of Hades to question the ghost of Tiresias of Thebes, and saw there all his old companions, and the mother who bore him and raised him; how he heard the Sirens singing on and on, and came to the Wandering Rocks, and dread Charybdis, and Scylla, whom no man ever passed unharmed; how his crew killed the cattle of the Sun, and Zeus struck the swift ship with a smoking thunderbolt, so that all his good men died together and he alone lived on; how he reached the island of Ogygia and the nymph Calypso, who kept him in her hollow cave and longed to make him her husband, and would have made him deathless and ageless forever, but never could win his heart; and how at last, after all his suffering, he came to the Phaeacians, who honored him like a god and sent him home in their ship with gifts of bronze and gold and clothing in plenty. This was the last thing he told her before a sweet sleep came over him and loosed the cares from his heart.

And Athena thought of one more thing. When she judged that Odysseus had had his fill of his wife and of sleep, she roused golden Dawn from the streams of Ocean to bring her light to mankind. Odysseus rose from the soft bed and said to Penelope, "My wife, we have both had our long share of trials — you here, weeping for my return, and I held back from home, year after year, aching to reach it. Now that we are together again at last, take care of all the goods that are left in the house. As for the flocks the suitors have wasted, I will take many myself in raids, and the Greeks shall make good the rest, until my pens are full again. But now I am going out to the wooded farm, to see my father, who has grieved so long for me. And to you, wise as you are, I give one word: at sunrise the news will spread that I have killed the suitors. So go up to your room with your women, and sit there, and see no one, and ask nothing."

With that he buckled on his armor. He woke Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd and had them all take up their weapons, and they armed. Then they opened the gates and went out, Odysseus leading. It was full daylight by now, but Athena wrapped them in darkness and led them quickly out of the town.

Meanwhile Hermes of Cyllene called up the ghosts of the suitors. In his hand he held the golden wand with which he closes the eyes of the living in sleep, or opens them again, whichever he pleases; with this he stirred the ghosts and led them off, and they followed him, squeaking. As bats squeak and flutter in the depths of some great cave when one of them drops from the cluster where they cling to the rock and to each other, so the ghosts went squeaking after him, while Hermes the deliverer led them down the dank ways of the dark. They passed the streams of Ocean and the White Rock, they passed the gates of the Sun and the country of dreams, and came at last to the meadow of asphodel, where the souls live on as phantoms of the dead.

There they found the ghost of Achilles son of Peleus, and with him Patroclus, and Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the best and the handsomest of all the Greeks after the matchless son of Peleus himself. These were gathered about Achilles when the ghost of Agamemnon came up to them, heavy with grief, and around him crowded the ghosts of all the men who had died with him in the house of Aegisthus. The ghost of Achilles spoke to him first.

"Son of Atreus," he said, "we always thought that Zeus loved you above all other heroes, first to last — you who were lord over so many brave men in the land of Troy, where we Greeks suffered together. And yet the hand of death, that no man living escapes, came down on you too soon. Better for you if you had fallen at Troy, at the height of your glory. The Greeks would have raised a great mound over your ashes, and your son would have inherited your name. Instead it was your fate to die the most pitiable death of all."

"Fortunate son of Peleus," answered the ghost of Agamemnon, "to have died at Troy, far from Argos, with the bravest of the Trojans and the bravest of the Greeks falling around you, fighting over your body. There you lay in the swirling dust, great and greatly fallen, your horsemanship forgotten. We fought for you the whole day long, and we would never have stopped if Zeus had not broken it off with a storm. Then we carried you out of the battle to the ships and laid you on a bier, and washed your fair body with warm water and anointed it with oil, and the Greeks wept around you and cut their hair for grief. Your mother heard, and came up out of the sea with her immortal nymphs, and a strange wailing rose across the water, so that the whole army shook with fear. They would have bolted for the ships if wise old Nestor had not held them — he whose counsel was always best. 'Hold, men of Argos,' he cried. 'Do not run, sons of the Greeks. This is his mother, come up from the sea with her immortal nymphs to look on the face of her dead son.' At his word their fear let go of them.

"The daughters of the old man of the sea stood about you, weeping, and wrapped you in clothing fit for the gods. The nine Muses came too, and lifted their lovely voices in the dirge, answering one to another, and there was not a man among the Greeks but wept, so deeply that singing pierced the heart. Seventeen days and seventeen nights we mourned you, mortals and immortals together, and on the eighteenth we gave you to the fire. We killed many a fat sheep and many a shambling ox around your pyre. You burned in the clothing of the gods, in deep myrrh and sweet honey, while the Greek heroes paraded in their armor around the blaze, both on foot and in their chariots, and a great noise of them went up. When the god's fire had done its work, we gathered your white bones at dawn, Achilles, and laid them in unmixed wine and oil. Your mother gave us a golden jar to hold them — the gift of Dionysus, she said, and the work of Hephaestus' own hands — and in it we mingled your white bones with those of Patroclus who had died before you, and set apart, close beside them, the bones of Antilochus, whom you had loved above all your living companions once Patroclus was gone.

"Over you the army of the Greeks heaped up a great and shining mound, on a headland thrust out over the wide Hellespont, so that it could be seen far out at sea by men now living and by those still to be born. And your mother begged splendid prizes from the gods and set them up in the middle of the games, for the best of the Greeks to contend over.
